title: Can Netanyahu survive another storm? Israel votes after October 7, Gaza and Iran wars
text: A wartime leader on trial at the ballot box: Netanyahu fights to stay in power Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a crucial test of his political future in Tuesday's election, with voters weighing his leadership following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks, successive wars in Gaza and with Iran, and Israel's growing international isolation, news agency Reuters reported. Despite the mounting challenges, Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, remains a formidable political survivor. With nationalist politics firmly entrenched and the country's fragmented electoral system making coalition-building decisive, he could still emerge best placed to form the next government. Opinion polls point to a close contest between Netanyahu's Likud party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk who has attracted support from both right-wing and centrist voters. Netanyahu has made his wartime leadership and close relationship with US President Donald Trump central to his campaign. Trump has endorsed the Israeli leader, with the two countries joining forces in the war against Iran. Watch Revealed: Iran's Anti-US-Israel Masterplan; Pezeshkian Pushes For Powerful 'Islamic NATO' Bloc On Sunday, Netanyahu said Trump was prepared to act again to âfinallyâ remove the Iranian threat, but only if he remained in power. Eisenkot, however, accused the prime minister of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats," adding that Trump would work "in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people." Netanyahu may once again need the support of far-right leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to secure a governing majority. Both have faced sanctions from some Western countries over allegations of inciting violence against Palestinians. Meanwhile, Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party has gained ground in opinion polls. Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear route to power. If neither manages to assemble a coalition in Israel's 120-member parliament, Netanyahu could remain in office as caretaker prime minister until another election is held next year. Polling stations are scheduled to remain open from 7 am to 10 pm (0500 to 2000 GMT). The October 7 reckoning The election comes after one of the most turbulent periods in Israel's history since its establishment in 1948. The trauma of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks, Israel's subsequent military offensive in Gaza and deep divisions over Netanyahu's right-wing government have dominated the country's political landscape. For many of Netanyahu's opponents, the vote is also a referendum on accountability for the security failures that preceded October 7, Israel's deadliest day. Mali Hajaj, an education ministry employee who supports Eisenkot, said a national inquiry into the attacks was essential for the country to begin healing. "the most important thing is the establishment of a national inquiry because that's where our healing will come from," she said. Lisa Tortor, another voter opposed to Netanyahu, said she hoped he would leave office and a new government would begin repairing the damage to Israel's international standing and the wider Jewish community. She said she hoped Netanyahu would go and "they can form a new government and do some of the repairing of the damage that Bibi has done for Jews all over the world and for Israel, and Israel's image." Not all voters, however, believe the prime minister should be held responsible for the October 7 attacks. Nof Gabay, an 18-year-old Likud supporter, dismissed that criticism and backed Netanyahu's leadership during the war. Gabay called him "the right man for the state of Israel" and said, "Netanyahu managed the war in the best possible way." Netanyahu's wartime record under scrutiny The election campaign has unfolded against the backdrop of years of military conflict that have reshaped Israel's security and diplomatic position. After the October 7 attacks, in which Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage, Israel launched a military offensive that devastated much of Gaza. Gaza health authorities say Israeli attacks have killed 74,000 people. Israel also dealt major blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and exchanged strikes with Iran before launching a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025. The conflict escalated further this year with a joint US-Israeli war against Iran. Netanyahu has presented his handling of these conflicts as evidence of his leadership and ability to confront Israel's security threats. His alliance with Trump has also become a key part of his pitch to voters, particularly as tensions with Iran remain central to the campaign. Eisenkot, meanwhile, has argued that Israel's next government must ensure Iran does not acquire a military nuclear capability. He has said this could be achieved through military action or an "arrangement", including a diplomatic solution backed by the United States. The competing positions underline how security policy remains central to the election, even as voters grapple with questions about accountability, the future of the Gaza conflict and Israel's standing abroad. Coalition arithmetic could decide the outcome Even if Eisenkot's alliance makes gains, forming a government could prove difficult. Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, his camp opposes the two-state solution that has underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians. Eisenkot has, however, criticised violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Such violence has surged since 2023, straining Israel's ties with Western countries. He has also opposed Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich. Meanwhile, dissatisfaction with Netanyahu has prompted some voters in traditional Likud strongholds to campaign against him. Others have turned away from the prime minister as he continues to fight corruption charges in a long-running criminal trial, which he denies. The participation of Israel's Arab minority could also influence the outcome. Arab citizens of Israel, who are Palestinian by heritage, could help shift the balance in a closely contested election if turnout is high. Although Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, analysts believe they could still support a minority government led by him. Such an arrangement could offer a route to removing Netanyahu from office without formally joining his coalition. The country's fragmented political system means that winning the most votes may not be enough. The ability to secure support from smaller parties and assemble a parliamentary majority could ultimately determine who governs Israel. Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute expects the result to be closely fought, with neither side securing a decisive mandate. title: Kamala Harris slams Biden & Trump over Gaza war, says US should have acted âsooner, more forcefullyâ
text: Former US vice president Kamala Harris. Former US vice president Kamala Harris has criticised both the Joe Biden and Donald Trump administrations for failing to use Washingtonâs influence to control Israelâs military campaign in Gaza, saying the US should have acted âsooner and more forcefullyâ. Speaking at the Asan Memorial Lecture organised by the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul, South Korea, on Wednesday, Harris described the failure to use American leverage to curb the Israeli governmentâs conduct during the war in Gaza as a major shortcoming of US policy. âMost recently, the failure to use our leverage to curtail the Israeli governmentâs horrific conduct in the war in Gaza, both under the current administration, which offers [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu a blank check, and our administration before, where we should have acted sooner and more forcefully,â Harris said. Her remarks amounted to a criticism of the Biden administration, under which she served as vice president, as well as the current Trump administration, which she accused of giving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unconditional support. Republican Jewish Coalition hits back at Harris Harrisâs comments drew criticism from the Republican Jewish Coalition, which described her position as âunsurprisingâ. The group cited her absence from Netanyahuâs 2024 address to the US Congress and her opposition to legislation targeting the boycott, divestment and sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel. The organisation also criticised Harris for calling for a halt to Israeli military operations in Rafah, a city in southern Gaza, and for agreeing with a student in 2021 who accused Israel of âethnic genocideâ. Warren Kinsella, an attorney and author who worked on Harrisâs 2024 presidential campaign, also expressed disappointment over her latest remarks, writing on social media that he was âashamed to have worked with herâ. Harris says US foreign policy needs a rethink Beyond the Gaza conflict, Harris spoke about the changing nature of American power and the need to rethink traditional approaches to foreign policy. She argued that economic innovation, markets, minerals and semiconductor technology were becoming increasingly important sources of global influence, alongside military strength. âComing out of world wars, and into the Cold War, military might was the primary source of power,â she said. âBut now more than ever, economic innovation, markets and minerals, chips and computers, have greater influence.â Harris also stressed the importance of strengthening US alliances, pointing to closer ties among China, Russia, Iran and North Korea as a development Washington and its partners needed to monitor. Harris puts 2026 midterms ahead of 2028 presidential race Harris expressed confidence that Democrats would win the November 2026 midterm elections but sidestepped a direct question about whether she planned to run for president in 2028. â2028, from my perspective, doesnât matter if we donât win 2026,â she said, indicating that the immediate priority for Democrats was the upcoming congressional elections. title: Israelâs electoral deadlock: Netanyahu, Eisenkot and the Persistence of hardline security politics
text: Gadi Eisenkot, Benjamin Netanyahu, Mansour Abbas Israelâs parliamentary election has produced a political deadlock, raising questions about Benjamin Netanyahu âs political future and the direction of Israeli foreign and security policy. With nearly 90% of votes counted, Netanyahuâs right-wing bloc was projected to secure 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Arab parties, projected to win 19 seats, could become influential in coalition negotiations. Neither bloc has secured the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority. Although Netanyahu has lost his governing majority, his political survival remains possible. More importantly, those expecting his departure to herald a fundamental moderation of Israeli policy towards Palestine and Hamas may be seriously mistaken. The election represents more than a contest between two political personalities. It reflects Israelâs continuing struggle over national security, political accountability and its strategic direction following the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks and subsequent regional conflicts. Netanyahu, Israelâs longest-serving prime minister, has built his political career around military strength, opposition to Iran and close strategic relations with Washington. However, the security failures surrounding October 7, prolonged military operations in Gaza and growing domestic divisions have weakened his political standing. Yet his principal challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, is hardly a moderate alternative on Israelâs fundamental security priorities. Eisenkot, who served as Chief of Staff of the Israel Defense Forces from 2015 to 2019, is a seasoned military strategist associated with the controversial Dahiyeh doctrine, which advocates overwhelming military force against hostile organisations. His security outlook is uncompromising. He has explicitly rejected Palestinian statehood, describing the two-state formula as a mistake, and insists that Israel must retain overriding security responsibility between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea. He has also demanded the destruction or dismantling of Hamasâs military capabilities and an end to its governing authority in Gaza. His position suggests that an Eisenkot government could pursue military objectives against Hamas with considerable determination, potentially adopting an even more forceful operational approach than Netanyahu in certain circumstances. Significantly, Eisenkotâs differences with Netanyahu are primarily over leadership, strategic execution and political accountability rather than Israelâs fundamental security objectives. Eisenkot joined Netanyahuâs emergency war cabinet following the October 2023 attacks but resigned alongside Benny Gantz in June 2024, criticising Netanyahuâs handling of the conflict and failure to achieve clearly defined military objectives. He has questioned Netanyahuâs claims of total victory when Hamasâs military and governing capabilities have not been completely dismantled. His departure was therefore not a rejection of Israelâs military campaign against Hamas but reflected dissatisfaction with its conduct, effectiveness and political management. Nevertheless, differences between the two leaders should not be overlooked. Eisenkot opposes Netanyahuâs far-right coalition partners, criticises settler violence and has questioned certain settlement expansion plans that could undermine Israelâs broader strategic interests. However, he supports Jewish settlements under specified conditions and rejects Palestinian sovereignty. These distinctions may influence Israelâs domestic politics and international diplomatic engagement, but they do not establish Eisenkot as a liberal alternative on the Palestinian question. Indeed, his military credentials and commitment to dismantling Hamas could make him an equally uncompromising, and potentially more operationally decisive, leader. For Palestinians, therefore, Netanyahuâs possible departure offers no guarantee of a fundamental policy transformation. Both leaders oppose Palestinian statehood and insist that Hamas must cease to exist as an effective military and governing organisation. The distinction may lie in how these objectives are pursued rather than the objectives themselves. Eisenkot has pledged to replace Hamasâs administration in Gaza within 18 months of taking office, through a US-backed arrangement or military force. An Eisenkot government might seek different arrangements for Gazaâs administration or coordinate more closely with Washington, but such possibilities should not be confused with an embrace of Palestinian independence. The unresolved challenge remains reconciling Israelâs security concerns with Palestinian political aspirations and the humanitarian consequences of prolonged conflict. The implications extend well beyond Israel and Palestine. The United States remains Israelâs indispensable strategic partner, providing military assistance, intelligence cooperation and diplomatic support. President Donald Trump has maintained strong relations with Netanyahu, particularly over Iran and regional security. Washingtonâs strategic commitment to Israel, however, transcends individual leaders. An Eisenkot government would almost certainly preserve this partnership, including cooperation against Iranâs nuclear ambitions and regional military networks. Nevertheless, differences could emerge over the timing and scale of military operations, particularly against Tehran, where Eisenkot has also acknowledged the possibility of American-backed diplomatic arrangements. Netanyahu, meanwhile, has consistently emphasised military pressure and the opportunity to eliminate Iranâs strategic threat. For the wider Middle East, Israelâs political uncertainty comes at a critical moment. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Jordan remain concerned about regional escalation, Gazaâs future and the consequences of confrontation with Iran. The Abraham Accords demonstrated the potential for ArabâIsraeli strategic cooperation, but further normalisation, particularly involving Saudi Arabia, remains constrained by the unresolved Palestinian question. Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot presently offers a clear pathway towards Palestinian statehood. Consequently, a change in Israeli leadership alone is unlikely to overcome the political obstacles to wider regional normalisation. For India, the electoral outcome is significant but unlikely to fundamentally alter its strategic partnership with Israel. Over three decades, bilateral relations have expanded across defence, intelligence, counterterrorism, agriculture, cybersecurity and emerging technologies. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has strengthened these ties while maintaining Indiaâs longstanding support for Palestinian aspirations and close relations with Arab states. New Delhiâs strategic interests require continuity in cooperation with Israel alongside strong energy, economic and security partnerships with the Gulf. Regional instability also threatens connectivity initiatives such as the IndiaâMiddle EastâEurope Economic Corridor. India will therefore favour stability, diplomatic engagement and the avoidance of further escalation, regardless of who eventually forms Israelâs government. The immediate political challenge remains coalition formation. Netanyahuâs bloc has emerged ahead of Eisenkotâs, although neither commands a majority. Eisenkot faces particular difficulties because forming an alternative government could require Arab-party support, which he has resisted. A Netanyahu-led coalition, a broader unity government or another election remain possible outcomes. Netanyahuâs political career has repeatedly demonstrated his capacity to survive apparently decisive setbacks. Ultimately, Israelâs election should not be viewed merely as a contest between two political rivals, but between two leaders committed to an uncompromising national security doctrine. While Netanyahu has pursued an aggressive military strategy against Hamas, Eisenkot, a former IDF chief, represents an equally hawkish and potentially more determined military-security approach. His explicit rejection of Palestinian statehood, commitment to dismantling Hamasâs military and governing capabilities, and criticism of Netanyahuâs failure to achieve decisive military objectives suggest that an Eisenkot government could pursue these objectives with even greater operational resolve. Far from representing a softer alternative, Eisenkot could prove more formidable in implementing Israelâs security priorities. Netanyahuâs departure, therefore, would not necessarily bring relief to Palestinians or a fundamental change in Israeli policy. Indeed, a change in leadership could produce greater military determination rather than moderation, even as the two leaders differ over political governance, strategic execution and regional diplomacy. The larger geopolitical question is therefore not merely who governs Israel, but whether its next government can translate military strength into sustainable security, regional stability and a viable political future. Changing Israelâs leadership may prove easier than changing the strategic realities shaping the Middle East. Disclaimer : Views expressed above are the author's own.

title: Who is Gadi Eisenkot? Ex-army chief of Israel is Netanyahu's biggest challenger in PM race
text: Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, visits the Western Wall, the holiest site where Jews can pray, in Jerusalem's Old City (Credit: AP) Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), is challenging Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with a campaign centred on security, leadership and accountability for the failures surrounding Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack. Eisenkot, who founded the Yashar party in 2025, has emerged as a key challenger to Netanyahu ahead of Israel's October 27 election. Unlike Netanyahu, a veteran and combative politician, Eisenkot has cultivated an image of a reserved, straightforward leader with strong military credentials. His family has also suffered personal losses during the Gaza war, with his son and two nephews killed while fighting there. From military chief to political challenger The son of Moroccan immigrants, Eisenkot served in the Israeli military for 41 years, rising to become its chief of staff from 2015 to 2019. He commanded troops in the West Bank during the second intifada and served during Israel's 2006 war against Hezbollah in Lebanon. During the Lebanon conflict, he employed what became known as the âDahiyeh doctrineâ, a strategy involving overwhelming force against areas used by militant groups, including the destruction of civilian infrastructure. The approach drew criticism over its humanitarian consequences. Eisenkot entered frontline politics after the October 7 attacks, joining Netanyahu's war cabinet as an observer. He left after eight months, criticising the prime minister's leadership and arguing that Israel had failed to achieve its declared objective of destroying Hamas' military and governing capabilities. He has also argued that freeing the hostages taken by Hamas was the only war objective Israel had achieved. Where he stands on security and Palestinians Despite presenting an alternative to Netanyahu's leadership and far-right coalition partners, Eisenkot maintains a hardline position on security. He says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled and that Israel must prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, either through military action or a diplomatic agreement backed by the United States. Eisenkot opposes Palestinian statehood, describing the idea of âtwo states for two peoplesâ as a mistake. He has argued that Israel must retain overriding security responsibility in the territory between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea. He also supports Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank, while saying they should serve Israeli national interests and be legal. He has criticised settler violence against Palestinians and opposed some of the Netanyahu government's settlement plans, including construction in the E1 area, which critics say would further divide the West Bank. Eisenkot has rejected partnering with parties representing Arab Israelis, saying they do not accept his core security principles. This position could complicate his efforts to assemble a parliamentary majority, even if his party performs strongly. Can he replace Netanyahu? Eisenkot's campaign offers voters an alternative to Netanyahu's leadership without a major shift away from Israel's hardline security outlook. His military background, personal losses during the Gaza war and criticism of the government's handling of the October 7 aftermath have shaped his public profile. Opinion polls cited by news agency Reuters show his party leading Netanyahu's Likud, although Israel's fragmented political landscape could make forming a government difficult for either leader. title: Israel elections 2026: What's at stake for Netanyahu? Key challengers, seats needed to win and more
text: Israel set to vote for the first time since Oct 7 attack; Netanyahu faces major test Israel is set to vote on Tuesday, marking its first national election since Hamasâ October 7, 2023, attack, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu âs leadership, security record and political future at the centre of the campaign. Voters are weighing his handling of the attack and the conflicts that followed against concerns over military service exemptions, judicial reforms and the rising cost of living. With Netanyahu facing a challenge from rival parties, the election is expected to test his ability to retain power after years of conflict and political divisions. However, with no single party expected to win a majority in the 120-member Knesset, the next government will depend on post-election coalition negotiations as much as the vote itself. What will decide Israelâs election Israelâs first national election since Hamasâ October 7, 2023, attack is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahuâs leadership. While the attack and the security failures surrounding it remain central to the campaign, the debate has focused largely on Netanyahuâs accountability, his handling of the aftermath and his leadership rather than Israelâs military conduct in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, which has broad domestic support. One of the biggest issues is the exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from compulsory military service. With Israel facing a shortage of soldiers and reservists repeatedly called up during wars, the exemptions have fuelled resentment among secular Israelis. Netanyahuâs dependence on ultra-Orthodox parties has made the issue particularly contentious, with his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, promising to end the exemptions. Netanyahuâs proposed judicial overhaul, which triggered mass protests in 2023, remains another point of division. Critics see the changes as an attempt to weaken the Supreme Court and undermine democratic institutions, while Netanyahu has defended them as a way to curb judicial power. The economy and the rising cost of living are also concerns, although they have received relatively little attention during the campaign despite many Israelis struggling with affordability. Leadership is likely to be a decisive factor, with voters weighing Netanyahuâs experience and security record against criticism of his handling of October 7 and the wars that followed.However, neither of the main political blocs is advocating a major shift on the Palestinian question: both are dominated by parties that support Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank and oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state. With no party expected to win an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset, the outcome will also depend on which leader can assemble a governing coalition. Who are the leading candidates? Benjamin Netanyahu: Israelâs longest-serving prime minister, Netanyahu has been in power for much of the period since 2009. His supporters see him as a strong leader capable of defending Israel, but his political standing has been weakened by the security failures surrounding Hamasâ October 7, 2023, attack, his corruption trial and an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes in Gaza, which he denies. His Likud party has faced a decline in opinion polls, though Netanyahu remains a formidable political survivor and is seeking to form a broad national government. Gadi Eisenkot: The former military chief, 66, leads the centrist Yashar party and has positioned himself as a security-focused alternative to Netanyahu. Having lost his son in combat in Gaza, Eisenkot has highlighted his military background and personal sacrifices. He has also pledged to end the exemptions from compulsory military service enjoyed by ultra-Orthodox men, an issue that has become a major source of public anger. Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid: Former prime ministers Bennett, 54, and Lapid have joined forces under a new party called Together. Bennett is a former commando and a right-wing politician, while Lapid comes from the centre. Despite their different political backgrounds, the two previously worked together to oust Netanyahu in 2021. Their campaign has focused on national unity and getting Israel back on track after years of conflict and political division. Avigdor Lieberman: The former defence minister, 68, leads the right-wing Israel Our Home party, which draws considerable support from Israelâs ex-Soviet immigrant community. Once a close ally of Netanyahu, Lieberman left his government in 2018, accusing him of being too soft on Palestinian militants in Gaza. He has since become one of the prime ministerâs most vocal critics. Yair Golan: The former general, 64, heads the Democrats, a left-wing party formed from the remnants of Israelâs Labour party and Meretz. Golan was praised for helping rescue people from a site targeted during the October 7 attack. Key figures backing Netanyahu Finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, 46, and national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, 50, are prominent far-right allies of Netanyahu. Smotrich has pushed for expanding Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and opposed Palestinian statehood. Ben-Gvir has advocated tougher measures against Palestinian prisoners, capital punishment for convicted Palestinian militants and expanded gun ownership for Israelis. Both have also backed the expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza and Israeli resettlement of the enclave. Netanyahu has also depended on the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism to maintain his governing coalitions. Their demand to preserve exemptions from compulsory military service for many ultra-Orthodox men has become increasingly contentious as Israel faces wartime manpower shortages. Who could hold the balance of power? Parties that are not firmly aligned with either major bloc could prove decisive in determining who forms the next government. These include Raam and the Joint List, which represent Israelâs Arab minority, as well as the new right-wing People of Israel party and the centre-right Reservists party. Their final strength and willingness to join either camp could shape coalition negotiations after the vote. With no party typically winning a majority outright, forming a coalition of at least 61 lawmakers is key to forming the government How elections work in Israel Israel follows a proportional representation system to elect the 120 members of its parliament, the Knesset. Voters choose political parties rather than individual candidates, and seats are distributed according to each partyâs share of the national vote. Parties must secure at least 3.25% of the vote to enter parliament. Since no single party has ever won an outright majority, forming a government typically requires alliances between multiple parties. The leader who can assemble a coalition with the support of at least 61 lawmakers can form the government, giving smaller parties considerable influence over negotiations and policy decisions. The election comes after a period of political instability between 2019 and 2022, when Israel held repeated elections. He argued that Israel had failed to achieve its stated objective of destroying Hamasâ military and governing capabilities. The son of Jewish Moroccan immigrants, he entered frontline politics alongside another former chief of defence staff, Benny Gantz, after the October 7 attacks. His son and two nephews were killed in combat in Gaza, according to Israeli media reports. Despite presenting himself as an alternative to Netanyahuâs leadership, Eisenkot maintains a hardline position on security. title: Israel elections: Netanyahu faces crucial test; reports of fraud attempts, missing ballots - top developments
text: Benjamin Netanyahu stands next to his wife Sara as they cast their ballots. Israelis are voting in a crucial parliamentary election on Tuesday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu facing a major test of his leadership amid unresolved conflicts, divisions over the country's future and growing international criticism of its conduct in Gaza. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking to retain power against a group of parties hoping to unseat him, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. The election is the country's first national vote since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack that triggered the war in Gaza and related regional conflicts. The election has also been clouded by allegations of missing, damaged and defaced ballot slips. Several parties reported irregularities at polling stations, prompting concerns about election integrity. However, the CEC said there was no evidence of systematic ballot tampering. 1. Netanyahu faces a crucial test The election is a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership and the direction Israel should take, with voters divided over security, military conscription, judicial independence and the country's international standing. Netanyahu's supporters see him as an experienced leader who has guided Israel through multiple wars and defended its Jewish identity. His critics accuse him of prolonging the war in Gaza and the hostage crisis for political reasons, weakening judicial independence and allowing ultra-Orthodox religious men to avoid compulsory military service. âThe present government is driving the country into the ground,â voter Angela Bengur said in Jerusalem, the Associated Press reported. Eisenkot's supporters see him as a leader with strong security credentials who could improve Israel's international standing and strengthen democratic institutions. His personal losses during the Gaza war have also shaped his public image: his son and two nephews were killed while fighting in Gaza. The campaign has been dominated by security concerns and the October 7 attack, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage to Gaza, according to the figures cited in the supplied reports. The opposition has criticised Netanyahu over the security failures that preceded the attack, while his supporters have emphasised his experience in handling regional threats. 2. Voter turnout reaches record levels Turnout in Israel's parliamentary election has risen sharply throughout Tuesday, reaching levels not seen at comparable times in previous elections. According to the CEC, 31.5% of eligible voters had cast their ballots by noon, the highest turnout recorded at that hour since 1973, The Times of Israel reported. The participation rate continued to climb through the afternoon. By 4 pm, turnout had reached 55.7%. Voter turnout has reached record levels, with 66.7% of eligible voters casting their ballots by 6 pm local time, according to the Central Elections Committee (CEC). The figure was significantly higher than the 57.7% recorded at the same time during the 2022 election. Polling is scheduled to continue until 10 pm local time, although some stations have different operating hours. The strong turnout reflects intense public interest in an election that could reshape Israel's political landscape. Around 330,000 young Israelis are eligible to vote for the first time. Turnout among Israel Defense Forces (IDF) personnel has also been high. The military reported that more than 68% of soldiers had voted by 5 pm, compared with 65% at the same stage of the 2022 election. 3. Netanyahu warns of Arab-backed government as Arab-led parties eye key role Arab-led parties could play a decisive role in government formation if the rival political blocs fail to secure a majority. Netanyahu urged Likud supporters to vote in large numbers, warning that the country's future was at stake. âThis is an emergency call to Likud voters! Today no one stays home. No sea, no barbecue. Making sure that the family, friends, and neighbors also get to the polling station,â he wrote on X, sharing a video. âThe future of our Jewish state is on the line: a strong right-wing government or a left-wing government supported by the Arab parties. Going out to vote with all our might!â he added. In another post, Netanyahu said buses were heading to polling stations and long queues were being reported in Arab communities, while right-wing strongholds had yet to see a comparable turnout. âIf we don't go out to vote now, we'll find ourselves with a government of the Arab parties. We must not stay home. Every vote counts! Going out now to vote - Machal, Likud,â he wrote. Arab citizens account for around one-fifth of Israel's population. Their participation could prove significant in a close election, particularly if neither of the main political blocs can assemble a majority independently. Arab voter turnout is expected to be substantially higher than in 2022, when it was just over 50%. Pollsters have projected participation of up to 70% in Arab communities. The two main Arab-led political groups: Mansour Abbas's Ra'am party and the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen in the supplied report, could influence the balance of power. Although most leading Jewish parties have ruled out formal cooperation with Arab-led parties, they could still provide parliamentary support from outside a governing coalition. Earlier this month, Jabareen said his party was willing to act as a âsafety netâ to help remove Netanyahu from power. âOur vote will change the government,â Abbas said after casting his ballot, adding that he hoped turnout in Arab communities would exceed 70%. âThis is essential to changing our situation and addressing the problems we face as an Arab community, such as violence, crime, home demolitions, fines, racism, and incitement,â Abbas said, CNN reported. âThe vote is an important tool for changing the political situation. A government that came to power through the ballot box can be removed through the ballot box.â However, cooperation with Arab-led parties remains contentious among right-wing politicians. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir warned that âit will be Mansour Abbasâ governmentâ if Netanyahu and his allies fail to secure a victory. 4. Yashar party alleges ballot tampering Allegations of ballot irregularities have added another layer of tension to election day. Eisenkot's Yashar party filed a complaint with the CEC after receiving reports that ballot slips bearing its designated voting symbol, âDerechâ, were missing, damaged or defaced at polling stations. The party said it had received complaints from several locations about ballot slips being removed, marked with pens or turned over inside voting booths. Such incidents could potentially lead to votes being disqualified. âAfter Likud's fake news campaign, we received numerous complaints about our ballot slips being defaced or removed,â party chairman Yoaz Hendel said, The Jerusalem Post reported. The party described the alleged incidents as a possible attempt to disrupt its vote and undermine election integrity. âAnyone who tries to steal ballot slips is trying to steal the election. This is a serious violation of election integrity and the fundamental right of Israeli citizens to vote,â the party said. Other leading parties also reported alleged irregularities at polling stations. However, the CEC said there was no evidence of systematic tampering with ballot slips. The allegations had not been independently established in the information available at the time of reporting. Separately, Talal al-Karnaw, mayor of the Bedouin city of Rahat in southern Israel, told Walla that power outages had affected some polling stations and neighbourhoods, creating what he described as a âserious problemâ for voters. 5. Eisenkot visits October 7-hit community before voting Eisenkot began election day by visiting Kibbutz Nir Oz, one of the communities hardest hit by the Hamas-led October 7 attack. He walked alongside former hostage Gadi Mozes towards his polling booth before leaving to cast his own vote elsewhere. âI am proud and moved to begin this day with Gadi Mozes, a symbol of the Israeli spirit and strength, of Israelisâ commitment to one another and their commitment to the state. I pledge to do everything I can to ensure that we are worthy of the price you paid, the price the kibbutz paid and the price we all paid, and to bring healing and repair to all citizens of Israel,â Eisenkot told reporters. Mozes spent 482 days in Hamas captivity and campaigned for Eisenkot, according to The Times of Israel . Eisenkot also criticised the government for not beginning election day in communities attacked on October 7. âIf someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here in the Gaza envelope,â he said. In Tel Aviv, families of people killed during the October 7 attack and former hostages observed a moment of silence. 6. President Herzog calls election a 'holiday of democracy' President Isaac Herzog urged Israelis to participate in the election, describing it as an opportunity for citizens to influence the country's future. âIt is a real holiday of democracy, and no one can be allowed to ruin it â quite the opposite, this is our opportunity, all of us, to influence our fate, the fate of our children, and the fate of our grandchildren. It is something that is deeply embedded inside of our spirit, as a very democratic nation,â The Times of Israel reported him as saying. âWe are putting different slips in the ballot, and we are expressing different opinions, in the end we have a common fate. A common fate in this land, a common fate in our beloved country, and this election process is another way to express our love for our country,â Herzog added. 7. Israel deploys 100,000 personnel for election day Israel has mounted a large logistical operation for the parliamentary election, with around 100,000 personnel, including election officials and workers, deployed across the country. Acting director general of the CEC Dean Livne said around 50,000 election workers had received training at approximately 2,140 venues. The committee prepared 12,018 polling stations, 18,000 ballot boxes, 12 million voting envelopes and 250 tonnes of paper for ballot materials. It also established 6,209 accessible polling stations. Special voting arrangements were made for more than 600,000 people who might be unable to vote at their designated polling stations, including soldiers, diplomats and hospitalised voters. These voters can use an outer-envelope system, with checks intended to prevent duplicate voting. Authorities also arranged free travel on 660 intercity public transport routes, including Israel Railways services, to help voters reach polling stations. Around 690 million shekels, or approximately $223 million, was allocated for the election. The CEC deployed around 15,000 cameras for electoral integrity inspectors to monitor polling stations and document voting and counting. The system is intended to protect ballot secrecy and help inspectors identify attempts to pressure or influence voters. 8. How Israel's electoral system works Israel is a parliamentary democracy in which voters elect lawmakers rather than directly choosing the prime minister. The government must retain the confidence of the Knesset to remain in power. The country uses proportional representation. Voters choose a party list, and the 120 seats in the Knesset are distributed broadly in proportion to the votes received by parties that cross the electoral threshold. Unlike many parliamentary democracies, Israel treats the entire country as a single constituency rather than dividing it into geographic electoral districts. This allows smaller parties representing religious, political and ethnic communities to win parliamentary representation. Parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes to enter the Knesset. The system often produces fragmented parliaments in which no single party wins an outright majority, making coalition negotiations central to government formation. 9. What happens after the votes are counted? After the results are finalised, President Herzog will consult the leaders of the elected parties before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a government. The person chosen does not necessarily have to lead the largest party. The key consideration is who appears most likely to assemble a coalition with sufficient parliamentary support. The designated lawmaker will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension. If the attempt fails, another lawmaker may be given 28 days to try. If that effort also fails, at least 61 lawmakers can request that the president assign the task to a particular member of the Knesset within a further 21-day period. A new government must win a confidence vote in parliament. A minority government may also take office if it receives more votes in favour than against, even without the backing of 61 lawmakers. The process could take weeks, leaving the identity of Israel's next prime minister uncertain even after the election results emerge. If all attempts to form a government fail, the country could face another election, with Netanyahu remaining caretaker prime minister until a new government takes office. 10. Iran tensions remain in the background The election is taking place amid continuing tensions with Iran and international criticism of Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Netanyahu warned that Iran would face âa devastating blowâ if it attacked Israel, keeping security and regional threats at the centre of the campaign. The election is also unfolding against a backdrop of strained international relations, including declining public support for Israel in the United States and sanctions imposed by some European and other partners. title: Israel elections: Can Benjamin Netanyahu turn security gains into a political victory?
text: People walk past a Likud party campaign billboard featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alongside opposition party leaders and bearing the Hebrew slogan "Right or Palestine," ahead of Israel's general election, in Beni Brak, Israel (AP Photo) Three years after the October 7 attack, Benjamin Netanyahu faces a crucial electoral test over security, political accountability and the direction of Israel. Donald Trumpâs endorsement and the unresolved confrontation with Iran have raised the stakes, but a divided opposition may struggle to turn its challenge into power. Israelis vote on Tuesday, October 27, in the country's first general election since Hamas's October 7, 2023, terrorist attack. The outcome could determine whether Bibi, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, extends his political career or loses power after three years of war and domestic turmoil. The final opinion polls suggest a close contest. Surveys published by Israel's three major television networks on Friday put Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party ahead of Netanyahu's Likud. Yet neither the prime minister's coalition nor the main opposition bloc is projected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. Yashar was projected to win around 22-23 seats, against 19-21 for Likud. Netanyahu's coalition was projected at about 50 seats, while the main opposition bloc was estimated at 52-56. Arab-led parties could win another 14-16 seats. These are projections, not results. But they point to the central question of the election: can Netanyahu survive the verdict on his leadership and can his opponents agree on an alternative? The challenger: Gadi Eisenkot Eisenkot, a former chief of the Israel Defence Forces (IDF), has emerged as Netanyahu's principal challenger. He served as military chief from 2015 to 2019 and joined the wartime government formed after the October 7 attack. He left the government in June 2024, arguing that political considerations were influencing decisions on the war. He subsequently broke with Benny Gantz and established Yashar in September 2025. Eisenkot's appeal rests on military experience, greater accountability and the argument that Israel needs a change of leadership without abandoning its security priorities. He is not a conventional left-wing challenger. His criticism centres on Netanyahu's handling of the war, the failures that preceded October 7 and the government's domestic agenda. Like several other opposition figures, he takes a hard line on Hamas and argues that Israel needs more effective security leadership. This distinction matters. The election is not a straightforward contest between hawkish and dovish approaches. Many of Netanyahu's opponents argue that his decisions have weakened Israel's security rather than strengthened it. October 7 and accountability The October 7 attack remains the defining test of Netanyahu's leadership. Hamas-led militants killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel and took 251 hostages, according to Israeli figures. The attack exposed major failures in intelligence, military preparedness and the government's assessment of Hamas's intentions. Netanyahu has emphasised the military campaigns that followed, presenting his government as determined to dismantle Hamas and confront threats from Iran and its regional allies. His critics argue that the attack happened under his watch and that the government has yet to provide an adequate account of how Israel's security establishment failed to prevent it. Opposition parties and critics have demanded an independent state commission of inquiry. Netanyahu has resisted such an investigation, which could scrutinise decisions taken by his government as well as the military and intelligence services. In recent weeks, reports said he had advance warning from the UAE and Egypt that Hamas was planning an attack. He calls the claims libellous and is taking legal action against the outlets that published them. His personal legal troubles add another layer. Netanyahu is on trial on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which he denies. In November 2025, he asked President Isaac Herzog for a pardon without admitting guilt, following public pressure from Trump. The trial remains a separate legal process. He is also subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes in Gaza, which he rejects. For his supporters, Netanyahu remains an experienced leader facing extraordinary security challenges. For his opponents, his political survival has become inseparable from questions of accountability. Dr Ashok Sharma, a visiting fellow at the University of New South Wales in Canberra, said the October 7 attacks had damaged Netanyahu's reputation as Israel's most experienced security-oriented leader. However, he cautioned against underestimating the prime minister's political resilience. âHis supporters increasingly assess his leadership through Israelâs subsequent military campaigns against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran,â Sharma said, adding that these operations had demonstrated Israel's military capabilities and determination to confront regional threats. For conservative and nationalist voters, he said, security remains a priority. The election will test whether accountability for October 7 outweighs confidence in Netanyahu's ability to confront continuing threats. Iran war: Security asset or political liability? Security is Netanyahu's central campaign argument and Iran is where it has become most consequential. Israel and the United States launched military operations against Iran on February 28, targeting its nuclear and military infrastructure. The conflict widened into a regional confrontation before a Pakistan-mediated process produced a ceasefire arrangement and a memorandum of understanding in June. The pause has not resolved the underlying disputes. Iran's nuclear programme, sanctions and the Strait of Hormuz remain sources of tension, while pressure on Iranian ports and continuing regional uncertainty have kept the risk of renewed fighting alive. Netanyahu has presented the campaign against Iran as a strategic achievement, arguing that military action has weakened a major threat to Israel. He maintains that further action may be necessary to prevent Tehran from rebuilding its capabilities or pursuing a nuclear weapon. But the war also raises questions about its costs, its long-term results and whether military operations have delivered a sustainable outcome. Sharma said the campaign had demonstrated Israel's intelligence capabilities, technological superiority and ability to project military power. However, he cautioned that Iran retained the capacity for asymmetric retaliation and could rebuild its military capabilities. âMilitary achievements alone cannot guarantee lasting security,â he said, arguing that the campaign's ultimate success would depend on whether military gains could be translated into sustainable deterrence, diplomatic arrangements and regional stability. The conflict has also highlighted Israel's dependence on American military assistance, intelligence cooperation and diplomatic support. Sharma described this as a strategic partnership rather than simply a vulnerability, while noting that the long-term outcome would depend on how effectively Israel converts its military gains into lasting security. A Financial Times report published earlier this week added a new dimension to the election. Citing people familiar with the plans, it reported that Netanyahu had instructed the Israeli military to prepare a major offensive against Iran for the weekend of October 10. The newspaper said Trump opposed restarting the fighting before the November 3 US midterm elections. Netanyahu subsequently rejected the account as incorrect and biased. The episode highlights a central question for Israeli voters: how much freedom does Netanyahu have to pursue his preferred military strategy without American backing? The US is Israel's most consequential international partner, providing military assistance and diplomatic support. Even when the two governments agree on the threat posed by Iran, they may differ over the timing and consequences of further attacks. For Netanyahu, the Iran campaign supports his longstanding argument that Israel needs a leader prepared to take decisive action. His opponents can counter that successive rounds of military escalation and ceasefires do not amount to a durable security strategy. A change of government would not necessarily bring a major shift in policy. Eisenkot and other opposition figures have also taken a hard line on Iran and have mostly attacked Netanyahu from the right, calling him soft on security. Hence, the difference may lie less in whether Israel regards Tehran as a threat than in how a new government chooses to manage it. Trump backs Netanyahu â but the relationship has limits Trump has made his preference clear. On October 18, he publicly endorsed Netanyahu's re-election, praising him as a strong leader and arguing that another prime minister might leave Washington to confront Iran alone. Netanyahu has used the endorsement to reinforce his claim that his personal relationship with Trump helps protect Israeli interests. Sharma said the endorsement strengthened Netanyahu's image as an internationally experienced leader capable of maintaining Washington's support. He pointed to the wider record of US-Israel cooperation, including American recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital and Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, as well as the Abraham Accords. But the relationship is not unconditional. The reported disagreement over a possible renewed offensive against Iran suggests that Washington's calculations, including the US domestic political calendar, may not always align with Netanyahu's military priorities. Netanyahu has disputed the reporting, but the broader tension remains relevant. Trump's endorsement also allows Netanyahu to present the election as a choice between continuity in Israel's relationship with Washington and a potentially less predictable alternative. Yet American support cannot by itself resolve his domestic difficulties or guarantee a parliamentary majority. Sharma said the endorsement could consolidate Netanyahu's support among conservative and security-conscious voters, but Israeli elections would still be shaped by domestic security, economic conditions and coalition politics. Netanyahu has also used his campaign to portray his opponents as aligned with forces hostile to Israel. In August, he shared an image of a Likud campaign billboard featuring New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani alongside Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Turkish President Recep Tayyip ErdoÄan and Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem. The message suggested that these figures wanted Netanyahu to lose and urged voters not to let them win. Mamdani, a vocal critic of Israel's conduct in Gaza, has called Netanyahu a war criminal and urged the US government to enforce the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant if he travelled to New York. Also read: 'Don't let them win' - Netanyahu's party puts Zohran Mamdani alongside Iran, Hezbollah leaders on billboard The billboard illustrated Netanyahu's attempt to frame the election as more than a domestic contest over governance. For his supporters, it reinforced the argument that Israel needs a leader prepared to confront its adversaries. Critics may see it as an effort to shift attention away from accountability and domestic problems. The US relationship itself has become more politically contested, particularly over the war in Gaza. Even if Netanyahu remains in office, he will have to manage American political divisions alongside the strategic partnership. Domestic fault lines Netanyahu's political strength has long depended on alliances among right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. These partnerships have enabled him to govern but have also constrained his room for manoeuvre. One of the sharpest disputes concerns military service. Ultra-Orthodox parties have defended exemptions for many men engaged in full-time religious study. As prolonged military operations have increased the demands on reservists and their families, the exemptions have become a more contentious political issue. Israel's Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that the broad legal basis for the exemptions could not continue as it had. Critics argue that the burden of defending the country should be shared more fairly, while ultra-Orthodox parties regard protecting religious study as a core commitment. Eisenkot has made broader military service one of his priorities, putting him at odds with parties that want to preserve the exemptions. The election also reopens the dispute over judicial reform. Netanyahu's government pursued controversial changes to the judicial system in 2023, prompting mass protests and warnings that the proposals would weaken checks on executive power. The war interrupted that confrontation but did not settle it. These disputes could complicate coalition negotiations even if Netanyahu's Likud performs strongly. They also give the opposition an opportunity to argue that a change of leadership could address domestic divisions without abandoning Israel's security priorities. Arithmetic problem Israel's parliamentary system means that winning the most seats does not automatically make a party's leader prime minister. The president consults political factions after the election before asking a candidate to form a government. That candidate normally has 28 days to assemble a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension. The key requirement is support from at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 members. This is where the opposition faces its biggest obstacle. Its parties may collectively win more seats than Netanyahu's coalition, but they disagree over which partners they are willing to accept. Arab-led parties could prove pivotal, with final polls projecting them at 14-16 seats combined. But Eisenkot and other opposition figures have faced pressure over whether they would rely on their support to form a government. That leaves several possibilities: an opposition-led government relying on Arab parties from outside the coalition, unexpected alliances or defections from Netanyahu-aligned parties. A national unity government is another possibility, although the failed 2020 power-sharing arrangement between Netanyahu and Benny Gantz offers little assurance of stability. Netanyahu has portrayed cooperation between his opponents and Arab parties as a threat, arguing that the election is a choice between the political right and a government that would concede too much to Palestinian interests. His opponents say the priority should be accountability and effective governance, but their divisions make it difficult to present a clear alternative. Sharma said the opposition's ideological differences could prove a major obstacle even if it secures enough seats collectively to challenge Netanyahu. Disagreements over national security, judicial reform, religious issues and relations with the Palestinians could also undermine the stability of any coalition it manages to form. Netanyahu, meanwhile, has extensive experience in coalition negotiations and has repeatedly demonstrated political resilience. Sharma said another fragmented Knesset, prolonged negotiations or political deadlock remained realistic possibilities. Netanyahu could therefore survive even if his coalition falls short of a majority, simply because his opponents cannot agree on a replacement. What happens next? The final polls are not guarantees. Netanyahu has beaten unfavourable surveys before, including in 2015, when the final polling picture underestimated his eventual performance. Smaller parties could also alter the balance if they unexpectedly cross or fail to cross the 3.25% threshold required to enter the Knesset. If no candidate can assemble a viable majority, Israel could face another election. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister in the interim, leaving the country with many of the same unresolved questions. The consequences would extend beyond domestic politics. Israel's next government will have to manage the confrontation with Iran, maintain its relationship with Washington, address the aftermath of the Gaza war and respond to questions about the security failures that preceded October 7. Those challenges will remain regardless of who wins. An opposition victory, however, would not necessarily mean a fundamental change in Israel's security and foreign policy. Sharma said countering Iran's nuclear ambitions and regional influence, maintaining military superiority and preserving the US-Israel strategic partnership would remain central priorities under any government. He also expects Israel's strategic relationship with India to remain largely unaffected by a change of leadership, given the established cooperation in defence technology, cybersecurity, intelligence and emerging technologies. An opposition government could place greater emphasis on diplomatic coordination with Washington, European partners and regional states, but the broader strategic direction would likely remain intact. âAn opposition victory would therefore be more likely to change Israelâs diplomatic style and regional engagement than fundamentally alter its strategic orientation,â Sharma said. For Netanyahu, Tuesday's vote is a test of whether his security-first strategy can survive the failures of October 7 and the consequences of the wars that followed. For Eisenkot and the opposition, the challenge is to convert dissatisfaction with the prime minister into a stable governing majority. Trump's endorsement and the Iran confrontation have given Netanyahu a powerful argument for continuity. But they have also exposed the limits of his control: Israeli military decisions remain tied to American calculations, while the costs of prolonged conflict continue to shape domestic politics. Netanyahu's future is on the ballot. Whether Israel's political direction changes with it will depend not only on the votes cast but on who can assemble the 61 seats needed to govern. Explosives were concealed inside the devices, allowing Israeli intelligence to turn ordinary communication equipment into remotely activated weapons. title: Economy, not ideology
text: When populists and autocrats lose elections, are voters rejecting their ideas or reacting to their economic problems? Research suggests that democracy is in danger. According to Swedenâs V-Dem Institute, the average person today has about the same democratic freedoms as in 1978. So, election results in Brazil and Serbia may look like victories for democracy. In Brazil, voters narrowly stopped Flavio Bolsonaro, who has shown strong authoritarian tendencies, from winning. They gave Lula another term instead. In Serbia, voters defeated strongman Aleksandar Vucic by a large margin. The result has attracted much attention because the winning side is a student protest movement supported by academics, doctors and others. Serbia has just 65 lakh people and a GDP of $112 billion. But these election results may not mean that democracy is making a comeback. As Harvard professor Steven Levitsky pointed out in 2024, voters may simply be unhappy with the people in power. In Brazil, even Lula lost the first round of voting before fighting back strongly. This trend has been clear since 2020, when Covid disrupted economies and governments adopted policies that made money easily available. The result was high inflation. Billionaires benefited, but the middle class and poorer people struggled. Levitsky noted that people had become deeply unhappy with their governments. In 41 of 55 elections and polls held between 2020 and 2024, the party in power lost. He said this was almost certainly linked to inflation caused by the pandemic. Were young Serbians, who protested against Vucic for two years, fighting for a political idea or for a better economic future? Britain offers another example. The Labour Party won a huge victory in the election, but became unpopular within months. Germanyâs Social Democrats are also struggling. In the US, voters first removed populist Donald Trump and elected Joe Biden, only to bring Trump back four years later. Now, with US midterm elections scheduled for November 3, voters may use their chance to weaken Trumpâs control of Congress. Why? He promised to tackle the rising cost of living, but his war on Iran has made peopleâs economic problems worse. Israel is another test for democracy, with elections taking place today. Opinion polls do not show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu winning a clear victory. But whoever wins is unlikely to take a softer stand towards Palestinians. Young Israelis, including first-time voters, do not appear to feel much sympathy for people in Gaza either. What they are tired of is endless war, the mental strain it causes and corruption. Everywhere, voters are asking their leaders a simple question: âWhat have you done for us and our future?â Leaders who are already in power are losing elections because they often have no convincing answer. title: Israel polls: Poll chief orders probe into 'foreign interference'; Netanyahu levels big charge - top developments
text: Israelâs international standing is also at stake following widespread criticism of its treatment of Palestinians in Gaza and growing violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank. Israelâs election chief has ordered a probe into alleged foreign interference in the October 28 election. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arab-led parties of stealing the vote and warned of a foreign takeover of parliament. The allegations emerged on Thursday as final results were awaited and neither Netanyahuâs bloc nor the opposition had secured a clear path to a majority in the 120-member Knesset. Israel's central elections committee chair, Justice Noam Sohlberg, asked Shin Bet chief David Zini to investigate suspicions of improper influence through foreign funding and alleged electoral bribery. Sohlberg said he could not confirm the validity of the claims but called for a thorough investigation. He asked Zini to submit findings within a week. Watch âWILL BURN THEM ALLâ: Iran âChases Offâ Israeli Jets With Fiery Warning Over Middle East | Watch Poll chief orders probe into alleged foreign interference Sohlberg directed the Shin Bet to investigate allegations that foreign entities had sought to influence the election through funding. In his letter to Zini, he wrote, âSerious suspicions have been brought to my attention regarding improper influence on the elections â exerted through funding provided by foreign entities acting against Israeli interests.â He added, âWhile I cannot attest to the substance of these suspicions, it is my view that â given they involve foreign entities â there is an obligation to investigate them thoroughly.â Sohlberg said the Shin Bet should use its authority to establish whether evidence supported or refuted the allegations. He called the investigation necessary to protect public confidence in the electoral process and democratic institutions. The allegations have not been independently established. Sohlberg did not identify the countries allegedly involved or provide further details about the suspected interference. Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of stealing elections Netanyahu seized on the investigation to intensify his attack on Arab-led parties and oppose any attempt by his rivals to form a government with their support. In a post on X, he said, âThe Ra'amgate affair is an earthquake. They stole the elections in Israel!â He added: âThis is an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of right-wing rule in order to lead to retreat and defeat of the IDF in all arenas - and primarily Iran.â Netanyahu also called for immediate action by the security agency and police. âWe demand to act immediately and with all means available to the Shin Bet and the police to investigate these crimes,â he said. Likud has argued that the allegations should rule out cooperation between Zionist parties and the Arab-led Raâam and Joint List parties. It warned against forming a government with their support or replacing the Knesset speaker through what it described as votes bought with cash. The accusations remain claims made by Netanyahu and his party. Police have previously said there was âno supporting evidenceâ for Likudâs allegation that Arab-led parties stole the election. Likud suspects Qatar and Turkey behind alleged funding Netanyahuâs Likud party suspects Qatar and Turkey may have funded get-out-the-vote groups targeting Arab citizens in Israel, according to Hebrew-language media reports. Channel 12 reported that the investigation was based on intelligence received by the Shin Bet and presented to Sohlberg. The reports said the channels allegedly used to transfer money to the organisations closely resembled those previously used to send funds for terrorism. However, the alleged involvement of Qatar and Turkey has not been established. Sohlberg did not identify any country as being behind the suspected interference. The allegations have taken on greater political significance because Arab-led parties could help Netanyahuâs opponents secure a majority. The investigation could therefore influence the debate over whether opposition parties should cooperate with them to form a government. Four arrested in alleged voter bribery case Four men were arrested on Thursday and were being questioned by the Lahav 433 major crimes unit over an alleged voter bribery scheme, Israeli police said. The arrests followed the detention of three southern Bedouin men on election day, Tuesday, on suspicion of planning to pay people to vote for Raâam. Raâam has identified the men as party activists and denied the allegations. It remains unclear whether the arrests are connected to the Shin Betâs investigation into suspected foreign interference. The separate bribery case has added to the political controversy surrounding the election. However, the arrests do not by themselves establish that the alleged scheme took place or that foreign actors were involved. Neither Netanyahu nor opposition has a clear majority The election has left Israel facing a difficult coalition-building process. Local media projections put Netanyahuâs bloc at 53 seats, opposition parties at 48 and Arab-led parties at 19 in the 120-member Knesset. A party or bloc needs at least 61 seats to secure a parliamentary majority. Neither Netanyahuâs allies nor the opposition can currently reach that threshold on their own. The Arab-led parties could therefore play a decisive role in determining the next government, even if they do not join a formal coalition. Netanyahuâs Likud party has received the most votes, but that does not automatically guarantee him another term. The president traditionally asks the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government, although this is not a legal requirement. Eisenkot open to cooperation with Arab-led parties Netanyahuâs chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has said he is open to working with Arab-led parties to reach the 61-seat threshold. Ahmad Tibi, head of the Joint List, told Army Radio that the opposition bloc had approached him about replacing the Knesset speaker. He said his party would support the blocâs candidate and urged Eisenkot to show political courage. The Joint List described the election result as an âunprecedented show of strengthâ by Arab voters and praised Jewish voters âwilling to swim against the tide of racism.â Small rallies were held overnight in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Such cooperation would be politically significant. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined an Israeli coalition government. The brief participation of an Arab party in a coalition that year marked a historic departure. Netanyahuâs party is seeking to use the foreign interference allegations to discourage such an arrangement. The opposition, meanwhile, faces the challenge of building a majority without abandoning its central campaign pledge to remove him from power. Final results expected after absentee ballots are counted Final election results could come as early as Thursday evening, once around half a million absentee ballots have been counted. The ballots include votes from military personnel, diplomats, prisoners, hospital patients and others. The votes are not expected to alter the overall result dramatically, according to the available projections. Israelâs election results must be certified by November 4. President Isaac Herzog is expected to task someone with forming the next government the following week. The swearing-in of the new parliament is scheduled for November 10. Eisenkot has warned political actors against using the investigation to influence the timing of the process. If coalition negotiations fail after multiple attempts, Israel could face another election early next year. Herzog has indicated that he wants to avoid that outcome. Political deadlock comes amid deep divisions The election has exposed divisions over security, religion and the future direction of Israel. One major issue is whether the fast-growing ultra-Orthodox population should continue to be exempt from compulsory military service. The question has become more contentious after three years of inconclusive wars and military losses. Netanyahu, Israelâs longest-serving prime minister, remains a polarising figure. He faces corruption allegations and accusations that he delayed a deal to secure the release of hostages held in Gaza for political gain. Israelâs international standing is also at stake following widespread criticism of its treatment of Palestinians in Gaza and growing violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank. Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israelâs population. Their stronger electoral showing has raised hopes among some voters that Arab-led parties could gain greater influence over government policy and parliamentary decisions. âGod willing, we will have something for us in the government, something that will bring us our rights,â said Brosli Elias, a resident of Nazareth. Possible renewed conflict with Iran adds uncertainty The possibility of further strikes against Iran could complicate Israelâs political situation. The Trump administration has spoken of new attacks after the US midterm elections on November 3. Experts have suggested that Netanyahu could use a renewed, large-scale conflict to push for a national unity government under his leadership. Such a development could also delay calls for a public inquiry into the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023, the deadliest extremist attack in Israelâs history, which triggered the war in Gaza. For now, the election investigation, the unresolved parliamentary arithmetic and the dispute over cooperation with Arab-led parties are likely to shape the next phase of government formation.
