title: Nukes, Netanyahu, and November: Tucker Carlson raises nuclear war alarm for Nth time
text: Tucker Carlson has raised eyebrows with his assertion that Trump might order a nuclear strike on Iran's Pickaxe Mountain site TOI Correspondent From Washington: Somewhere in Washington DC, the nuclear clock is apparently ticking. At least according to Tucker Carlson, a former Fox News host and penitent Trump loyalist, who says the U.S President may be hours away from ordering a nuclear strike on Iran under pressure from Benjamin Netanyahu. The target, according to Carlson, is Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified underground complex near Iran's Natanz nuclear facility. âBibi (Netanyahu) calls Trump about it every day,â Carlson quoted an âinformed observerâ as saying in a lengthy post on X, claiming that the Israeli PM is âcornered and desperateâ after last weekâs election results, and he canât form a government unless Trump helps him. "The only military option is a nuclear strike," Carlson wrote, alleging that the Trump administration has quietly rewritten the U.S nuclear doctrine since February to make battlefield nuclear weapons easier to use. Carlson also dragged in India, Pakistan, and other nations into his alarmism. A U.S strike, he warned, would unleash radioactive contamination across the Persian Gulf, potentially trigger nuclear escalation involving Russia, India, Pakistan and North Korea, and bring about World War III. "After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final,â he wrote, without explaining why others would get involved. Carlson has been sounding variations of this alarm for months, suggesting that even Armageddon has trouble keeping appointments. The latest post was greeted with ridicule in serious policy circles despite the adventurism of Trump and his MAGA cohorts. Indeed, there is a rather significant gap between the gravity of the claims and the evidence offered to substantiate it. Neither the White House nor the Pentagon has confirmed a change in nuclear doctrine. Carlson identifies no named American official, produces no documentary evidence and relies on anonymous sources for his central claims. Trump himself told Newsmax in October: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to." Still, U.S hardliners have been raising the prospect of an imminent nuclear confrontation with Iran for months, repeatedly drumming up the bogey of Tehran acquiring nuclear weapons within weeks or months. Carlsonâs own interview in March with former National Counterterrorism Center director Joe Kent was revealing. Asked whether Iran had been on the verge of acquiring a nuclear weapon, Kent replied: "No, they weren't three weeks ago when this started, and they weren't in June either. " He also said there was no intelligence indicating that Iran was about to abandon its policy against developing nuclear weapons. The American bogey of Iran getting nuclear weapons within weeks has now acquired a life of its own with one widely circulated meme features an ancient stone tablet supposedly dating to 1750 BC, bearing the inscription: "Iran is only weeks away from developing nuclear weapons." Another version has archaeologists discovering a 3,000-year-old tablet warning that Persia was weeks away from the bomb. Carlson is also accused of having his own agenda in cranking up the nuclear alarm. Once among Trump's most enthusiastic media champions, he has become one of the most consequential dissenting voices within the MAGA movement, and his break with Trump has been particularly pronounced over Israel and Iran. Carlson has argued that America should not subordinate its foreign policy to Israeli interests or be dragged into another Middle Eastern war. He has attacked Netanyahu's influence in Washington, questioned the rationale for American military intervention and challenged the longstanding assumption among Republican conservatives that supporting Israel is an unquestionable article of faith. The nickname "Qatarlson", popularised by his critics, including Laura Loomer and other pro-Israel conservatives, suggests that his criticism of Israel reflects Qatari influence rather than independent conviction. There are also larger ideological divisions at play here. One faction of MAGA believes America First means resisting foreign entanglements, particularly wars undertaken for Israel; another regards unwavering support for Israel as integral to U.S national security and conservative politics. Carlson has become a lightning rod in that battle, with critics accusing him of trafficking in conspiratorial anti-Israel rhetoric, while supporters view him challenging standard establishment thinking. title: Blue wave meets red flag: On cusp of big win, Democrats face internal sabotage
text: Rep. Haley Stevens (AP Photo) TOI Correspondent From Washington: Just when Democrats in America were beginning to entertain thoughts of a blue wave, possibly even a blue tsunami, along came Haley Stevens to remind them that nobody is quite as capable of complicating Democratic fortunes as a Democrat. In an extraordinary convulsion barely 48 hours before Tuesday's midterm elections, the Democratic Michigan congresswoman, who lost a bitter party primary (inner party election) to progressive Abdul El-Sayed, crossed the political aisle to endorse his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, in what would be called a last minute âdefectionâ in Indian political parlance. The immediate political damage is difficult to quantify, but the optics and the timing â coming just when many polls are showing a Republican rout â could hardly be worse for Democrats, who are trying to persuade voters that they are united and ready to take back control of Washington. Instead, one of their own has provided Republicans with a ready-made advertisement for Democratic disarray. MAGA boss Donald Trump immediately jumped on the break, praising her âbravery. â The Stevens-El-Sayed rupture had been simmering since a bitter August primary,, which El-Sayed won by less than one percent. It was not simply a case of a disappointed politician nursing wounded ambitions within the party; the two represent sharply different constituencies and political instincts, particularly over Israel and the Gaza war. Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, was bankrolled by the so-called âJewish lobby.â El-Sayed, a progressive son of Egyptian immigrants, campaigned on a more critical position towards Israeli policy and US military support for Israel. The primary exposed fault lines between pro-Israel Dems and the party's vocal progressive wing, and the schism is now threatening to play out nationally, undercutting polls pointing to a big win. Stevens initially endorsed El-Sayed after losing -- albeit without much enthusiasm -- but the truce was always more a marriage of political convenience than a true reconciliation. The trigger for the final explosion was an ad by El-Sayed supporters linking U.S financial support for Israel to the rising cost of groceries. Stevens considered the advertisement antisemitic and demanded that El-Sayed disavow it. He eventually rejected the ad's contents, but the dispute had gone personal by then, with El Sayed, likely emboldened by polls showing he was leading by 10+ points, torching a planned joint church appearance with Stevens and asking her to take a walk. She walked -- over to Republican candidate Mike Rogers. Such election-eve defections being rare in America, Democratic leaders were aghast, even as Trump and his flock welcomed her. Democratic Party boss and NY Senator Chuck Schumer, who had backed Stevens during the primary, called her decision a "despicable betrayal," while furious party flacks like James Carville used gross reproductive metaphors to warn her that Republicans would use her and discard. Democratic partisans are still hoping that a NYT/Siena poll showing the party leading in all seven crucial Senate -- five of them by +5 percent â--can withstand the last minute Stephens torpedo. The numbers are unbelievable for Dems, particularly in Kansas and Texas, where they have not won a Senate seat in decades. Even allowing for polling error, the geographical breadth of the Democratic advantage suggests a national political environment hostile to Republicans. Still, the Dem are nervous, and the feeling is not entirely irrational. The party has repeatedly discovered that the electorate it sees in surveys is not necessarily the one that turns up at polling stations. Donald Trump's political career has been built, in considerable measure, on voters who are difficult for traditional polling models to capture: less politically engaged people, rural and small-town voters, working-class whites, and those who are reluctant to identify openly with MAGA and some of its nativist and racist agenda. The 2016 election remains the defining example. Hillary Clinton's 97 percent winning certainty evaporated in the industrial Midwest and boondocks America, where Trump mobilised voters who had been insufficiently represented in polling samples and turnout assumptions. Even in 2024, Dems were surprised by the extent of Trump's support among working-class voters, including sections of the electorate that had previously been part of their coalition. This is the so-called hidden Trump voter: somebody who may not be particularly enthusiastic about the Republican Party, may not even like Trump personally, but will turn up to vote Republican when sufficiently motivated. There is another complication: Midterm elections generally have a different electorate from presidential contests. Older, more habitual voters tend to dominate, while younger and less politically engaged voters are more likely to stay home. That will favour Republicans if the Democratic advantage in current surveys â captured by a range of pollsters from Nate Silver to NYT, from Emerson College to Marist University â does not translate into actual turnout. Republicans, meanwhile, have their own problems. Trump's economic message of unprecedented prosperity is difficult to reconcile with voters worried about grocery bills, tariffs and household expenses. His rallies, which many now see as entertainment, may fill arenas but they do not necessarily fill ballot boxes. The most important question on Tuesday will therefore not be whether Democrats are ahead in the polls, which they are. It will be whether their lead survives the transition from the pollster's carefully constructed likely-voter sample to the rather less predictable business of actually voting. You use AI every day. title: Tel Aviv tells
text: Israel is deeply divided after the October 7 attacks. Netanyahu may stay in power, and fighting with Iran could begin again. The election results in Israel have revealed a deeply divided country. Even after more than 84% of the votes had been counted, neither of the two main political groups had won enough seats to form a government on its own. Benjamin Netanyahuâs Likud-led group was expected to win 54 seats, while the group led by challenger Eisenkot was expected to win 47. Arab political parties were also heading for a historic result, possibly winning 17 seats in the new Parliament, called the Knesset. Because no group had a clear majority, political leaders could spend weeks trying to build a government together. During this period, Netanyahu would continue as caretaker Prime Minister. Interestingly, this situation might suit Netanyahu just fine. Some experts believe he may have expected such an outcome. The election was really a test of whether Israelis wanted Netanyahu to continue leading the country. Supporters and opponents of Netanyahu were almost equally divided. This division reflects how Israeli society has changed since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. In the past, left-wing political groups had a stronger presence. Today, right-wing politics, especially those influenced by religion and Jewish nationalism, has become much more powerful. Even Netanyahuâs opponents face a problem. Some of them have promised not to work with Arab political parties, although joining forces with these parties might be their best chance of removing Netanyahu from power. This is one of Netanyahuâs biggest political successes. He has helped move Israeli politics towards the right. He has also encouraged the idea that opposing his government means supporting Israelâs enemies. This has made it harder for his opponents to unite and has divided the public even further. Arab citizens make up nearly one-fifth of Israelâs population. Their growing support for Arab political parties also shows how sharply divided the country has become. Meanwhile, the idea of a Two-State Solution â creating an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel â is becoming harder to achieve, even though many countries support it. Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank face a difficult situation. Their political leadership is divided between the Palestinian Authority, which has struggled to make progress, and Hamas, an armed group that refuses to accept Israelâs existence. This conflict also helps Netanyahu politically, because he can present himself as a leader who will protect Israel from its enemies. Arab governments in the region also seem increasingly tired of dealing with the Palestinian issue, even though many ordinary Arab citizens continue to care deeply about Palestinian rights. The election therefore points to a new reality: Netanyahu remains the central figure in Israeli politics, and the country is deeply divided over him. There is also a risk that the conflict with Iran could start again. US President Donald Trump has supported Netanyahu and said they need to âfinish the jobâ they started. If Netanyahu stays in power and Trump emerges from the US midterm elections with his political position weakened, tensions in West Asia could rise again. The big worry is that Israelâs political deadlock, combined with the rivalry between Israel, Iran and the United States, could lead to another round of fighting in an already troubled region. Speaking to Israeli television after voting wrapped on Tuesday night, Ra'am chief Mansour Abbas said: "I believe we can overcome the difficulties ... and I think that most voters for the (Eisenkot) bloc do want to see (a) govt with the Ra'am party." He said senior members of Eisenkot's bloc had discussed a possible deal with him even before the election. "Everyone is talking to us, not just the change bloc. A few days ago, a very, very senior member of the right approached me. " Eisenkot ruled out forming a govt with any of the Arab parties during the campaign, citing what he called a lack of shared values, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state. Netanyahu's Likud party confirmed it would not negotiate with any Arab party to try to form a govt. "Not a chance," spokesman Guy Levy said at the party's headquarters in Jerusalem. "It's not even a question that should be asked." Who is Mansour Abbas? Mansour Abbas (52) is an Arab-Israeli politician, dentist and leader of Ra'am. Elected to Knesset in 2019, he reshaped Arab politics by advocating a pragmatic, domestic-focused approach. Instead of making engagement conditional on the wider Israeli-Palestinian conflict, he prioritises civil gains for Arab citizens, focusing on crime, socioeconomic inequality, infrastructure and municipal funding. He also briefly served in an Israeli ruling coalition from 2021 to 2022. What is Joint List? Joint List is an alliance of Arab-majority parties in Israel, formed in 2015 to unite the vote of Arab citizens. It includes Ahmed Tibi's Ta'al and has historically brought together secular, nationalist and left-leaning parties such as Hadash. It campaigns on civil equality, tackling crime in Arab communities and ending the occupation, and has backed govts from outside rather than joining them. How are Arabs placed in Israel Arab citizens of Israel, who often identify as Arab Israelis or Palestine citizens of Israel, comprise 20% of the population, or roughly 2.1 million people. They are central to the medical sector. Data from Israeli ministry of health and Taub Center for Social Policy Studies in Israel show Arabs account for over 20% of physicians, nearly a quarter of nurses and almost half of licensed pharmacists. Two Arab citizens have served as Supreme Court judges, while Arab engineers, scholars, writers and athletes, have visible public roles. Arab parties' past support For decades, Arab parties provided outside support to governments. Cabinet representation was limited to individual appointments, including Druze lawmaker Salah Tarif in 2001, Labor's Raleb Majadele in 2007, and later Issawi Frej and Ayoob Kara. title: âDespicable betrayalâ: Top Democrat slams Haley Stevens for backing Republican candidate over El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race
text: Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate El-Sayed. A Democratic congresswoman in Michigan has endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her party's nominee Abdul El-Sayed, triggering a political storm within the party just before the US midterm elections. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary in August, announced her support for Rogers on Sunday after appearing alongside him at a church service in Detroit. Her endorsement came amid a rising bitter public feud with El-Sayed, who had reportedly asked her to stay away from a planned joint campaign appearance. "Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing her decision. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today." The move drew sharp criticism from Democratic leaders, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling it a "despicable betrayal". Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel accused Stevens of abandoning the values she claimed to support. El-Sayed, however, sought to play down the development, telling reporters that he was focused on issues affecting voters, including the rising cost of living. "At the end of the day I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding that "none of this matters". What led to Stevens' break with El-Sayed? The rift between the two Democrats has deepened since the August primary, reflecting wider divisions within the party over its political direction and US support for Israel. Stevens, a centrist Democrat and strong supporter of Israel, had called on El-Sayed to condemn an advertisement by an independent left-wing group linking US support for Israel to high grocery prices. El-Sayed criticised the advertisement and said it was not produced by his campaign. In a statement on Friday, Stevens said El-Sayed should stop blaming Israel for economic problems facing Michigan residents. "Abdul promises to get money out of politics," she wrote. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford." El-Sayed responded by accusing Stevens of trying to reopen a primary contest that had ended months earlier. He also said he did not agree with the advertisement. The two were originally expected to appear together at a church event on Sunday alongside other Democratic leaders in an effort to demonstrate party unity before Election Day. However, the planned joint appearance was called off, with Stevens instead attending a service with Rogers. Democrats react as Trump praises endorsement Stevens' decision also triggered turmoil within her own office. Her longtime chief of staff resigned following the announcement, while other staff members were expected to leave, according to a person familiar with the developments. "We are shocked and heartbroken," an aide said in a statement. Hertel said the endorsement showed that Stevens had "abandoned everything she claims to care about", while Schumer publicly condemned her decision to support the Republican candidate. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, praised Stevens, describing her move as an act of bravery and highlighting her support among Black and Jewish voters in Michigan. Speaking at a campaign rally in Iowa, House Speaker Mike Johnson also said he had spoken to Stevens after the endorsement and encouraged her to keep speaking out. Rogers welcomed the congresswoman's backing, saying he was honoured by her support. Why the Michigan Senate race matters The contest between El-Sayed and Rogers is among the closely watched Senate races in Tuesday's midterm elections. The seat is currently held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, and Republicans have not won it since 1994. Michigan is a key battleground state, having backed Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election before voting for Trump in 2024. For Democrats, holding the seat is crucial to their efforts to regain control of the Senate. The party needs a net gain of four seats to secure a majority, making Michigan one of the most consequential contests in the election. Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighbouring Oakland County during the August primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters. The primary was marked by bitter exchanges and heavy outside spending, including support for Stevens from a super PAC affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. title: Kamala Harris returns to campaign trail for US midterms amid speculation over 2028 presidential bid
text: Former US vice president Kamala Harris. Former US vice president Kamala Harris has returned to the campaign trail to support Democrats in closely contested races ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, as speculation grows over whether she will make another bid for the White House in 2028. According to news agency Reuters, Harris, the Democratic Party's 2024 presidential nominee, is campaigning in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. She has made relatively few public appearances this year but is now stepping up efforts to help Democrats challenge Republican control of Congress. Harris began her campaign tour in Las Vegas on Tuesday, criticising President Donald Trump and his administration over what she described as its cruelty and incompetence. Speaking alongside Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, she addressed members of the Culinary Workers Union. "We got a serious fight in front of us," Harris said, accusing the Trump administration of being corrupt, callous and incompetent. Ford, Nevada's first Black attorney general, is seeking to become the state's governor. Harris said his election would make him the first Black governor west of the Mississippi River. Harris continued her campaign appearances in Mississippi, where she rallied supporters of Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom in Columbus. Colom is attempting to become the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from Mississippi since 1982. He is facing Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in a closely contested race, Reuters reported. Addressing supporters, Harris encouraged young people not to let others' doubts limit their ambitions, drawing cheers from the crowd. Harris' popularity remains divided along party lines Harris' return to the campaign trail comes as both parties seek to mobilise voters ahead of the midterms. Trump has also been travelling across the country to campaign for Republican candidates facing competitive races. However, Harris continues to face challenges in winning support beyond the Democratic base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in June found that 39 per cent of Americans viewed her favourably. Her approval was significantly higher among Democrats, at 82 per cent, compared with 7 per cent among Republicans and 33 per cent among independents. Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee, said parties typically turn to their most prominent figures towards the end of an election campaign. "At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters," Kamarck was quoted as saying by Reuters, adding that this was the reason Harris and Trump were campaigning for their respective parties. Will Harris run for president again in 2028? Harris could emerge as one of the leading contenders if she decides to seek the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028. However, her political record includes two unsuccessful presidential campaigns. She lost to Trump in the 2024 election, while her first presidential campaign ended before the Democratic primaries began in 2020. A potential 2028 bid would also bring renewed scrutiny of the events surrounding the 2024 election, when then-president Joe Biden abandoned his re-election campaign amid concerns about his age and mental fitness, leaving Harris to take his place as the Democratic nominee. Harris later criticised Biden's decision to seek a second term as "reckless" in her memoir, 107 Days, named after the length of the presidential campaign she inherited. She has also become more vocal about the Biden administration's approach to Israel's war in Gaza. This month, Harris criticised the Israeli government's "horrific conduct" and said the US should have acted sooner and more forcefully. Harris says 2026 midterms come first Harris has not ruled out another presidential run, but she has repeatedly emphasised the importance of the upcoming midterm elections. During an appearance on the video podcast Baby, This Is Keke Palmer this month, actor Keke Palmer asked Harris whether she would run for president again. "Oh, girl, come on!" Harris replied, laughing. "I haven't decided yet." She then stressed that the immediate priority was the midterm elections. "2028 don't matter if we don't do 2026 right," Harris said. Her return to the campaign trail is likely to keep her in the political spotlight as Democrats seek to regain congressional ground and potential candidates begin positioning themselves for the next presidential election. title: Economy, not ideology
text: . When populists and autocrats lose, is the vote on political theory or economic reality? Thereâs a view, supported by research, that democracy is in danger. Per Swedenâs V-Dem Institute, the average person has about the same democratic freedoms now as in 1978. So, itâs tempting to read election results from Brazil and Serbia as an endorsement of democracy. In Brazil, voters narrowly denied Flavio Bolsonaro, a candidate with undisguised authoritarian tendencies, and gave Lula another term. In Serbia, they roundly defeated strongman Aleksandar Vucic. The Serbian result has got outsized attention â itâs a country of just 65L people and $112bn GDP â because the winning side is a student protest movement, fronted by academics, doctors, etc. Yet, this may not be the democratic revival many are hoping for. Rather, as Harvard Prof Steven Levitsky pointed out in 2024, such results could chiefly be anti-incumbency. Even Lula in Brazil lost the first round to Bolsonaro, before staging a spirited fightback. The trend has been clear since 2020, when Covid, and economic disruption, led govts to adopt easy-money policies. The resultant inflation worked for billionaires, but left the middle class, and everyone below, worse off. Levitsky noted that citizen distrust and discontent were running high, and in 41 of 55 polls between 2020 and 2024, the incumbent lost: âalmost certainly a product of and part of Covid inflationâ. Were young Serbians, who campaigned against Vucic for two years, fighting for an ideology or their economic future? Weâve seen how Labour won a landslide in UK, only to become unpopular within months. In Germany, Social Democrats arenât in a happy place either. Or look at US, which ousted Trump, a populist, for Biden, only to vote him back four years later. And now, with US midterms scheduled for Nov 3, it looks like Americans will pounce on the chance to clip Trumpâs wings in Congress. Why? Because, far from addressing their cost-of-living crisis, as he promised, heâs worsened their economic pain with the war on Iran. Israel, another test case for democracy, votes today. And while polls donât show Netanyahu winning outright, whoever wins is unlikely to go soft on Palestinians. In fact, young Israelis, first-time voters, donât appear to have much sympathy for Gazans either. What they are weary of is endless war and psychological hardship. And corruption. People everywhere are asking elected leaders, âWhat have you done for us, for our future?â And incumbents are losing because they usually donât have a convincing answer. title: âNo fine, no admission of wrongdoingâ: University of North Carolina strikes deal with Trump to end 18 probes
text: Members of the University of North Carolinaâs diverse student body make their way through campus The administration of US President Donald Trump has reached a settlement with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC) to close 18 federal investigations into alleged race discrimination and antisemitism at the university. The voluntary agreement does not require any monetary payment, and UNC has not admitted to wrongdoing or liability. The deal, which remains in effect until the end of 2028, allows the university to retain its eligibility for federal funding. It comes amid the Trump administrationâs broader crackdown on universities over pro-Palestinian protests against Israelâs military campaign in Gaza, diversity initiatives, transgender policies and climate programmes. Watch WATCH: Trump Stumped By Macronâs Iran War Attack Amid France Protests Unc to introduce mandatory antisemitism training Under the agreement, UNC will appoint an internal administrator and establish a coordinator position within its compliance office to address discrimination, including antisemitism. The university has appointed Elizabeth Hall, associate vice chancellor for university compliance, to fill both roles. She will also serve as the point of contact for the Justice Department and oversee the universityâs reporting obligations. The settlement requires mandatory antisemitism training for students, faculty and staff. It also prohibits face masks or coverings that conceal an individualâs identity during protests and states that student groups may face disciplinary action for antisemitic discriminatory conduct. Trump has accused pro-Palestinian protesters of antisemitism and supporting extremism. However, protesters, including some Jewish groups, have argued that opposition to Israelâs occupation of Palestinian territories and its military campaign in Gaza is not inherently antisemitic, and that advocating for Palestinian rights does not amount to supporting extremism. UNC will also be required to submit complaints involving antisemitism and race discrimination to the US Justice and Education departments every quarter. Unc must maintain non-discriminatory admissions policies The agreement requires UNC to maintain non-discriminatory admissions policies and prohibits the use of racial proxies. However, the university can consider how applicants have overcome personal adversity and take into account aspects of their family backgrounds, such as poverty, provided these factors are applied consistently. The settlement follows the US Supreme Courtâs 2023 decision to strike down race-conscious admissions programmes at Harvard University and UNC, effectively ending the use of affirmative action in college admissions. Other universities have also reached settlements with the administration. Columbia University agreed last year to pay more than $200 million to resolve federal investigations, while Brown University agreed to pay $50 million to support local workforce development. title: UN agency World Food Programme to cut food aid to Gaza as funding crisis threatens millions

London's Metropolitan Police said most of the arrests were related to people expressing support for a proscribed organisation. âOfficers remain at the scene and are continuing to make arrests," the police said in a statement, the Associared Press reported. More than 100 people took part in the demonstration, with several holding placards reading, âI oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.â Some protesters applauded and chanted âfree, free Palestineâ as those arrested were taken to police vans. A separate vigil in support of Palestine Action was held outside the US Consulate in Edinburgh, Scotland. Demonstrators carried placards similar to those seen in London. The protests came ahead of a November 4 hearing at the Supreme Court in an appeal against the UK government's decision to designate Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation. Supporters of the group have criticised the ban as draconian, arguing that it violates freedom of speech. Under UK law, membership in or support for a proscribed organisation is a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison. title: Iran claims downing US drone over Bandar Abbas after Trump hints at renewed strikes

The arrives came after the US President Donald Trump hinted at the possibility of renewed military action against Iran as early as Sunday, while leaving open the possibility of a diplomatic agreement. Speaking to reporters after casting his ballot in Florida on Saturday, Trump said Iran wanted a deal to reopen the waterway but questioned whether Tehran would honour any agreement. âDo you really think I would tell you that? title: Oil prices today: Crude falls over 1% as Iran-Qatar talks raise hopes of diplomatic progress
text: Representative image Oil prices fell more than 1% on Monday as Iranian and Qatari officials held talks for a third consecutive day aimed at securing an agreement to end the US-Israeli war on Iran, easing some immediate concerns over supply disruptions. Brent crude futures declined $1.59, or 1.40%, to $111.84 a barrel by 0011 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell $1.56, or 1.50%, to $102.56 a barrel, according to Reuters. The decline followed a strong rise last week, with Brent ending October at its highest level in six months amid concerns that the conflict between the US, Israel and Iran could escalate again after Tuesday's US midterm elections. Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade, said the fall reflected a technical correction after last week's gains, alongside hopes of progress in diplomatic efforts. "Oil is seeing a technical pullback this morning after last weekâs strong gains," Waterer said, as quoted by Reuters. "Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now." However, he cautioned that the market remained alert to the possibility of stronger rhetoric over Iran, which could push Brent crude towards $120 a barrel after the midterm elections. Iran-Qatar talks and Strait of Hormuz disruptions The latest price movement came as Iranian and Qatari officials continued consultations aimed at facilitating an agreement to restart direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the "ongoing and progressing" discussions was to continue consultations with Qatari mediators. He added that Tehran was prepared for "both defence and diplomacy". The diplomatic efforts are taking place against the backdrop of attacks on oil tankers travelling through the Strait of Hormuz, which have pushed up global energy and shipping costs. The waterway is a key route for global oil shipments, and disruptions to tanker movements have remained a concern for energy markets during the conflict. Opec+ keeps December output targets unchanged Meanwhile, the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, a grouping known as Opec+, kept their December production targets unchanged on Sunday. The decision was in line with market expectations and indicated that the group would not make further policy adjustments until next year, as it continues to face export disruptions linked to the Iran war. Separately, Saudi Arabia increased its crude oil exports in October compared with September, despite attacks by Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthi forces on its energy infrastructure, Reuters reported, citing two of three ship-tracking companies. The developments in the Gulf, the outcome of diplomatic efforts involving Iran and Qatar, and the possibility of renewed military escalation after the US midterm elections remain key factors for oil markets. title: Indian-origin woman Srishti Tarana Sharma charged in US over pro-Palestine intimidation campaign at Michigan university
text: Indian-origin Srishti Tarana SharmaÂ  charged in US over pro-Palestine threats at Michigan university/Image: AP An Indian-origin woman, Srishti Tarana Sharma, 23, is among four additional people charged in a federal investigation into alleged threats, vandalism and intimidation targeting Jewish organisations, University of Michigan officials and businesses perceived to have links to Israel. US Attorney Jerome F Gorgon Jr announced the new charges, taking the total number of defendants indicted in the case to 12. The other newly charged individuals are Henry David MacKeen-Shapiro, 23, Aaron Hunter Vonbargen, 25, and Joseph Mark Fisher, 23. According to the US Attorney's Office, two of the newly charged defendants, MacKeen-Shapiro and Vonbargen, were arrested last week and are due to make their initial court appearances. The remaining two, including Sharma, are still at large. The investigation centres on alleged conspiracies to intimidate the Jewish Federation of Detroit, University of Michigan leadership and law enforcement personnel, as well as businesses considered to have connections with Israel. As per the superseding indictment, the defendants and other alleged co-conspirators developed plans to pressure the university and private-sector organisations into cutting any perceived ties with Israel following the October 2023 Hamas attacks. Prosecutors allege that the group threatened further retaliation and escalating criminal activity if its demands were not met. The indictment also claims that members used encrypted messaging services, social media platforms and overseas collaboration tools to identify targets and coordinate their activities. The alleged incidents included spray-painting threats, smashing windows and throwing glass jars containing noxious chemicals into family homes. Investigators also allege that the suspects marked homes and workplaces with symbols associated with Hamas, including red handprints and inverted red triangles. The indictment further alleges that photographs of the incidents were subsequently shared on social media alongside additional threats. Prosecutors say the posts were intended to intimidate the immediate victims and send a warning to other members of the community who support Israel. Those allegedly targeted included the Jewish Federation of Detroit, two University of Michigan regents, other university officials, a university police lieutenant, a student and two businesses perceived to have links to Israel. Commenting on the latest charges, Gorgon said the alleged threats against Jewish communities and public officials were part of a wider pattern of intimidation. âThese alleged attempts to terrorize our Jewish community and government officials are nothing new,â he said. title: After losing their home in Gaza, a Palestinian potter turned clay into dome-shaped shelter for his parents as shortages of cement and steel stall reconstruction
text: After spending two years living in a tent, Palestinian potter Jaafar Atallah decided to turn the very earth beneath his feet into a home for his parents. With cement and steel difficult to obtain in Gaza, he gathered around 15 people, collected local clay and experimented with mud bricks until they managed to build a dome-shaped dwelling. The Financial Times reported on Atallahâs effort in June 2026, describing how his familyâs traditional pottery skills had become a way to seek shelter amid widespread destruction and shortages of construction materials. For Atallah, the project was about more than building walls. It was an attempt to give his parents a measure of protection and dignity after their home was destroyed during the war. The dome drew on a familiar shape from his familyâs pottery tradition: the bread ovens they had made for generations. This time, however, the structure was large enough for people to live in. Watch âNO FASCISM HEREâ: Ben Gvir Heckled As Anti-War Demonstrators Target Netanyahu Ahead Of Elections From pottery to building homes Atallah had earned his living making bowls, vases and other pottery items using clay found near his home in northern Gaza. The war destroyed the familyâs home and pottery factory, forcing them to relocate and rebuild their lives elsewhere in the territory. After enduring life in a tent, he began exploring whether the same material used in his craft could help create a more substantial shelter. With help from family members and other workers, including his father, who was also a potter, he collected clay and shaped it into bricks. The process was not straightforward. The team experimented with different mixtures and tested several prototypes before finding a combination that could hold together. The mixture included clay, water, ash and powdered glass. Atallah also developed a waterproof glaze for the bricks, attempting to make the structure more resistant to the elements. The result was a domed clay dwelling that the team described as strong enough for a person to stand on top of it. The construction offered an alternative to the fragile tents in which many displaced Palestinians continue to live. Atallah explained the practical difference in an interview with the Financial Times, saying that food could be stored in the clay structure, unlike in a tent where fresh produce could spoil quickly in the summer heat. He described the heat inside tents as torture, underscoring how extreme weather compounds the hardship of displacement. A housing crisis with few alternatives Atallahâs initiative comes amid a severe housing crisis in Gaza, where years of bombardment have damaged or destroyed homes, public infrastructure and businesses. The Financial Times and Asharq Al-Awsat reported that shortages of essential construction materials, including cement and steel, have pushed residents towards improvised methods of repairing or rebuilding shelters. According to UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, Israel has restricted the entry of construction materials into Gaza, calling them 'dual-use' mateirals and citing concerns that items such as cement and steel could be diverted by Hamas for military purposes, including tunnel construction. The restrictions have left residents and humanitarian organisations struggling to find materials for reconstruction. Israeli authoritiesâ security rationale and the consequences for civilian housing are central to the wider dispute over rebuilding the territory. According to figures cited in the Financial Times report from the United Nations, around 1.9 million people in Gaza were displaced or living in tents. Many shelters lack adequate sanitation and basic utilities, leaving families exposed to heat, cold and flooding. With conventional construction materials scarce, residents have turned to whatever they can recover locally. Some collect stones and concrete fragments from destroyed buildings, while others reuse steel reinforcement bars or make mud-based mortar. These approaches may help protect a tent or repair a damaged wall, but they are not a substitute for a comprehensive reconstruction effort. The Norwegian Refugee Councilâs Gaza shelter coordinator, Iyad Abu Hamam, cautioned that recycled concrete does not achieve the strength required for many building applications. The improvised use of rubble and mud therefore has significant limits, particularly when it comes to roofs and structures that must meet safety standards. Turning rubble into a resource Atallah is not the only Gazan trying to find building materials in the remains of destroyed homes. Teenage sisters Tala and Farah Moussa have been experimenting with bricks made from crushed concrete debris, mud, ash and powdered glass. Their idea emerged after their own house was bombed. The sisters, who had been displaced multiple times with their family, began crushing concrete into smaller pieces and testing different mixtures to make usable blocks. After five or six prototypes, they developed a mixture suitable for applications such as pavements and partitions. In May 2026, the sisters won a youth innovation award from the Swiss-based Earth Foundation, receiving $12,500 that they hoped to use to organise workshops and teach others their technique, according to the Financial Times and Asharq Al-Awsat. Their work reflects a broader effort to reuse materials that would otherwise remain part of Gaza's enormous rubble piles. However, the sisters' bricks and Atallah's clay structures should not be mistaken for fully tested replacements for conventional construction materials. Builders have also salvaged steel reinforcement bars from destroyed buildings, although corrosion can limit their usefulness. Others have collected cement that reportedly surfaced in the Maghazi area after Israeli forces pumped material into a tunnel to seal it. Sharing a possible way forward Atallah's project has attracted attention beyond his immediate community. After he shared videos of the construction process online, pottery groups around the world offered support. The videos also helped spread the idea that locally available clay could be used to create shelters when conventional supplies were unavailable. Khalil Abu Ramadan, a social media personality known for making clay sculptures, documented the construction and helped promote the approach. Atallah subsequently began working on another clay home for himself and his wife. The aim is to encourage other families to explore similar methods. For people living in tents, the prospect of a more substantial shelter is compelling, particularly when temporary accommodation offers little protection from extreme temperatures or other hazards. Yet building with locally available materials is not necessarily inexpensive. Even clay, rubble and other resources can involve considerable labour and costs in Gaza's wartime economy. Nor does a dome's apparent strength establish that it can withstand every structural or weather-related risk. Hope amid the destruction As per a New York Times report, efforts such as Atallah's within a broader picture of Palestinians attempting to rebuild their lives. Even after a ceasefire agreement, residents have continued to face destruction, displacement and uncertainty. Families are trying to restore livelihoods, children are attending makeshift classrooms, and communities are searching for ways to reclaim everyday routines. The clay homes represent one small part of that struggle. They cannot replace the scale of reconstruction required across Gaza, but they demonstrate how traditional skills and locally available materials can be adapted to meet urgent needs. For Atallah, pottery has taken on a different purpose. The clay that once supplied his family's livelihood is now being used to create shelter for those who lost their home. His work offers a glimpse of what rebuilding can look like when families cannot wait for conventional supplies to become available. The larger challenge remains unresolved: improvised homes can provide some relief, but lasting recovery will require safe access to construction materials, adequate infrastructure, technical expertise and the resources needed to rebuild damaged communities. title: Israel poll results deadlocked amid historic showing by Arab parties
text: File photo: Benjamin Netanyahuâs (left) Likud party faces Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party. Anxious Israelis watched election results near completion Wednesday, as no clear winner emerged and weeks of negotiating could lie ahead for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an array of opposition parties trying to unseat him. Arab-led parties put up a historic showing, but it's not clear if the other opponents of Netanyahu's far-right govt would form a coalition with them for a majority of seats in parliament. Issues around the Palestinians and their descendants remain sensitive in Israel. In defiant comments - which showed his Likud party losing ground since 2022 election - Netanyahu dismissed the idea of partnering with Arab parties as treasonous. He won't work with the Arab-led parties, whose constituents make up 20% of Israel's population, and they have also ruled out any partnership. His top challenger, centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has left the door open to partnering with Arab parties under certain conditions, including their recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and of Hamas as an extremist group. Emerging results indicated that neither Netanyahu's nor Eisenkot's coalition blocs would reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in 120-seat Knesset. Media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties and 19 for Arab-led parties. With 85% of votes counted, Bibiâs party has 20.8%, Eisenkotâs 16.1% Israeli voters choose parties, not individuals. With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahuâs Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkotâs Yashar party has 16.1%. Arab-led parties had 14.9%. Itâs not clear whether some of Eisenkotâs likely partners who have ruled out such an alliance will change their minds to force Netanyahu from office. Counting absentee ballots will last until Thursday evening. There are an estimated half-million of them from military personnel and diplomats. Nearly 78% of voters turned out, the highest since 1999. Voting reflected unease over Netanyahuâs alliance with the far-right and anger in a war-weary nation over military draft exemptions for the significant ultra-Orthodox Jewish population. The Likud partyâs share of the vote declined from 23.4% in 2022. But results suggest opponents were unable to capitalise on the grief caused by the Hamas-led Oct 7, 2023, attack to decisively push him from office. One far-right partner losing support was national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. For many Israelis, he represented the worst strain of Netanyahuâs govt, openly taunting Palestinian detainees. Vote-counting suggested Likud would remain the largest party and most likely to be tapped to form a govt by Israelâs president, Isaac Herzog. The president, however, isnât required to task the leader of the party holding the most seats. âWe must do everything we can, to avoid another round of elections,â Herzog said. title: From Tehran's pupils to missile makers: Why Houthis are a bigger threat now
text: Iran has supplied weapons, money and training to the Houthis, formally known as Ansar Allah, for more than a decade. Tehran has denied arming the group in violation of a United Nations arms embargo. Houthi rebels in Yemen are becoming less dependent on Iranian weapons after years of training and technical assistance from Tehran. This is allowing the group to assemble its own drones and missiles, posing a growing threat to Saudi Arabia as the US-Iran war strains regional air defences and depletes stocks of missile interceptors. The shift has become increasingly significant after Houthi attacks on Riyadh international airport and the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi Arabia's defences. Weapons and regional experts say the group's growing ability to produce its own weapons could make it harder to contain, even if Iranian supply routes are disrupted. Iran's strategy: Teach the Houthis to build weapons Iran has supplied weapons, money and training to the Houthis, formally known as Ansar Allah, for more than a decade. Tehran has denied arming the group in violation of a United Nations arms embargo. However, according to a report by news agency Reuters, Iran has also helped the Houthis develop the skills needed to assemble their own weapons. This includes drones and missiles made using dual-use components, which can serve both civilian and military purposes. Andreas Krieg, a senior security studies lecturer at King's College London, said Iran's Revolutionary Guards and members of the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah initially helped the Houthis understand missile systems and how to operate them. "Former Yemeni military engineers and a growing generation of locally trained specialists have helped institutionalise these capabilities," he said. "Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted." The strategy was designed to ensure that the Houthis could continue developing their military capabilities even if they lost access to direct Iranian supplies. "The Revolutionary Guards were forward-looking. They looked at what happened if the Houthis couldn't receive equipment or weapons directly (from Iran), or if these were seized by US-allied forces," said Hamid Nikou, a former political advisor to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Nikou said the strategy included teaching the Houthis how to assemble dual-use parts to make drones and even ballistic missiles. "Iran has basically taught the Houthis how to fish," Nikou said. Iranian analysts say this has made the Houthis one of Tehran's most cost-effective and valuable military proxies. Chinese components add to Houthi capabilities The Houthis are also diversifying their sources of weapons components, reducing their reliance on equipment supplied directly by Iran. Conflict Armament Research said in a report this week that the group was attempting to manufacture advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using components shipped from China. Yemen's internationally recognised government seized one such shipment. "China has emerged as a particularly important commercial source, while Iran continues to provide specialised military technology, technical expertise and components that are difficult to obtain commercially," Krieg said. The development could complicate efforts to restrict the Houthis' weapons programme. Intercepting shipments and disrupting supply routes may not be enough if the group can obtain components through commercial channels and assemble weapons locally. The Houthis have also reportedly explored the use of artificial intelligence to improve their weapons. Anthropic said last month that "a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen" had used its Claude AI assistant to help develop software for a guided rocket, a planned ballistic missile with a range of more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) and a missile variant incorporating a hypersonic glide vehicle. These reported efforts point to the group's ambitions to expand its capabilities. They do not, by themselves, establish that all the weapons described have been successfully developed or deployed. US-Iran war puts Saudi air defences under pressure The Houthis' expanding capabilities come as US allies in the Gulf face mounting pressure on their air defences. Since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, the United States has used large quantities of missile interceptors to protect its bases and allies, including Israel and Gulf countries. The depletion of these stocks has added to the challenges facing Saudi Arabia as it confronts the Houthi threat. Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute, said Saudi Arabia's air-defence network was not yet as sophisticated as those of Israel or Ukraine. "Saudi Arabia, in terms of the sophistication of the military and the development of an integrated air defence network, is not really yet at the level of either Israel or Ukraine, and it just has a very tough job to do," he said. Saudi Arabia's size also makes it harder to defend against aerial attacks than Israel or a US military base, Sabet added. The latest attacks have raised concerns about the kingdom's ability to protect strategic infrastructure. They also threaten Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract foreign investment and diversify its economy beyond oil. Years of conflict have made the Houthis more capable The Houthis' growing military capabilities reflect years of conflict and adaptation. The group has fought Saudi-backed forces in Yemen since 2014. The civil war settled into a fragile ceasefire in 2022. After Israel's assault on Gaza in 2023, which followed deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel, the Houthis began firing rockets at Israel and targeting commercial shipping in the Red Sea. The subsequent US-Iran war reignited the conflict in Yemen, by which time the group had gained further operational experience and diversified its supply chains. "They haven't been sitting still," Sabet said. "They were basically diversifying their supply chains... and as they gain operational experience, they're able to make those weapons more sophisticated." The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis has said it intercepted several missiles fired at Saudi cities and destroyed 127 Houthi weapons storage facilities and launch platforms. Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said the group had acquired advanced military technology with help from "regional actors". This included ballistic missiles, drones and fast boats carrying explosives. The growing challenge for Saudi Arabia and its allies is that disrupting weapons shipments or destroying launch sites may not be sufficient to neutralise a group that is learning to manufacture and improve its own weapons. Speaking at a memorial ceremony for Israelâs first president, Chaim Weizmann, Herzog said the results were an established fact and called on political leaders to âstop climbing up trees and face realityâ. Herzog is scheduled to receive the certified election results from the Central Elections Committee on November 4, after which he will begin consultations with party representatives at the Presidentâs Residence. The newly elected Knesset is due to be sworn in on November 10. Eisenkot has said he intends to use the oppositionâs parliamentary majority to establish what he described as a âZionist and statesmanlike governmentâ. The willingness of the Arab factions to recommend and support an opposition candidate could strengthen that effort, but the refusal of several Zionist parties to sit in a coalition with them remains a significant obstacle. title: India, Israel vote against Pakistan-backed UN arms control resolution: What it means
text: In a significant move, India and Israel opposed a UN resolution proposed by Pakistan and Belarus concerning regional arms control. India and Israel have voted against a Pakistan- and Belarus-sponsored draft resolution at the united nations seeking conventional arms control at regional and subregional levels, with New Delhi arguing that national security concerns cannot be restricted by geographical boundaries. The draft resolution, titled âGeneral and complete disarmament: Conventional arms control at the regional and subregional levelsâ, was adopted by the UN general assemblyâs First Committee on Monday, receiving 180 votes in favour, two against and no abstentions. According to the news agency PTI, India and Israel were the only two countries among the 193 UN member states to oppose the resolution. Explaining India's position, Anmol Sher Bedi, first secretary at India's permanent mission to the UN, maintained that conventional arms control was a global issue and should not be addressed primarily through regional and subregional frameworks. âWe are not fully convinced that it should be pursued primarily in regional and sub-regional contexts,â Bedi said while presenting India's explanation of vote before the UNGA first committee. He added that New Delhi's opposition was in line with its consistent position on the matter. Watch 'Hindus And Jews Vs Muslims': Asim Munir's Twisted, New Anti-India Plot In Tehran Exposes Pak India also raised questions over the resolution's call for the UN disarmament commission to develop principles that could provide a framework for regional agreements on conventional arms control. âWe read this request with a certain degree of curiosity,â Bedi said, pointing out that the commission had already reached three consensus-based outcomes on related issues. These included guidelines and recommendations on regional disarmament adopted in 1993, guidelines on conventional arms control and disarmament finalised in 1999, and recommendations on practical confidence-building measures concerning conventional weapons agreed upon in 2017. âThat makes three consensus outcomes on this very subject in the very body now being asked to start from scratch,â he said. Questioning the need for further discussions, Bedi said it was difficult to understand why an issue that had already undergone extensive deliberations needed to be taken up again, unless the intention was to keep the UN's disarmament machinery occupied. India also criticised the resolution's emphasis on maintaining a balance in defence capabilities within regional and subregional settings. Bedi argued that the approach wrongly presumed that countries' security interests were confined to their immediate geographical neighbourhoods. âThis assumes that the security concerns of States politely stop at their regional borders. They do not,â he said. He further stressed that national security considerations often extend beyond narrowly defined regional boundaries, adding that the idea of maintaining a military balance within a particular region or subregion was unrealistic. The resolution argues that conventional arms control should primarily be pursued at regional and subregional levels, as most threats to international peace and security in the post-Cold War period have emerged among countries within the same geographical regions. Separately, India voted against a paragraph referring to conventional arms control proposals concerning South Asia. The paragraph took note of initiatives undertaken in various regions, including consultations among certain latin American countries and proposals for conventional arms control in South Asia, while acknowledging the importance of such measures for regional security. The resolution further states that militarily significant countries and nations possessing greater military capabilities have a special responsibility to advance agreements aimed at strengthening regional peace and security. title: Australia eyes Israelâs Iron Dome: Why is Canberra building a missile shield?
text: Israelâs Iron Dome is a short- to medium-range air defence system developed by Israeli defence company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems (Photo: AP). Australia is considering acquiring missile interceptors developed for Israelâs Iron Dome as part of efforts to establish an air defence system, officials told a parliamentary committee on Thursday. Defence officials said Australia aimed to have a ground-based missile defence system in place by the early 2030s, citing lessons from rapidly changing warfare in Ukraine and the Middle East. The options under discussion include the US Patriot missile defence system and interceptor missiles developed by Israeli defence company Rafael Advanced Defence Systems for Iron Dome. The interceptors have recently been used in a new system developed for the US Marine Corps and are jointly manufactured with US company Raytheon, AFP reported. The Iron Dome Israelâs Iron Dome is a short- to medium-range air defence system developed by Israeli defence company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. According to Rafael, the system has recorded more than 10,000 successful interceptions since 2011, with a success rate exceeding 90 per cent. It is designed to intercept a range of aerial threats, including rockets, artillery shells, mortars, cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The company says the system can operate in different weather conditions and respond to multiple incoming threats simultaneously. Watch Project 18A: Indiaâs â¹75,000 Crore Plan for Bigger, Deadlier Next-Gen Navy Destroyers The Iron Dome Iron Dome system is part of a wider family of air defence systems that includes C-Dome, its naval variant, and I-Dome, a mobile configuration. These systems are designed to protect civilian population centres, military forces, maritime assets and strategic infrastructure. According to the company, Iron Domeâs architecture can be integrated with other sensors and command-and-control systems as part of a layered air defence network. Rafael also says the United States Marine Corps selected the system to strengthen its expeditionary air defence capabilities. Truck-mounted, medium-range interceptors were tested by the US Marines in Guam in June during a regional military exercise that Australia also participated in, AFP reported. Australia does not supply weapons to Israel, and potential purchases of Israeli defence equipment have come under political scrutiny. âThe government will always seek to deliver the most suitable military technology,â government minister Murray Watt told the committee when asked about the issue. Air Marshal Robert Chipman said the defence force would make recommendations to the government next year following a competitive selection process linked to the Talisman Sabre military exercise in 2027.

title: What if the next US president turns hostile? Netanyahu's answer lies partly in India
text: Warning of hostile US prez in future, Bibi seeks India alliance Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has warned that a future US president could be hostile towards Israel, calling for new alliances with countries such as India and nations in Latin America to safeguard his country's strategic interests. Netanyahu unveiled his security doctrine on Sunday, nine days before Israel's October 27 election, arguing that Israel must prepare for a possible shift in Washington's approach. His remarks came hours before US President Donald Trump publicly endorsed his re-election bid. Watch 'NETANYAHU HAS FAILED ISRAEL!': Massive Protests Erupt Against Bibi Over War And Election Anger "In two years, a President, man or woman, could come to power who is very hostile to Israel," Netanyahu said. "How would you deal with that? How would you operate in relation to the United States? And beyond that, what solutions would be necessary?", he questioned. The Israeli premier stressed that his government must make the most of the remaining years of Trump's presidency while preparing for an uncertain political future in the US. "First, we must do everything we can during these two years, and during the following two years, in the American arena, through good times and bad," he said. Netanyahu also called for Israel to broaden its network of international partners, pointing to India as a key ally beyond the US. "The second thing is to create other alliances. That is what I am working on now with many countries in our region and outside it. India is not a small country, and there are many others," the Israeli Prime Minister emphasised. He also pointed to shifting political dynamics in Latin America as an opportunity to expand Israel's diplomatic reach. "There is a major shift in Latin America, and there could be an enormous change in Brazil in just a few days," Netanyahu said, adding, "We must expand our pool of alliances and develop capabilities that make us valuable to everyone." Netanyahu has repeatedly cited his relationship with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and India's ties with Israel to counter perceptions that his country is becoming diplomatically isolated. In May this year, amid a prolonged war and growing international criticism, he described the relationship with India as "unique", calling the country a "huge power" where there is "crazy love" for Israel. Netanyahu's US dilemma Netanyahu's warning comes amid concerns in Israel over declining support among Democrats in the US. Analysts have attributed some of the strain to his strained relations with Democratic presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden. Those tensions have also featured in Netanyahu's political messaging. He has presented his willingness to challenge American presidents as a sign of a strong leader prepared to defend Israel's interests, a strategy analysts believe has helped him politically over the years. Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister. Rival slams security doctrine Netanyahu's presentation drew sharp criticism from Gadi Eisenkot, his main challenger in the upcoming election. The former Israel Defence Forces chief dismissed the announcement as a political exercise that offered little substance as the country continued to face security challenges. "Nine days before the election and three years after the gravest failure and disaster in Israel's history, with every war front still open, Netanyahu decided to present his 'security doctrine' to the public," Eisenkot said. "Two hollow pages, full of slogans that have nothing whatsoever to do with a security doctrine, reveal more than anything the strategic vacuum Netanyahu has left the State of Israel in and his disregard for the security of Israeli citizens," he said. Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of using fear and political messaging to influence voters ahead of the election. "This is Netanyahu's method: manipulating perceptions, frightening people and trying to divert attention from the parade of lies and racism surrounding his campaign tonight," he said.
