title: 3 years after October 7 Hamas attack: A scarred Israel, a devastated Gaza and a Middle East no longer the same
text: Israelis mark the October 7 anniversary in Israel as Gaza continues to bear the warâs devastating toll Three years after Hamasâs October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the shockwaves of that day continue to shape lives, politics and security across the Middle East. What began as a devastating assault on southern Israel grew into a prolonged war in Gaza and then widened into a regional confrontation involving Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran and Iran-backed groups. Watch October 7, Three Years Later: How The Hamas Attack Reshaped The Middle East The conflict has left behind two deeply traumatic realities - the Israeli experience of the attack, hostage-taking and continuing security fears, and the Palestinian devastation caused by the war in Gaza. Beyond the immediate human cost, the conflict has also altered alliances, weakened Iranâs regional network, changed Israelâs military calculations and disrupted diplomatic efforts across the region. For those who lived through October 7, however, the consequences are not measured only in geopolitical shifts. They remain embedded in ordinary moments, places and memories, reminders of a day that transformed the meaning of safety, freedom and home. âThe smell of hell.â That is how one Israeli resident describes what a barbecue now smells like. Living close to Gaza, Deganit Bar Hay told AP the smell of burnt flesh has become a trigger, making it difficult for her to barbecue. Benny and Maggy Solomon, parents of Oct 7 victim Hila Solomon, attend a memorial at the Nova festival site in southern Israel (Credit: AP) Along the highway running parallel to the Gaza Strip, where people were gunned down while trying to flee on October 7, memorials now stand beside the road. Cars smashed and riddled with bullets have been preserved elsewhere, stacked in rusting heaps. Portraits of young female military spotters, whose warnings about a possible attack were disregarded, mark another set of lives lost that day. For those who survived the attack and those who were taken hostage, the meaning of ordinary life changed too. âFreedom has completely changed the way I see life,â Emily Damari, who was abducted wounded from her home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza and released in January 2025, told Reuters. After captivity, she said, even opening a refrigerator or drinking cold water felt like something to be grateful for. âBeing free, at home, surrounded by my family and my people is something I will never take for granted again.â Eli Sharabi, taken hostage from nearby Kibbutz Be'eri, spent 491 days in captivity. His wife Lianne and daughters Noiya and Yahel were killed in the October 7 attack, while his brother Yossi was taken hostage and died in Gaza. Released in February 2025 emaciated after what he said was prolonged hunger, shackling and beatings, Sharabi told Reuters: âI choose life. I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do. â Three years later, those memories remain raw in Israel. But there is another landscape of memory just across the border. In Gaza, children are growing up with different reminders of the same war - lost parents, amputations, displacement, damaged homes and years without anything resembling a normal childhood. DW reported the stories of 15-year-old Mahmoud Abu Shadaq, recovering from injuries caused by an airstrike, and eight-year-old Layan Abed, who lost her father during the conflict. Aid groups are providing rehabilitation and mental-health support, but the scars are likely to outlast the fighting. That is the paradox at the heart of the three years since October 7. One attack produced two vastly different but deeply traumatic legacies - the Israeli trauma of the assault and hostage-taking, and the Palestinian devastation that followed Israel's military campaign in Gaza. And the consequences did not stop at Gaza's borders. What began with Hamas's assault on southern Israel became a war in Gaza, then a wider confrontation involving Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran and Iran-backed groups across the region. It has altered Israel's security doctrine, weakened Iran's regional network, unsettled Arab states, disrupted diplomacy and pushed the Middle East into a new and still uncertain balance of power. Three years on, the question is no longer simply what happened on October 7. It is what October 7 set in motion. October 7, 2023: Day the âironâ wall broke Just before 6.30am on October 7, 2023, Israelâs much-vaunted âiron wallâ along Gaza began to fail. Explosives dropped by drones knocked out communication towers and remote-controlled guns, while snipers targeted sensors and cameras. Israeli defenders were left staring at blank screens as roughly 2,200 rockets rained towards southern and central Israel. A minute-by-minute look at how the October 7 assault broke through Israelâs border defences. Then came the breach. Hamas fighters cut through the 20-foot-high fence or blew openings into it. Motorbikes, pickup trucks and bulldozers poured through, followed by hundreds of armed men. Others arrived on motorised paragliders. About 30 breaches were eventually made, allowing an estimated 1,500 fighters into Israel, The Guardian reported. It was more than a fence being breached. It was the collapse of an assumption â that Israelâs technology, intelligence and military superiority had made a large-scale assault from Gaza almost impossible. âWe have decided to put an end to all of the occupationâs crimes,â Hamas commander Mohammed Deif announced as the attack began, declaring the âal-Aqsa delugeâ. Within hours, the assault had turned deadly. Fighters stormed military positions and nearby communities, reaching the Supernova music festival, where at least 260 people were killed and others taken hostage. In kibbutzim such as Beâeri, residents barricaded themselves inside reinforced rooms as gunmen moved through the communities. At Zikim, soldiers at a military base were overwhelmed before reinforcements arrived. Files, images, and data analysis are unavailable until usage resets tomorrow at 2:01â¯AM. Continue chatting with text only, or upgrade for more access. The scale of the failure soon became clear. Israeli intelligence had detected increased communications activity among militants in Gaza before the attack. Egyptian security services had also warned of an impending event. But Israeli officials assessed the activity as connected to a military exercise and decided that the alert level did not need to be raised, The Guardian reported. Three surveillance balloons used to monitor the border had also broken down and had not been replaced. The result was a catastrophic intelligence and preparedness failure: a border designed to keep Gaza's militants out became a route into Israel, while the forces meant to respond were caught unprepared. For people inside the communities along the border, the technological failure quickly became intensely personal. In Nirim, resident Eldad Hess and his family hid inside a reinforced shelter as gunfire erupted outside. âTen minutes later we heard automatic rifle shots outside the house,â Hess told The Guardian. âI understood what was happening but in my heart I couldn't believe what was happening.â His family survived. Others did not. By late morning, Israel had declared war. At 10.34am, Israeli strikes began hitting Gaza. At 11.35am, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Israelis: âCitizens of Israel, we are at war. Not an operation, not a round â at war.â The language of the conflict changed almost as quickly as its geography. The attack had begun as a meticulously planned assault on southern Israel. Within hours, it had become the opening act of a war that would transform Gaza, redraw Israel's security calculations and eventually pull much of the Middle East into its orbit. Palestinian children walk amid the rubble of buildings destroyed during Gaza war (Credit: Reuters) Gaza became war's price, and its unfinished question The military campaign that followed October 7 devastated Gaza. Entire neighbourhoods were destroyed, millions were displaced and a generation of children has grown up amid death, injury and uncertainty. The humanitarian crisis became one of the defining consequences of the war. Even after a ceasefire agreement in October 2025 secured the release of the remaining hostages and hundreds of Palestinian prisoners and detainees, the larger Gaza question remained unresolved. According to Reuters, Israeli strikes have continued despite the ceasefire. Gaza's health ministry says at least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the truce, while Israel says its strikes target Hamas and accuses the group of trying to rearm and carry out attacks. Hamas denies the accusation. Meanwhile, Israel's effective control over Gaza has expanded to around two-thirds of the enclave, Reuters reported. The advance of the Israeli-controlled âyellow lineâ has squeezed Gaza's roughly 2 million residents into a shrinking coastal area where many live in tents or damaged buildings. The numbers tell one part of the story. The more difficult question is what happens next. Trump's plan envisaged Hamas disarming, Israeli forces gradually withdrawing, an International Stabilization Force taking over security and a new Palestinian technocratic administration governing Gaza. None of those pieces has fully fallen into place. The proposed force has a commander and commitments from several countries but has yet to be assembled. A Palestinian technocratic governing body appointed in January has yet to enter Gaza. Hamas has indicated a willingness to hand its weapons over for storage under a US-backed Palestinian administration, but Israel has rejected any withdrawal before complete disarmament. And reconstruction is barely beginning. A $2.45 billion plan announced by the Board of Peace in September is dwarfed by an EU-UN estimate of $71.4 billion needed for recovery and reconstruction over the next decade, Reuters reported. The war may have ended in parts of Gaza. The question of what Gaza becomes has not. Even after years of war, the biggest questions over Gazaâs governance, security, disarmament and rebuilding remain open The war crossed the fence, then crossed borders The first major regional spillover came from Lebanon. Hezbollah, Iran's most powerful regional ally, entered the conflict, opening another front along Israel's northern border. What had been a long-running Israel-Hezbollah confrontation now became part of the October 7 war. Then came Yemen. The Houthis attacked Israel and targeted shipping in the Red Sea, turning a conflict thousands of kilometres away into a threat to one of the world's busiest maritime corridors. US and British military action followed. Iran-backed groups in Iraq and Syria also became part of the wider confrontation. The significance was larger than the individual attacks. October 7 demonstrated that a war involving Israel and Hamas could activate an entire network of armed groups built over decades. And then the network itself began to fracture. Iran's âaxis of resistanceâ stopped looking invincible Before October 7, Iran's regional influence appeared formidable. Hamas governed Gaza. Hezbollah possessed a vast arsenal in Lebanon. Bashar al-Assad remained in power in Syria. The Houthis controlled large parts of Yemen and threatened shipping lanes. Behind them stood Iran, whose missiles and nuclear programme had long been central to Israeli and Western security calculations. Three years later, that picture has been transformed. Hamas lost its top leadership, including Yahya Sinwar, who was killed by Israel in October 2024. Hezbollah suffered major losses. Assad is no longer in power in Syria. Iran's own territory has come under direct Israeli and US military attack. âThe old order â Iran as the region's disruptive spine, its proxies as the tools of pressure and deterrence â is gone,â Bilal Saab, a Chatham House fellow and former Pentagon official, told The Washington Post. Ali Vaez, director of the Iran Project at the International Crisis Group, put the change more starkly: âThis has changed the region forever.â But a weakened Iran does not automatically mean a more stable Middle East. The conflict widened from Gaza to Lebanon, the Red Sea, Iraq, Syria and eventually direct Israel-Iran confrontation Shadow war finally came into open For decades, Israel and Iran largely fought without declaring a conventional war against each other â through proxies, covert operations, assassinations, cyberattacks and strikes on Iranian-linked targets. October 7 accelerated the collapse of that distance. The confrontation increasingly moved from the shadows into direct exchanges of missiles and drones, exposing the limits of the old system of indirect deterrence. For Israel, the result has been a dramatic increase in military dominance. A former senior Israeli military official told The Washington Post that, despite the continuing trauma of October 7 and the ongoing war, Israel had reached a position few had imagined possible. âWe are still traumatized from 7th October. There is still war,â the official said. âIsrael is not untouchable, but we have made it very expensive to touch us.â That may be Israel's biggest strategic transformation since the attack: October 7 produced not only a determination to prevent another such assault, but a willingness to use overwhelming force far beyond its immediate borders. Israel won battlefield. What does it do with power? Military dominance brings its own dilemma. Israel's neighbours may have welcomed the weakening of Iran and its allies, but the emergence of an Israel with fewer regional constraints has also created unease. âThe focus on security comforts Israelis but unnerves their neighbors,â The Washington Post reported, citing regional analysts. An Israel less constrained by powerful rivals raises questions about whether military superiority could turn into overreach, particularly in the West Bank. Saab told the paper that Gulf leaders, while wanting to see the Iranian regime weakened, also worry about âthe trigger-happiness of Israelâ. Inside Israel, however, the emerging philosophy is increasingly being framed as security through strength. âWhen this is over, I think you're going hear our leaders talk about Israel's desire for peace through strength,â an Israeli official told The Washington Post. âWe are going to fight our enemies as strongly as possible and hug our friends as close as possible.â The shift is significant. For much of its history, Israel's military strength was primarily presented as a shield. After October 7, the war has pushed Israel towards using that strength to actively reshape the strategic environment around it. Whether that creates lasting security remains one of the region's biggest unanswered questions. Palestinians at centre, increasingly without control There is another paradox. The war has put the Palestinian question back at the centre of international diplomacy. Yet Palestinians themselves have little control over what comes next. Gaza has been devastated and its population repeatedly displaced. The future of its governance remains unsettled. In the West Bank, settlement expansion and calls for Palestinian displacement have intensified. The debate over Gaza's future has also exposed sharply different visions. Trump's plan says Gaza should be rebuilt for its people. Israeli right-wing politicians have called for âvoluntary emigrationâ. Israel's defence ministry established an office in 2025 to oversee such departures after Trump had suggested Gazans could be permanently displaced. Trump later backed away from the idea following strong opposition from Arab states and international criticism. The competing visions leave Gaza caught between reconstruction, Israeli security demands, Hamas's future and the unresolved question of Palestinian statehood. The October 7 attack was intended by Hamas to alter the regional balance. Instead, Palestinians have emerged from the war facing a destroyed territory and an uncertain political future. Gulf states no longer just watching from sidelines The war has also changed the calculations of countries that were not direct combatants. Saudi Arabia had been moving towards a potentially transformative relationship with Israel before October 7. The war disrupted that trajectory and pushed the Palestinian question back into the centre of Arab diplomacy. At the same time, Gulf states have had to watch Iran's missiles and drones reach closer to their own territory. Saudi Arabia and Turkey are emerging as important players in the next regional order. Both are deepening relationships with China, maintaining channels with Russia and continuing to work with Washington â a form of strategic hedging as they assess what a more powerful Israel and a less predictable US presence mean for them. The Gulf's old calculation was relatively straightforward: American security guarantees, economic stability and the containment of regional rivalries. After October 7, none of those assumptions looks quite as secure. Three years of war have reshaped the balance of power across the Middle East 3 years on, Oct 7 is still reshaping map The most consequential change may be that the region no longer has the same centre of gravity. Before October 7, Iran's network of armed allies was at the height of its influence. Israel was powerful but largely operated within a familiar system of deterrence. Arab states were cautiously pursuing normalisation and economic integration. The Palestinian issue, while unresolved, had increasingly been pushed into the background of regional diplomacy. The attack shattered that equilibrium. Israel emerged more militarily dominant but also more isolated. Gaza emerged devastated. Iran's regional network was badly weakened, but the collapse of that network created uncertainty rather than a settled alternative. Saudi Arabia and Turkey gained greater room to manoeuvre. Gulf states became more conscious of their own vulnerability. The US remained indispensable but its regional choices became more consequential â and more controversial. The result is not necessarily a new Middle East yet. It is a Middle East in transition. âThis has changed the region forever,â Vaez told The Washington Post. âBut with what consequences still has to play out.â And perhaps that is the clearest measure of what three years of war have changed. For an Israeli survivor, the smell of a barbecue can still bring October 7 back. For a child in Gaza, an airstrike can mean a missing parent, an injured body or another lost home. For Iran, Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and the Gulf states, the same three years have rewritten calculations about power and security. The attack began with a breach in a border fence. Three years later, the breach has become a fault line running through the entire Middle East. From Gazaâs ruins to a global shock The deepest consequences of October 7 are still visible in Gaza, where three years of war have transformed everyday life. Homes, neighbourhoods and essential infrastructure have been devastated, while repeated displacement has uprooted much of the territoryâs roughly two million people. The destruction has extended far beyond buildings. Gazaâs economy has been pushed into collapse, with 92% of economic establishments damaged or destroyed and unemployment reaching 78%, according to UN figures cited in September. Nearly 98% of schools have been damaged or destroyed, while Gazaâs health system has been left barely functioning. For many families, access to water, electricity, shelter, healthcare and education has become a daily struggle. The war has also reshaped the geography of Gaza. Israeli military control and restrictions have pushed Palestinians into increasingly smaller areas, while the so-called Yellow Line has become a new dividing point inside the territory. The result is a population living amid destroyed homes, damaged infrastructure and limited access to basic services, even after the October 2025 ceasefire. But the economic consequences did not remain confined to Gaza or the Middle East. The war disrupted energy markets and global supply chains, with the Strait of Hormuz emerging as a critical pressure point. Around 25-30% of global oil and about 20% of liquefied natural gas pass through the waterway, exposing major energy importers in Asia and Europe to higher fuel and power costs. Shipping disruptions have increased freight and insurance costs, while interruptions to fertiliser supplies have raised concerns over food prices. The shock is particularly severe for poorer countries, where food accounts for a larger share of household spending and governments have less fiscal space to absorb higher costs. Financial markets have also felt the effects, with higher borrowing costs, tighter financial conditions and increased volatility adding to pressures on economies already carrying heavy debt burdens. The IMF has described the shock as global but uneven: energy importers are more exposed than exporters, poorer countries more than richer ones, and economies with limited reserves more than those with stronger buffers. That may be the widest legacy of October 7. The attack began in southern Israel, but its consequences have travelled through Gaza's ruins, across the region's borders and into the world's energy, food, trade and financial systems. Three years on, October 7 is no longer only a date that changed the Middle East. It has become a fault line whose economic and geopolitical aftershocks continue to reach far beyond it. title: US grand strategy falls short of delivering victory in Iran
text: A Patriot missile launcher stands on guard as a B-1 bomber of the US Air Force takes to the air. (Image credit: US DoW) In spite of glaring differences in capabilities of the US-Israeli combine vis-Ã -vis the Iranians, Operation Epic Fury has not led to a victory for the Americans. Somewhere in their planning process, the strategic, political and economic aspects were not enmeshed adequately to arrive at the grand strategy required to achieve victory. A bleak situation has evolved, with Houthis re-entering the fray, and putting under the scanner Saudi Arabiaâs military capabilities. An analysis of the US miscalculations leads to the conclusion, that much as the Americans have achieved militarily, they have not been able to impose their will on Iran. As the shortfalls are studied, itâs also essential to identify major dilemmas that await the Americans at the next turn. American miscalculations impeding evolving of grand strategy Underestimating the Opponents Capabilities. The renowned military thinker Sun Tzu has stated, âIf you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will suffer a defeat.â Incorrect appreciation of the enemy capabilities can be the gravest of flaws in battle. The American assessment of Iranians resilience, especially the ability to absorb loss of top rung leaders, destruction of critical military and industrial capabilities, was flawed. They expected the Iranians to foldup once the decapitation campaign was successful. The resounding success in Venezuela, leading to capture of Maduro in January, 2026, possibly fanned euphoric deductions that proved untenable in Iran. The deduction that simultaneous with a successful decapitation campaign, the Iranians would rise up against an oppressive regime, proved wrong. Iran has a history that goes back thousands of years. It provides the nation a strong foundation and identity. These factors surface sharply to complement national cohesion when a nation is in danger. The US miscalculations are not new, though. When the US led coalition entered Baghdad, Iraq in April 2003, they expected a rousing reception that wasnât quite there. Damage to Global Trade by Denial of Straits. The criticality of Strait of Hormuz was well known before the first American salvoes of missiles, aircraft, drones were released, however, did the Americans evaluate the force required to fully dominate the Hormuz with multi-layered Air Defence cover, physical occupation of its banks, disallowing Iranian minelaying endeavour, and also sustaining such deployment? Further, It doesnât require sinking a super tanker to initiate a spike in freight costs. The insurance companies need barely an assessment of heightened risks to hike their rates. The possibility of Bab el Mandeb further choking global trade wasnât perhaps fully factored into the costs of war. That the Houthis will resurface as a force in being, wasnât possibly fully considered either. US Defence Pacts with Other Nations: The Myths. The US has its bases all over the West Asian region to create a defensive envelope that host countries had mostly taken as an impregnable shield. However, the Iranians have been able to penetrate the shield, fairly successfully. The US bases in the region include those at Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Jordan. These bases have faced Iranian attacks. The faith nations had in the US to be possessing the will and capability to protect allies and partners has been substantially eroded. Disproportionate Costs of Sustaining War. The American economy has produced the worldâs greatest military machine. They have run possibly the best intelligence-based operations that we have witnessed. The flip side of the coin is its cost thatâs straining the worldâs largest economy. When a USD 35,000-dollar UAV of the Iranians triggers the launch of a top end 2.1-million-dollar interceptor of the US Navy, the cost of the war pinches. Admiral Brad Cooper, Commander of U.S. Central Command is on record stating that the Persian Gulf countries are split over their support to a war against Iran. These countries, having allowed the use of the bases to the Americans for striking Iran, invited waves of attacks from the Iranians. Under such circumstances itâs not strange for alliances being stressed, differences arising and well entrenched relationships feeling the tug. Geo Economics: The Tariff Battleground. With a tariff war running the course simultaneously, nations have begun to wonder, which way are geopolitical alliances headed. President Trump has literally opened an economic warfare battlefront against most of the world. The price of a gallon of petrol was already shooting up when his tariff follies hit across geographies for citizens to feel the pinch in procuring their daily bread and butter. title: FREYJA missile shield: Ukraine's new bet against Russian ballistic missiles
text: German soldiers unload the US made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile (SAM) system Ukraine has completed its part of a new multinational missile defence system designed to intercept ballistic missiles, but the programme is still waiting for critical components from European partners before it can move towards testing. The development marks a major step in Kyiv's effort to build an alternative to US-made Patriot systems as Russia continues to intensify missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities. According to Defence News, the system, called FREYJA, is being developed through a coalition of Ukraine and European countries. Ukrainian defence company Fire Point has completed its assigned work on the FP-7.X interceptor and launcher, while European partners are responsible for supplying key technologies, including radar, infrared seekers and command-and-control systems. Watch Putin's Army ANNIHILATES Ukrainian Military Aircraft Mid-Air, 600+ Shot Down In 24 hours | Watch The programme is targeting initial testing by the end of 2026, with battlefield deployment planned for 2027. However, the timeline depends on the delivery and integration of the remaining European components. "Ukraine has done what it was supposed to do, and that is good news," Zelenskyy told journalists, adding that 10 countries were participating in the programme and working on their respective contributions. "People work on systems like this for decades. We want it very fast, because there is no time," he said, highlighting the urgency of developing an indigenous capability to intercept ballistic missiles. Which countries are involved and what are they contributing? The Integrated Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was formally established on July 13, 2026, in Paris. According to the joint declaration published by the Swedish government, its 10 founding members are Ukraine, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. Ukraine is developing the FP-7.X interceptor missile and launcher through its defence company Fire Point. Germany is contributing radar technology through Hensoldt, including its TRML-4D radar, while Diehl Defence is involved in infrared seeker development. Norway's Kongsberg Defence and Aerospace is developing the command-and-control centre. Other potential technology suppliers include Sweden's Saab and France's Thales for long-range surveillance radar, and Denmark's Weibel Scientific and Italy's Leonardo for fire-control radar. These are proposed contributions in the preliminary design, not all confirmed contracts. Poland joined the coalition in September, while Canada has expressed readiness to contribute technology. How FREYJA will work and why Ukraine needs its own missile shield FREYJA is being designed as an integrated ballistic missile defence network combining Ukraine's FP-7.X interceptor and launcher with European radar, tracking, guidance and command-and-control technologies. Its surveillance radars will detect incoming ballistic missiles, while tracking radars monitor their trajectory and relay information to a central command centre being developed by Norway's Kongsberg. The system will use NATO's Link 16 communication standard to connect with Ukraine's wider air defence network, while the Asterix protocol will facilitate radar-data exchange. The initial FP-7.X interceptor is designed to engage threats at an altitude of approximately 20 to 25 kilometres using a blast-fragmentation warhead, with a hit-to-kill version planned for the future. The architecture is modular, allowing components from different manufacturers to be integrated or replaced. Ukraine's push to develop FREYJA is driven by its growing dependence on the US-made Patriot air defence system to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. However, the supply of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors remains limited, with high production costs and growing international demand adding to the pressure. According to Defense News, a PAC-3 interceptor costs approximately $3.8 million, while Ukrainian defence company Fire Point is targeting a production cost of less than $1.2 million for its FP-7.X interceptor in serial production. The shortage has become more pressing after the US-Israel war with Iran depleted an estimated two-thirds of America's prewar PAC-3 interceptor stockpile. With Russia continuing to launch ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and large numbers of drones against Ukrainian cities, Kyiv wants to build a more affordable and sustainable missile defence capability. FREYJA could help Ukraine expand its interceptor supplies, reduce dependence on American weapons and strengthen its domestic defence industry through European technological cooperation.

Neither camp was projected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. As counting progressed, partial results published by the Central Elections Committee showed Netanyahuâs bloc with 57 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 47, with 41.9% of ballot boxes counted as of 5:58 am (local time). However, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have expressed reservations about relying on these parties to form a government. In his election-night speech, Netanyahu reiterated his opposition to a government dependent on Arab-led parties. Eisenkot has indicated he could work with them under certain conditions, a move that could complicate negotiations with other opposition partners. Israeli political analyst Asaf Ronel told news agency Al Jazeera, that the exit polls raised questions about whether opposition leaders would cooperate with Arab-led groups. âThe question now is whether they can let go of their racist elections promise, otherwise the most likely scenarios is that we are back to another round of elections in the next few months,â he said. October 7 and military service shape vote The election was held against the backdrop of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks and the subsequent wars. Netanyahuâs opponents have demanded accountability for the security failures, while his supporters point to Israelâs military campaigns since the attacks. The exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from military service was another major campaign issue. Eisenkot has pledged to end the de facto exemptions, which have become increasingly contentious amid prolonged military mobilisation. Turnout reached 77.7%, according to Israelâs Central Elections Committee, the highest since 1999 and more than seven percentage points above the figure recorded at the same stage in the 2022 election. What happens next? Once final results are announced, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders before asking the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government to assemble a coalition. The designated candidate will initially have 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. If negotiations fail, another candidate could be invited to try. If no government can be formed, the Knesset could be dissolved and fresh elections called within 90 days. Until then, Netanyahuâs government would remain in office in a caretaker capacity. Has it happened before? Israel has experienced repeated political deadlock in recent years. Between April 2019 and March 2020, the country held three elections as parties failed to secure a stable majority in the Knesset. The impasse ended with a power-sharing agreement between Benjamin Netanyahu and his then-rival Benny Gantz, under which the two were supposed to rotate as prime minister. title: Italy's students take to streets over cost of living, dockworkers block arms trade
text: The protests were largely peaceful, despite clashes earlier this month in which demonstrators fought with police, looted shops and vandalised property. Tens of thousands of people, mostly students and workers, took to the streets across Italy on Friday to demand higher wages, better public services and relief from rising living costs. They also opposed increased military spending and the use of ports for arms shipments amid conflicts in the Middle East and elsewhere. The demonstrations were held in more than 40 cities as grassroots union Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) called a 24-hour general strike. The action was part of a wider international campaign by dockworkers against the transport of weapons through ports and for better working conditions. The protests were largely peaceful, despite clashes earlier this month in which demonstrators fought with police, looted shops and vandalised property. In Turin, however, police used a water cannon to push back students and left-wing activists who approached security cordons around the prefecture building. In Rome, a large march passed near the Colosseum. Protesters said they planned to put up tents and stay there over the weekend. Some rubbish bins were placed across streets and set on fire. In Milan, demonstrators marched onto the city's ring road before ending their march outside the Politecnico di Milano university. In Genoa, around 15,000 port workers, students and other demonstrators entered the port. They protested against the use of ports for arms shipments and highlighted the deaths of seafarers in conflicts stretching from the Gulf to the Black Sea. The Italian demonstrations coincided with strikes and protests in several other countries. Unions in France, Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey and Morocco had jointly called for an end to wars in the Middle East, including the conflict in Gaza, and âan end to the militarization of ports.â âPorts must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops,â the joint statement said. âDockworkers do not work for war!â Organisers said more than 100 ports across several countries had joined the campaign. The action was expected to affect operations across Europe, the Mediterranean and North America. In Greece, dockworkers' unions called a strike at Piraeus, the country's largest port. A separate seafarers' strike over pay, working conditions and safety also kept ships docked at several ports, disrupting ferry services. Giorgos Gogos, president of the Dockworkers Union of Piraeus Port Authority, said: âWe donât want to participate in any war, all around the world. We donât want our ports to be hubs of military material, transferred so as to kill people.â In Turkey, protesters gathered outside Istanbul's Haydarpasa port under a banner reading: âNo to war, no to armament!â In France, the CGT ports and docks federation called a one-day strike at major ports, including Le Havre, Marseille, Dunkirk and Rouen. It opposed what it described as the militarisation of port facilities under European policies and French government budget proposals that it said threatened social protections. The scale of disruption remained unclear, with participation expected to range from full-day strikes to shorter walkouts and demonstrations. In Italy, the general strike caused less disruption to transport than anticipated after the government ordered transport workers back to work. Supply chain management company C.H. Robinson warned clients of possible operational disruptions and shipment delays. However, experts expected the impact on global supply chains to remain limited. Marcus Baker, global head of marine, cargo and logistics at insurance broker and risk adviser Marsh, said a 24-hour strike was unlikely to significantly disrupt global trade, although it could affect perishable goods and time-sensitive shipments. He said the action would further complicate supply chains already under pressure from Middle East tensions, climate-related events including El NiÃ±o, restrictions affecting the Rhine and Panama Canal, and shifting tariffs. Judah Levine, head of research at online shipping marketplace Freightos, said the strike could worsen congestion at ports such as Genoa, where vessels already face waits of one to two days for a berth. Ed Anderson, a professor of supply chain and operations management at the University of Texas' McCombs School of Business, said the protests were unlikely to cause outright shortages. âJust one day is not that much in terms of disruption,â he said. title: Israel elections 'stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism': Netanyahu
text: Netanyahu's Likud party accused Arab parties of attempting to undermine the election through alleged criminal activities. title: Netanyahu orders sweeping West Bank offensive after deadly Hebron attack days before Israel election
text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has initiated preparations for a military operation in the West Bank Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered preparations for a sweeping military operation across the occupied West Bank after a shooting near Hebron killed two Israeli soldiers, raising fears of further escalation and widespread restrictions on Palestinian movement just days before Israel's October 27 election. According to The Guardian, Netanyahu ordered security forces to impose a cordon around Hebron and prepare for a wider lockdown of the West Bank following the attack on October 23. The Israeli military said the two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron after failing to reach a nearby highway, where they were suspected of planning an attack on civilians. Watch Iran War: U.S. Quietly Removes Troops From Mideast Bases, Orders Diplomats to Leave Gulf Nation According to a preliminary military investigation, the ensuing gunfight lasted more than 20 minutes and left five Israelis wounded, two of whom later died. Israeli forces subsequently shot and killed both gunmen. Following an emergency meeting with his security cabinet and senior military officials, Netanyahu said Israeli forces would enter the neighbourhood where the attackers lived, evacuate residents and conduct house-to-house searches to seize weapons and dismantle what Israel describes as militant infrastructure. He compared the planned operation with Israel's 2025 military offensive in northern West Bank refugee camps, which displaced tens of thousands of Palestinians, according to the UN human rights office. Israeli forces also began tightening restrictions across the occupied West Bank, with checkpoints and road gates limiting movement between Palestinian towns and villages. The Guardian reported that the closure was the fourth territory-wide restriction imposed by Israel in a month. The measures could disrupt daily life for Palestinians, while roads remained accessible to Israeli drivers, including settlers. The escalation comes just days before Israel's October 27 election, putting security and Netanyahu's handling of Palestinian attacks at the centre of the political debate. Netanyahu can use the response to reinforce his image as a leader who takes a hard line on security, while pressure from far-right coalition partners for a broader offensive adds to calls for tougher action against Palestinians. Reuters reported that opinion polls showed Netanyahu's right-wing coalition at risk of losing its parliamentary majority, with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot emerging as a leading challenger. The October 27 vote is the first Israeli national election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack and the subsequent wars that reshaped the country's security debate. The latest escalation in the West Bank could further intensify the campaign's focus on national security, although Netanyahu's political future will also depend on coalition negotiations after the vote. title: Israel-Britain ties hit new low as Jerusalem consulate loses its diplomatic status
text: A view of the British consulate with signage removed, on the deadline set by Israel for its closure. (Reuters photo) The diplomatic relationship between Britain and Israel has suffered a fresh setback after Israel said the British Consulate in east Jerusalem would no longer function as a consulate, with 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, set to leave the country. Britain, however, said the building would remain open and continue to provide services, with a smaller diplomatic team working from the site. The move marks the latest deterioration in ties between the two long-standing allies. Britain to retain smaller diplomatic presence Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar said the consulate would continue operating with a seven-member diplomatic âtask forceâ and a âvery limitedâ scope of activity. âIsrael will no longer turn its cheek to diplomatic attacks against it," Saar said in a statement to news agency Reuters. The sign outside the consulate was removed, but British officials said the building would remain open. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said it would now âbe known as the UK Mission, Jerusalemâ following discussions with the Israeli government. A small team of diplomats will continue working there, Miliband said. âThis will ensure that we maintain our longstanding British presence and the U.K.âs role in support of a two-state solution,â he added. Britain had previously threatened to expel Israeli diplomats if Israel closed the consulate. London has now decided against that step for the time being, saying it wants to work with Israel to expand its diplomatic presence again. âWe will work in the coming months to build back up our presence,â Miliband said. Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty said British diplomats would continue working on relations with Palestinians and helping British nationals visiting the area. Dispute follows West Bank trade ban The latest dispute follows Britain's decision last month to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The move represented a significant hardening of Britain's position towards Israel. The United Nations and much of the international community consider the settlements illegal. Miliband also rejected Israel's authority to close the British consulate, saying Britain âdoes not accept that the government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, which has been there for nearly 200 years.â He reiterated the British position that east Jerusalem âis occupied territory.â Despite the diplomatic dispute, Doughty said the UK continued to have âa strong and ongoing relationship with Israelâ. Ties strained over Gaza and settlements Britain and Israel continue to cooperate closely on defence and security, but their wider diplomatic relationship has deteriorated over Israel's conduct of the war against Hamas in Gaza and Britain's decision last year to recognise a Palestinian state. The dispute over the consulate comes against the backdrop of the wider Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Israel captured the West Bank, Gaza and east Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war. The Palestinians claim these territories for a future independent state. Israel has since established scores of settlements in the West Bank, which are now home to more than 500,000 Jewish settlers. Many have developed into large residential communities. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government, described as Israel's most nationalist and religious in history, regards the West Bank as the biblical and historical homeland of the Jewish people and considers the settlements important for security. title: Oil prices slip as peace hopes ease supply fears, Middle East tensions limit losses
text: Crude prices relax Oil prices declined on Thursday as traders weighed the possibility of fresh diplomatic developments between the US and Iran against the risk of further supply disruptions from escalating attacks in the Middle East. Brent crude fell by $0.85, or 0.74%, to $114.50 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) dropped $0.91, or 0.89%, to $101.90. The decline pared gains made in the previous session, when Brent advanced 1.3% and WTI climbed 3%. The prospect of a diplomatic breakthrough emerged after US vice president JD Vance sent a letter to Iranian security council chief Mohsen Rezaei in an effort to restart peace negotiations, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter. The possibility of further negotiations has offered some relief to oil markets, but the threat of an intensification in regional hostilities continues to weigh on the outlook for supplies. Concerns include renewed attacks by Yemen's Houthis and the possibility that the US could launch an attack on Iran after its mid-term elections on November 3. Houthi attacks keep supply concerns alive Fresh developments in the conflict involving the Houthis and Saudi Arabia added to uncertainty on Thursday. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired towards the kingdom's eastern region early in the day, with hostilities between the two sides showing no signs of easing. The latest incident followed an attack on Aden airport on Wednesday, according to Yemeni government forces. A day earlier, the Houthis had said they struck Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery with a missile, escalating their attacks against the world's second-largest crude producer after the United States. Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed the reported strike on the refinery, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day. The continuing attacks have kept concerns over potential supply disruptions in focus even as diplomatic efforts offer the possibility of easing tensions. Conflicting signals from US-Iran peace efforts Efforts to find a way to end the war involving the US, Israel and Iran have produced mixed signals. An official briefed on the negotiations said Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft agreement to end the conflict. However, a senior Iranian official rejected the proposals, describing them as unacceptable ideas that did not constitute an offer. Iran's foreign minister said on Wednesday that Tehran was continuing to give diplomacy a chance to succeed. The minister also flagged the possibility of completing Iran's seven-day plan in less than a week if it was adopted. The contrasting positions leave the prospects for a diplomatic resolution uncertain, while the possibility of renewed negotiations has contributed to the downward movement in crude prices. Meanwhile, US inventory data provided another factor for oil markets to follow. The US Energy Information Administration said that energy companies had withdrawn 1.9 million barrels of crude oil from storage during the week ended October 23. Gasoline inventories, however, increased by 3.9 million barrels, against analysts' expectations of a decline of 900,000 barrels. The opposing movements in crude and gasoline stockpiles added to the mixed signals facing oil markets as traders assessed the impact of diplomatic developments, regional attacks and US inventory data on prices. title: As Trump mulls fresh strikes after midterms, Vance writes to Iran, Tehran says 'won't surrender'
text: US-Iran war tensions escalate as midterms approach: Vance writes to Iran; Tehran pushes for 7-day ceasefire NEW DELHI: Iran is pursuing a seven-day plan to secure a ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz as diplomatic efforts intensify amid the possibility of renewed US military strikes after the November 3 midterm elections. US Vice President JD Vance has reportedly reached out to Iranâs security leadership to explore a framework for negotiations, even as Washington warns Gulf allies to prepare for a potential escalation. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Wednesday that Tehran was working with regional mediators to advance the proposal, which Iran had previously conveyed to the United States through Qatar. He said the plan could be implemented in less than a week if the necessary conditions were met. Watch JD Vance-Linked Group In Bolsonaro Poll Probe! Brazil Investigates Alleged Plot Against Lula "While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed," Araghchi said in a post on X. "We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week." The proposal dates back to September, when the Iranian delegation was in New York for the United Nations General Assembly. It has resurfaced following recent diplomatic engagements in the region, particularly Qatar's involvement, according to Al Jazeera's reporting from Tehran. An Iranian security source told Al Jazeera that the plan was not fundamentally new. Tehran has also indicated that the seven-day period could be shortened, suggesting that the central question is whether Iran's demands and conditions can be met. Under the proposal, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen within seven days if conditions, including a ceasefire across the Middle East, were fulfilled. Iran has also demanded the unfreezing of its assets held abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade. Vance contacts Iran's security chief as Washington explores talks The diplomatic push comes as The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance had sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), in an effort to revive negotiations and avert renewed American attacks. The report said the contact was made at the direction of US President Donald Trump. The letter and subsequent discussions between US and Iranian officials focused on exploring a framework for negotiations rather than the details of a comprehensive peace proposal. Separately, US news website Axios reported that regional mediators led by Qatar were pushing for an agreement to restart US-Iran talks and prevent a resumption of hostilities after the November 3 US midterm elections. Trump has not made a final decision on whether to launch fresh strikes against Iran, according to diplomats briefed on the matter and cited by The Associated Press (AP). Washington has warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible "short, intense military campaign" against Iran after the elections, The Wall Street Journal reported. US officials have also urged regional allies to prepare for potential Iranian retaliation against energy facilities and other critical infrastructure. Iran warns of economic fallout from renewed attacks Tehran has warned that renewed military action could have far-reaching consequences for global energy markets, particularly if fighting disrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. âDevastating impact on intâl markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Arabian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers,â Araghchi said in a post on X, referring to discussions at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow. The Strait of Hormuz is a critical shipping route through which around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies previously passed. Iran has restricted maritime traffic through the waterway since the war began in late February and has attacked vessels attempting to cross without its authorisation. The United States, meanwhile, has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports to put pressure on Tehran's economy. Iran has warned that any renewed attack would trigger a broader response. Rezaei has threatened strikes against US-linked infrastructure, including data centres and facilities associated with artificial intelligence. Concerns over the safety of American personnel have also intensified. In a memo dated October 23 and reviewed by Reuters, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran had stepped up efforts to target American personnel and that alleged plots against US citizens had reached advanced stages. "Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel," Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," he added. Trump keeps military option open ahead of midterms Trump has repeatedly suggested that the conflict could end soon while keeping open the possibility of renewed bombing after the November 3 elections. During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the conflict could come âin a couple of weeks, if you donât mind.â âSomebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?â Trump said earlier in the same address. âI said, âWhenever I want it to end.â Itâll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.â The conflict has become a political challenge for Republicans ahead of the midterms, with rising petrol prices adding to voter concerns about its economic consequences. The Pentagon's latest estimate to Congress put the cost of the war to American taxpayers at $47.1 billion. The military situation has also become more complicated as the conflict has spread across the region. Iran-backed Houthi rebels have attacked Saudi oil infrastructure and airports, while a Saudi-led coalition has carried out strikes against Houthi-held territory in Yemen. The United Arab Emirates foreign ministry has urged the parties to âexercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensionsâ and prevent a return to full-scale military operations. Mojtaba Khamenei calls for end to 'neither war nor peace' situation Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei has called for an end to the region's state of 'neither war nor peace', as Tehran prepares for the possibility of renewed military confrontation with the United States and Israel. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the country's cabinet on Wednesday that the government would pursue the implementation of the supreme leader's directive with full commitment and resources, according to Iran's state news agency IRNA. The Iranian cabinet discussed the country's prevailing conditions, strengthening national resilience and countering external threats. Pezeshkian stressed the need for continuous preparedness to deal with different possible scenarios. "All ministers, heads and deputies of the executive branches are obliged to maintain full readiness based on requirements, and use the existing capacities to increase productivity and strengthen the national power," he said. Pezeshkian also called for greater resilience against threats, sanctions and external pressure. "Enemies should not think they can weaken the will of the Iranian nation and force the country to surrender," he stressed. During the meeting, Araghchi briefed the cabinet on diplomatic developments and regional consultations, particularly those involving a visiting Qatari delegation and Pakistan's army chief. The remarks come as Tehran pursues diplomatic efforts to revive negotiations while preparing for a possible confrontation. Vance's reported outreach to Rezaei and the proposed seven-day plan indicate that diplomatic channels remain active, even as Washington keeps the military option open. Whether the proposal can meet Iran's demands, secure a ceasefire and restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains uncertain as the November 3 US midterm elections approach. title: Can Trump defy history? The big battles shaping US midterms
text: A referendum on Trump? Why US midterms matter for his presidency The central question in the US midterm elections is whether MAGA supremo Donald Trump can retain control of Congress or whether voters will hand Democrats the opportunity to challenge his agenda during the final two years of his presidency. With Americans heading to the polls on Tuesday, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up for grabs. Republicans currently control both chambers, but Trump's falling approval ratings, rising living costs and the war with Iran have given Democrats fresh hope of making gains. According to a BBC report, the elections could determine how much freedom Trump has to push his policies through Congress and how effectively Democrats can challenge his administration. Why midterms matter for Trump The midterm elections are traditionally a test of the sitting president's popularity. The party in power often loses seats as voters use the elections to express dissatisfaction with the administration. Trump's approval ratings have added to Republican concerns. According to polling data cited by the BBC, his approval rating began his second term at just over 50% but subsequently fell into the 40s. It dropped below 40% after the US and Israel launched air strikes against Iran at the end of February and currently stands at around 38%. Historically, the president's party has lost an average of 27 House seats in midterm elections since 1934. It has gained seats in only three of the 23 elections held during that period, the BBC reported. Watch Vance Grilled On Cam: âWhy Are Trumpâs Approval Ratings âUnderwaterâ? VP Abruptly Ends Gaggle The political stakes are particularly high because Republicans have only narrow control of the House. A Democratic takeover of either chamber could make it harder for Trump to advance his legislative agenda. House battle: Republicans face a narrow majority The Republicans currently hold 218 seats in the 435-member House of Representatives, giving them a razor-thin majority. All 435 seats are being contested because House members serve two-year terms. Chart explaining the midterms in numbers However, not every constituency is expected to witness a close contest. According to the Cook Political Report, only 18 seats are considered toss-ups, meaning either party has a realistic chance of winning them. Of these, 14 are currently held by Republicans and four by Democrats. Democrats could also take control by winning seats in constituencies already classified as likely or leaning towards them. The narrow Republican majority means even a relatively small shift in voter support could change control of the House. Senate race: Democrats face a tougher challenge The battle for the Senate is more complicated for Democrats. Republicans currently hold 53 of the 100 seats, while Democrats have 45. Two independents also vote with the Democrats. Unlike the House, only about one-third of Senate seats are contested every two years because senators serve six-year terms. This time, 35 seats are up for election. The Senate race The Cook Political Report identifies seven Senate races as toss-ups, six of which are currently held by Republicans. Democrats would need to win four of these seats, along with four seats classified as likely or leaning Democratic, to reach the 51-seat majority. Among the closely watched contests is Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent. Democrats are also targeting traditionally Republican states, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. Texas is another key battleground, where Democrat James Talarico is challenging Republican Ken Paxton. A Talarico victory would give Democrats their first Senate seat in the state since 1988, according to the BBC. Cost of living, healthcare and immigration dominate voter concerns The economy remains one of the biggest challenges for Republicans heading into the elections. Trump had promised to bring down inflation and make everyday life more affordable during his 2024 campaign, but rising costs have remained a major concern for American households. The war with Iran has added to the pressure. Trump had highlighted falling petrol prices in his State of the Union address on February 24, saying prices were below $2.30 per gallon in most states. However, the conflict with Iran began four days later, disrupting energy supplies from the Middle East and pushing petrol prices to around $4 per gallon. Issues in US elections The war has also become increasingly unpopular among Americans. A poll conducted in August found that 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the conflict, the BBC reported. Healthcare and immigration are other major issues shaping the campaign. Democratic candidates have focused on the rising cost of health insurance and concerns over access to healthcare under Trump's policies. Republicans, meanwhile, have highlighted the administration's immigration measures, with Trump pointing to a sharp fall in illegal border crossings as evidence of their success. Can Trump overcome the political headwinds? Despite the challenges, Republicans have an advantage when it comes to campaign funding. According to figures cited by the BBC, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had around $320 million in cash reserves in mid-October, compared with just under $230 million for Democrats. Trump's political fundraising group, MAGA Inc, had an additional $160 million or more at its disposal. Republicans have used their financial advantage to step up advertising ahead of the vote. More than $1 billion worth of political advertisements were aired in September, according to research firm AdImpact. Republicans outspent Democrats by around $200 million and had higher advertising expenditure in nearly all closely contested Senate races. The late campaign push is aimed at mobilising Republican voters and limiting potential losses in both chambers. While the overall political environment appears favourable to Democrats, Trump and his party have previously performed better than expected in elections despite unfavourable polling. What happens after the midterms? The outcome will shape the final two years of Trump's presidency. If Democrats take control of either chamber, they could use their position to challenge his policies, scrutinise his administration and make it harder for Republicans to pass legislation. If Republicans retain control of both chambers, Trump will have greater room to pursue his legislative priorities. The elections will also set the stage for the next presidential race in 2028. With Trump constitutionally barred from seeking a third term, political attention is likely to shift towards the next generation of leadership and what Democrats offer voters beyond opposition to the Republican president. title: A Nevada manganese mine that left arsenic and lead in the ground is undergoing an estimated $257 million cleanup; a 3.5-acre park has now opened on the former site, with more than 3,000 homes planned nearby
text: Nevada mine site gets a new park amid $257 million cleanup and plans for 3,000 homes (Image Credit: Nevada Division of Environmental Division) What was once a mining site associated with potentially harmful industrial waste is now making way for neighbourhood parks, walking trails and thousands of homes. In Henderson, Nevada, a former manganese mine that operated for decades and left behind contamination is being transformed into a large residential community. The opening of Greenbow Park marks a new phase in that redevelopment. According to the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (NDEP), the Three Kids Mine site has been the subject of extensive environmental assessments and a cleanup programme, with the estimated remediation cost reaching approximately $257 million. From wartime manganese production to an abandoned mining site The Three Kids Mine has a history dating back more than a century. Manganese ore was discovered at the site in Clark County, Nevada, in 1917. However, mining operations took place intermittently, including between 1942 and 1943 and again from 1953 to 1961. Manganese was an important industrial mineral, particularly during World War II, when demand increased for materials used in military equipment and steel production. According to the NDEP, an on-site processing mill was constructed in 1942 to meet the renewed demand for manganese during World War II. The mill reopened in 1951, and mining resumed in 1953. Mining continued until the open pits were exhausted, and operations permanently stopped in 1961. The end of mining, however, did not mean the end of the site's environmental problems. Former mine features included open pits, waste rock, an ore yard, processing facilities and tailings ponds. Environmental assessments identified dust, residues and processing waste containing lead, arsenic, manganese and petroleum. The contamination raised concerns about the condition of the land and the work needed before it could be considered suitable for redevelopment. Why the cleanup carries a $257 million price tag The scale of the environmental work is reflected in the estimated cost. The NDEP's November 2023 Record of Decision placed the total estimated cleanup cost at approximately $257.5 million. The wider Three Kids Mine property covers around 1,165 acres, although the former mining operations affected a smaller portion of the site. The area affected by the former mining operations covered approximately 410 acres, distinguishing the contaminated mine area from the larger property earmarked for redevelopment. Environmental investigations and feasibility studies were undertaken to identify contaminants and determine the appropriate remediation measures. The federal Three Kids Mine Remediation and Reclamation Act was enacted in July 2014, creating a framework for transferring federally owned land through the City of Henderson Redevelopment Agency so that assessment, remediation and reclamation could take place. The land transfer was completed in February 2024, while major cleanup activities began in May 2024. The NDEP also established a perimeter air monitoring plan to monitor air quality during the work. The contamination identified at the site was not limited to lead and arsenic. Investigations also identified manganese, petroleum-related materials and other industrial waste. The environmental work therefore involved addressing several types of contamination rather than simply clearing away the remains of the old mine. Greenbow Park brings a new public space to the former mine One of the most visible signs of the transformation is Greenbow Park, a new 3.5-acre recreational space that has opened on the former mine property. According to FOX5 Vegas, the park is part of the Aries master-planned community in Henderson. Its facilities include pickleball courts, playgrounds, shaded gathering areas and more than 3,000 feet of trails. Visitors can also enjoy views of the Las Vegas skyline from the walking routes. The park adds recreational space to an area being developed into a residential neighbourhood. Its opening is significant because the former industrial property is now being incorporated into a community designed around housing, outdoor activities and shared public spaces. Rather than leaving the former mining land as an isolated industrial site, the redevelopment is intended to give it a new role in Henderson's expanding urban landscape. More than 3,000 homes planned across 24 neighbourhoods Greenbow Park is part of a much larger development plan. The Aries master-planned community is expected to include more than 3,000 homes spread across 24 residential neighbourhoods. The redevelopment covers more than 1,100 acres, making it a substantial addition to Henderson's residential growth. The community is being developed on the former Three Kids Mine property, with housing and recreational facilities planned as part of the wider project. The transformation also highlights the challenges involved in bringing previously industrial land back into urban use. Former mining properties can offer substantial redevelopment opportunities, but their conversion requires careful environmental assessment, remediation and long-term planning. There is also an important distinction between the progress of the redevelopment and the environmental project's official status. While Henderson's redevelopment director told the Las Vegas Review-Journal that remediation work had been completed, the NDEP's public project page continues to describe the overall cleanup as ongoing and lists site closure reports and monitoring documents. For Henderson, the opening of Greenbow Park offers a visible glimpse of what the former mine site could become. A property once associated with manganese production and industrial contamination is gradually taking on the appearance of a residential community, with parks, trails and thousands of homes planned as part of its next chapter.

text: The end of BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War marks more than the conclusion of a major anime project. For director Tomohisa Taguchi , it also closes a creative chapter that lasted seven years. After spending years bringing Tite Kubo's celebrated manga back to television, the director is beginning to feel the weight of its conclusion. His latest comments offer a personal look at the emotions behind the anime's final chapter and the changing future of its production studio, Pierrot Films. Tomohisa Taguchi reflects on his seven-year journey with BLEACH For Taguchi, the connection with BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War began long before viewers saw the final episodes. He revealed that the project first came his way around 2019, giving him seven years to work on an anime that has remained close to the hearts of longtime fans. Now that the production has reached its conclusion, the reality of moving on is becoming harder to ignore. In a recent comment shared by Anime Tokki, the director spoke about the emotional impact of watching Pierrot Films move its production focus towards other projects. He said: "Watching Pierrot films shift its production to other projects, the feeling that 'it's really over' has finally sunk in. I was approached around 2019, so I spent 7 years with BLEACH TYBW." His words highlight how much time and creative energy went into bringing the final arc of Tite Kubo's manga to the screen. For audiences, the ending means saying goodbye to Ichigo Kurosaki's latest journey. For the people behind the scenes, it also means leaving behind years of planning, production and collaboration. The director's reaction carries particular weight because BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War was not simply another anime assignment. The revival brought back a franchise that had been absent from television for a decade, creating enormous expectations among viewers who had followed the original series. BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War marks a major chapter for Pierrot Films The final arc has been released in four parts, beginning in October 2022. Each instalment brought viewers closer to the long-awaited conflict between the Soul Reapers and Yhwach's Quincy army. The final instalment, titled The Calamity, premiered on July 25, 2026, with Pierrot Films handling animation production. The studio's involvement also reflects a wider change in its approach to anime production. Pierrot Films was introduced as a dedicated production branch in 2024, with plans to work on manga adaptations aimed at adult audiences as well as original projects. BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War became one of its major productions. The final two episodes were pushed back to October to allow more time for production quality. The concluding episode aired on October 26 in Japan, bringing the Thousand-Year Blood War adaptation to its end. Taguchi's comments offer a reminder that an anime's ending affects more than its audience. Behind every major battle, emotional scene and dramatic reveal is a team that has spent years bringing the story to life. For fans, the conclusion closes an important chapter in Ichigo's story. For Taguchi and the production team, it marks the end of a seven-year commitment. And as Pierrot Films turns towards new projects, the director's words capture the bittersweet feeling of finally moving on from a world that has occupied so much of his working life.
