title: First Mahatma Gandhi statue in North Dakota unveiled at Bismarck's Peace Park
text: First Mahatma Gandhi statue in North Dakota unveiled at Bismarck's Peace Park. The first life-size statue of Mahatma Gandhi in North Dakota was unveiled at Peace Park in downtown Bismarck, the state's capital, in a ceremony attended by the state's first lady Kjersti Armstrong and agriculture commissioner Doug Goehring. The statue was installed with the assistance of the Consulate General of India in Seattle, with technical support from the Indian American community in North Dakota and the North Dakota Trade Office, the consulate said in a press release. The unveiling ceremony began with the national anthems of India and the United States, followed by musical renditions of Gandhi's favourite hymns by school students from North Dakota. Officials from the Bismarck Parks and Recreation District and members of the Indian American community also attended the event. The unveiling took place during the month of Gandhi Jayanti , observed worldwide on October 2 as the International Day of Non-Violence. It also marked the year of Gandhi's 157th birth anniversary. Addressing the gathering, North Dakota agriculture commissioner Doug Goehring highlighted the growing friendship between India and North Dakota. He said Gandhi's message resonated not only with India and the rest of the world but also with people in North Dakota. Goehring described the statue as a symbol of peace and non-violence and recalled Gandhi's timeless message. North Dakota first lady Kjersti Armstrong expressed her admiration for Gandhi, saying it was an honour to celebrate his legacy, which she described as being more important today than it had been in a very long time. Peace Park adds Gandhi statue to public art installations Located at 400 East Front Avenue in downtown Bismarck, Peace Park was developed shortly after the September 11, 2001, attacks. It is also home to a Peace Pole installed by the Gandhi Peace Network of North Dakota, along with other bronze sculptural artefacts. The Gandhi statue joins these installations, adding to the public art heritage of North Dakota's capital city. The consulate described Gandhi's life and message as universal symbols of peace and non-violence. The installation also comes amid growing engagement between India and North Dakota since the establishment of the Consulate General of India in Seattle. According to the consulate, visits by the Consul General to North Dakota in 2024 and 2026 included meetings with the governor, the mayor of Bismarck and leaders from the agriculture, business and education sectors. The consulate has also organised cultural and consular outreach programmes in Fargo, including the International Day of Yoga 2026 and a consular camp in February 2026. Senior delegates from the North Dakota Trade Office also visited India earlier this year as part of ongoing exchanges between the two sides. Fifth Gandhi monument under Seattle consulate's jurisdiction The Bismarck installation is the latest addition to the Consulate General of India's initiative to establish Gandhi monuments across the US Pacific North and Midwest. Watch Mahatma Gandhi Statue Restored: From Attack to Renewal on International Day of Non-Violence Earlier statues were installed at the base of the Space Needle in Seattle in October 2024, at the State Capitol in Lincoln, Nebraska, in December 2024, and at the Mansfield Center at the University of Montana in Missoula in March 2026. Along with the statue installed at Bellevue Public Library in October 2009, the Bismarck monument is the fifth Mahatma Gandhi statue within the jurisdiction of the Consulate General of India in Seattle, the press release said. title: Mimi Chakraborty calls for end to Kolkataâs horse-drawn carriage rides, pushes for electric alternatives
text: Following the death of another frail and severely dehydrated horse that collapsed on a Kolkata road, actor Mimi Chakraborty has appealed for the city's horse-drawn tourist carriages to be permanently replaced with heritage-style electric alternatives. In a letter to the West Bengal Urban Development and Municipal Affairs Minister, Chakraborty, a PETA India supporter, has urged the government to expedite its reported pilot project for electric carriages. She said she was âdeeply shakenâ by the recent horse's suffering and death, despite efforts by people nearby to save the animal. Pic: PETA Citing PETA India's records, she pointed out that at least 19 horses in Kolkata have reportedly died or succumbed to road accidents and other injuries since 2024. The actor also referred to a 2026 incident in which police registered an FIR after a horse pulling a tourist carriage collapsed on the road. Her appeal comes as New York City has passed Romanch's Law, which will phase out its horse-drawn carriage industry by 2028. The legislation honours 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died after jumping from a runaway horse-drawn carriage in Central Park in an attempt to help his mother. His father, Deepak Mahajan, has separately appealed for Kolkata to make a similar transition. The renewed calls have brought the spotlight back on the need for a more humane alternative to horse-drawn tourism in Kolkata. Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. title: Vance sends letter to Iran hard-liner in bid to revive peace talks as Trump threatens strikes: Report
text: File photo: US Vice President JD Vance and Mohsen Rezaei US vice president JD Vance has opened a direct channel to one of Iranâs most powerful hard-liners in an attempt to revive peace negotiations according to a report by the Wall Street Journal. This developments comes even as US president Donald Trump threatens to resume military strikes in the coming weeks. Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iranâs Supreme National Security Council and a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), in an outreach intended to test whether Washington and Tehran can agree on a framework for negotiations. The letter was sent at Trumpâs direction, according to one person familiar with the matter cited by WSJ, and the president is aware of the initiative. Separately, Trump has denied directing Vance to initiate peace negotiations with Iran, saying the vice presidentâs contact concerned medical supplies. âIran needs help with medical supplies. Basically, itâs getting supplies in to help people that are not well,â Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews when asked whether he had instructed Vance to begin peace talks. The effort comes as Trump weighs a short, intense new attack on Iran after next weekâs US midterm elections. Vance is seeking to establish whether diplomacy can avert another round of fighting, though the discussions have yet to produce a detailed peace proposal. Rezaei said last week that Iran would not negotiate with Washington until its core demands were met. The outreach marks a delicate balancing act for Vance, who has publicly backed the war but privately expressed reservations about prolonging it. Before Trump launched âOperation Epic Furyâ in February, Vance argued for more robust diplomacy. Trump later appointed him lead negotiator, and the vice president travelled abroad twice to meet Iranian counterparts in pursuit of an agreement to end the conflict. A memorandum of understanding reached in June collapsed just two weeks after it was signed, amid competing interpretations of how shipping through the Strait of Hormuz would be restored. Subsequent negotiations, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan, have failed to break the deadlock. Washington wants Iran to make nuclear concessions upfront, while Tehran is demanding immediate economic relief. Rezaeiâs emergence as a key interlocutor could also reshape the diplomatic process, potentially sidelining figures such as Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. title: Rare White House visit by top US commander puts Trump's Iran strike options in focus
text: Adm. Brad Cooper and US president Trump The top US military commander in the Middle East held a rare in-person briefing with US president Donald Trump on Thursday to discuss the state of the Iran war, including the effectiveness of Washingtonâs naval blockade and military options for a possible resumption of major combat operations, according to reports by The Wall Street Journal and Axios. Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command (CENTCOM), met Trump at the White House alongside defence secretary Pete Hegseth, joint chiefs chairman General Dan Caine and other senior officials. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent and White House envoy Steve Witkoff also attended, Axios reported, citing two US officials. Cooper briefed Trump on whether the naval blockade was achieving its objectives, the operation to guide oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz towards global energy markets, and the economic pressure campaign being conducted by the military in coordination with the Treasury Department, according to Axios. WSJ separately reported that the meeting covered military options for Iran and came as Washington weighs resuming major combat operations. The rare in-person briefing comes as Trump pursues two tracks: trying to revive negotiations with Tehran while preparing for the possibility of renewed strikes after the US midterm elections. WSJ has reported that US officials have told Arab Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign after the elections. Trump hinted at the possibility of renewed military action last week. âWe may do another little Epic Fury,â he said at a rally, referring to the US-Israeli bombing campaign in the spring. âOr theyâll agree.â Diplomacy continues amid military preparations Regional mediators led by Qatar are trying to prevent a resumption of hostilities after the midterms and steer Washington and Tehran back towards negotiations. âThe mediation is at a very sensitive stage,â a regional source told Axios. Qatari mediators recently delivered a letter from vice-president JD Vance to Iranâs Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, proposing a restart of negotiations while stressing that any talks would have to address Iranâs nuclear programme, Axios reported. The Journal has also reported that Vance engaged the Iranian hard-liner in an effort to revive peace negotiations. Trump and Vance met on Wednesday to discuss a possible gesture of goodwill towards Iran, such as sending humanitarian supplies, including food and medicine, according to a source cited by Axios. title: US lost nearly 10 million acres of forests to development and cropland between 1990 and 2017, with 11 states accounting for 70% of the loss
text: Image: Canva United States deforestation has permanently removed nearly 10 million acres of forest between 1990 and 2017, according to new research on land conversion and forest loss across the country. Woodland cleared for development and cropland disappeared at a pace of as many as 350,000 acres every year, roughly one football field every two minutes, year after year for 28 years. The researchers behind the analysis describe the national scale of permanent forest loss as both significant and increasing, a finding with direct and far-reaching consequences for land conservation, for climate change impacts and for the carbon stored in American trees. How the Forest Monitor separates lasting forest loss from timber harvests and wildfire damage The United States Forest Monitor, built by researchers at Clark University for the Open Space Institute, concentrates on clearing that lasts. According to the Clark University report, it uses annual land cover records from the United States Geological Survey and picks out ground that was forest, became non-forest and stayed that way for at least five years. That conservative filter avoids year-to-year swings in classification. Only conversion to development or cropland is kept, because those uses typically persist for decades, while pasture, shrub, scrub and barren land are excluded since they often revert to forest. The system works at a resolution of 30 metres, roughly one-quarter of an acre per pixel. Development and cropland drive the loss, and the rate is rising again after the Great Recession The two drivers leave very different footprints. Development-driven loss clusters around urban centres and expanding metropolitan and suburban regions, making it easy to spot on a map. Cropland expansion accounts for roughly half of all forest loss nationwide, yet it is spread more thinly across the landscape, so its signature is far less visible. Development-driven loss declined after the Great Recession of 2008, but the researchers point to growing evidence that rates of loss have begun to increase again. They also focus on gross conversion rather than net change, because mature forests generally provide greater ecological and climate benefits than younger ones, and many other monitoring approaches count harvests and wildfires that are often followed by recovery. Image: Canva Hotspots reveal 61 areas of concentrated forest loss, and past clearing points to future losses The analysis identified 46 development-driven hotspots and 15 cropland-driven hotspots, the places where losses are packed most tightly together. Example maps show intensive conversion for development around Raleigh and Richmond, and cropland expansion in areas spanning Alabama and Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina, and Mississippi. Recent conversion often sits close to development and cropland that existed before 1990, which makes past forest loss a good indicator of future loss. Loss outside the hotspots can matter too, particularly where it affects large intact forested areas, and the researchers flag that as a subject for further inquiry. Southern states carry the heaviest burden, with six states responsible for half of all forest loss Half of all conversion occurred in just six states: Georgia, Texas, North Carolina, Florida, Arkansas and Alabama. Adding Virginia, Mississippi, Missouri, South Carolina and Tennessee takes the total to 11 states, and approximately 70 per cent of national loss, and all of the top 13 states are in the southeastern or south central regions. The 10 states with the greatest area lost account for 67 per cent of the national total. Six of the top 20 sit outside the region: Washington, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, New York and Minnesota. Loss rates reach as high as 42,000 acres per year, the equivalent of clearing an area the size of the District of Columbia annually. Measured by share of forest lost, Georgia passes four per cent and Virginia counties lose the most Measured against the forest each state had in 1990, the same southern states dominate, joined by some northeastern surprises. Georgia, North Carolina, Florida, South Carolina, Texas, Arkansas and Virginia appear among the 10 states with the largest percentage of forestland permanently converted, alongside Delaware, New Jersey and Massachusetts. Each lost 2.7 per cent or more of its 1990 forestland, and Georgia lost 4 per cent. Some counties lost as much as 40 per cent of their initial forest within a few decades, nearly all of them in the southeast, with a few in the Pacific Northwest, and almost all close to rapidly expanding urban centres. The three hardest-hit counties are all in Virginia. The climate toll: 2.3 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent committed to the atmosphere Gross loss amounted to roughly 2 per cent of the nationâs forestland, and the Clark University report reaches its climate figure by counting both direct carbon emissions and the loss of expected future carbon storage. About 65 per cent of the total comes from direct emissions and roughly 35 per cent from foregone sequestration. Albedo change, the extra sunlight reflected back into space once forest becomes developed land or cropland, partly offsets the damage, reducing the total by about 15 per cent. Annual deforestation equals approximately 8 per cent of the carbon absorbed each year by remaining forests, 29 per cent of emissions from harvested wood products and roughly 1 per cent of fossil fuel emissions across all sectors in the 2020s. Six states cause half the climate burden, and Washington ranks higher for carbon than for acres Rankings change when the measure is climate impact rather than acreage, because forest carbon stocks, storage potential and albedo change differ from place to place. Half of the burden comes from Georgia, North Carolina, Texas, Florida, Virginia and Alabama. Adding South Carolina, Arkansas, Mississippi and Washington brings the share to 70 per cent. Washington ranks 14th for the amount of forest lost but 10th for carbon burden, thanks to the high carbon storage of its western forests. What the report leaves out, and how the next version aims to close the gaps through 2024 The researchers are open about what the first version misses. Its cautious approach omits some conversions, including forest turned to pasture, which is often confused with shrubland, savanna and areas of partial tree cover loss. The five-year persistence test also delays reporting, and no formal accuracy assessment has been carried out because it is not currently funded. Over the coming year the team plans to extend tracking to 2024, and it is exploring an early warning system that flags probable recent conversion. State-level reports, with Pennsylvania as the worked example, are in development, and the findings are aimed at land trusts, state climate strategies and carbon offset markets seeking to prioritise forest protection.

text: Nicole Richie and Joel Madden, PC: Wikipedia Nicole Richie and Joel Madden sold their Beverly Hills mansion for approximately $10.18 million in May 2025, after putting the property on the market for $12.95 million in July 2024. The final sale price was about $2.77 million below the original asking price. title: In 1969, Chicago soldier Frank Kowalczyk recorded a 43-minute audio letter to his mother from Vietnam, speaking roughly 8,600 words as helicopters passed overhead; 57 years later, the Smithsonian preserves his voice
text: In March 1969, a 21-year-old American soldier stationed in Vietnam decided to do something different from writing a letter home. Frank A. Kowalczyk switched on a reel-to-reel tape recorder and began speaking to his mother in Illinois, sharing updates about his fellow soldiers, life in the Army, family gossip and his plans for the future. During the approximately 43-minute recording, he spoke more than 8,600 words, while the sound of a helicopter passing overhead captured the reality of a war thousands of miles from home. Fifty-seven years later, the recording is preserved by the Smithsonianâs National Postal Museum in Washington, DC. Kowalczyk, a US Army private first class from the Chicago area, was serving with Headquarters, 46th Engineers Battalion, 20th Brigade, at Long Binh Post near Saigon. He had bought the recording machine from another soldier and preferred speaking into a microphone to putting his thoughts on paper. âI figured Iâd just sit down and instead of writing you a letter just make use of tape,â he said at the beginning of the recording, explaining that it would be easier because he hated writing. The museumâs catalogue describes the message as having been recorded over several sessions in March 1969. While Smithsonian Magazine describes it as a 43-minute tape, the National Postal Museumâs object record rounds its duration to approximately 45 minutes. What followed was not a carefully prepared account of military service, but a long, informal conversation with his family back home in Calumet City, Illinois. From family gossip to the realities of war Kowalczykâs recording moved between the ordinary details of life and the unsettling circumstances surrounding him. He asked his mother about his fatherâs work schedule, checked on his siblings and wondered whether neighbours back home had married. He also discussed his friends, his experiences in the Army and his frustration with the routine duties imposed on soldiers at Long Binh Post. The everyday questions gave the recording an intimacy that a formal account of military life might have lacked. He was not simply documenting his deployment; he was trying to remain part of the family life continuing without him. He also talked about the differences between life in Vietnam and the world he had left behind. He described the military routine, the weather, the food and his experiences travelling around Saigon and nearby places. He mentioned learning Vietnamese and joked about how difficult it might be to stop using the language after returning home. Yet the recording also contained glimpses of the warâs harsher realities. Kowalczyk referred to a fellow soldier who had bled to death in a bunker because help had not arrived. He expressed a preference for being assigned outside the main base, where he felt soldiers were treated with greater respect. The conversation was not a polished historical account, and its value lies partly in that informality. His remarks captured the concerns, frustrations and familiar routines of a young man trying to make sense of military life while staying connected to people he missed. The helicopter that brought the war into the room One of the most striking moments comes when Kowalczyk draws his motherâs attention to a helicopter flying overhead. âRight now in the background, youâll probably hear a chopper flying over,â he says in the recording. He goes on to explain that helicopters passed over the area frequently throughout the day. For his daughter, Manda Kowalczyk, the sound has become one of the recordingâs most powerful elements. Speaking to Smithsonian Magazine, she explained that the helicopter was a reminder of the distance between her fatherâs home and the place where he was serving. âThese helicopters are not in Chicago. This is happening in Vietnam,â she said. Lynn Heidelbaugh, a curator at the National Postal Museum, similarly highlighted what the recording preserves beyond its spoken words. The helicopterâs noise is something a written letter could not convey, giving listeners a sense of the environment surrounding the soldier as he spoke. Kowalczyk also asked his mother to record a reply and send it back with news, weather reports or television audio. Hearing familiar sounds from home, he suggested, would be strange in the best possible way because such material was rarely available to him in Vietnam. How audio letters connected soldiers with home Audio correspondence had become a way for military personnel and their families to exchange more personal messages during periods of separation. By the Vietnam War era, reel-to-reel recorders were increasingly accessible, allowing some service members to record their own tapes. The American Red Cross also operated recording facilities in Vietnam and the Pacific, while its âVoices from Homeâ programme helped families record messages for relatives serving overseas. Such recordings allowed loved ones to hear familiar voices rather than relying exclusively on handwritten letters. Military postal arrangements made it possible to send eligible personal recordings from designated areas without ordinary postage charges. The Post Office Department also used the âspace available militaryâ transportation programme to move mail overseas. Kowalczyk himself referred to the free-mail rules during his recording, demonstrating that he was familiar with the arrangements. A family recording becomes part of the Smithsonian The tape remained a personal family possession for decades. Kowalczykâs daughter knew about it but did not recall hearing it until it became part of the Smithsonian collection. The family eventually donated it to the National Postal Museum in 2011, when Heidelbaugh was researching material for the museumâs âMail Callâ exhibition. Kowalczyk, who died in 2024, reportedly found it amusing that anyone would be interested in a recording he regarded as little more than a long conversation about weather, insects and everyday life. For his daughter, however, hearing the tape offered a glimpse of her father as a young man, before she could have known him in the same way. She told Smithsonian Magazine that hearing his Chicago accent made his voice sound like home. The National Postal Museum now preserves the recording and makes it available alongside a transcript, allowing listeners to hear Kowalczykâs words and the sounds around him. More than half a century after he pressed record, the tape remains a document of both military history and family life. Its significance is not only in what Kowalczyk said about Vietnam, but also in what he wanted his mother to know about home, his friends and himself. title: After polio left her unable to walk, Elsie MacGill returned to engineering and supervised production of more than 1,450 Hawker Hurricane aircraft, earning the nickname âQueen of the Hurricanesâ
text: Hawker Hurricane. Image Credit: Wikipedia Elsie MacGill became one of Canadaâs most influential engineers at a time when women faced considerable barriers in technical professions. After contracting polio and losing the ability to walk, she returned to engineering and took on a major role in producing Hawker Hurricane fighter aircraft during the Second World War. Her work helped keep aircraft production moving as Britain and its allies faced an urgent need for military planes. Known as the Queen of the Hurricanes, MacGill later became equally recognised for challenging discrimination against women and advocating for their rights. How did Elsie MacGill return to engineering after polio According to the Government of Canada, Elizabeth Muriel Gregory MacGill, known as Elsie MacGill, was born in Vancouver, British Columbia, on 27 March 1905. She grew up in a family that valued education and public engagement. Her mother, Helen Gregory MacGill, was a prominent advocate for womenâs rights and became British Columbiaâs first woman judge. This environment helped shape MacGillâs belief that women should have opportunities to participate in professional life. MacGill pursued engineering at a time when very few women entered the field. She studied electrical engineering at the University of British Columbia before continuing her education at the University of Toronto, where she earned a degree in electrical engineering. She later completed a masterâs degree in aeronautical engineering at the University of Michigan, becoming the first woman in North America to earn a masterâs degree in that subject, according to the Canadian Aviation Hall of Fame. Her progress was interrupted in 1929 when she contracted polio. The illness left her unable to walk, and she faced a long period of recovery. Rather than abandoning her career, she adapted to her physical limitations and continued working towards her professional goals. Her determination became a defining feature of her story, although her achievements rested on technical knowledge and practical experience as much as personal resilience. Her work transformed Canadian aircraft manufacturing MacGill began working in the aviation industry in the late 1920s and early 1930s, when aircraft engineering was developing rapidly. She worked for Fairchild Aircraft in the United States before moving to Canada, where she became involved with Canadian Car and Foundry, commonly known as Can Car, in Fort William, Ontario, now part of Thunder Bay. In 1938, MacGill became chief aeronautical engineer at Can Car. The appointment placed her in a senior technical position just as the threat of war was increasing demand for military aircraft. Her responsibilities involved designing, testing and improving aircraft, as well as helping the factory prepare for large-scale production. According to the Royal Canadian Mint, MacGill played a significant role in producing Hawker Hurricane fighter planes at the Canadian factory during the Second World War. The aircraft had an important place in Allied air operations, including the Battle of Britain in 1940, when British and Allied pilots fought to prevent German control of the skies. The Hurricane was not simply a design that could be manufactured without difficulty. Producing military aircraft in large numbers required detailed engineering work, skilled employees, reliable supplies and an organised factory. MacGill helped address those challenges while overseeing production and ensuring that the aircraft met the required standards. The Hawker Hurricane was adapted for cold weather One of MacGillâs most important contributions was helping the factory adapt the British-designed Hurricane for Canadian conditions. The aircraft needed to operate in colder environments, so she worked on improvements that included equipment to prevent ice from building up on its wings and tail. According to the Royal Canadian Mint, she also helped develop adaptations such as ski landing gear and de-icing systems. These changes mattered because ice could interfere with an aircraftâs ability to fly safely. MacGillâs engineering work helped make the Hurricane more suitable for the conditions in which Canadian-built planes might be used. Her role combined practical problem-solving with the larger challenge of supplying aircraft to the Allied war effort. The factory itself underwent a major transformation. Veterans Affairs Canada reports that, within a year, the plant was producing 3 fighter aircraft a day, supported by a workforce of around 4,500 people. The operation produced approximately 1,450 Hurricanes in just two years. The scale of the achievement was particularly striking because Can Car had not previously operated at this level of fighter-aircraft production. MacGill helped guide the engineering work required to turn the factory into a major supplier during wartime. How did MacGill earn the Queen of the Hurricanes nickname MacGillâs wartime contribution brought her public recognition beyond the engineering community. In 1942, she was featured in True Comics, which used the nickname Queen of the Hurricanes to describe her achievements. The name reflected her responsibility for the engineering work behind the production of more than 1,450 aircraft. Her career did not end with the Hurricane programme. After the contract was completed, she became responsible for production of 835 Curtiss Helldiver aircraft for the US Navy, according to Veterans Affairs Canada. Her experience showed that her skills extended beyond a single aircraft model or manufacturing project. MacGill also used her standing to advocate for women. The Government of Canada records her involvement with the Canadian Federation of Business and Professional Womenâs Clubs, where she served as national president. She argued for greater opportunities for women in professional and public life, at a time when their access to many careers remained restricted. In 1967, she joined the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada. The commission examined the position of women in Canadian society and helped bring questions of equality into national debate. Her participation reflected a broader commitment that had developed alongside her engineering career. The Royal Aviation Museum of Western Canada also notes that MacGill became a technical adviser to the United Nations International Civil Aviation Organization after the war. Her achievements remain part of Canada's engineering history MacGill died in a car accident in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 4 November 1980, aged 75, according to Veterans Affairs Canada. Her legacy has since been recognised through engineering and aviation honours, as well as public commemorations. In August 2023, the Royal Canadian Mint issued a commemorative one-dollar circulation coin honouring her. Designed by Claire Watson, the coin depicts MacGill holding rolled-up blueprints, with the Maple Leaf Trainer II she designed and a Canadian-made Hawker Hurricane shown alongside her. The Mint presented the coin as recognition of both her engineering achievements and her contribution to women's rights. The title Queen of the Hurricanes captures only one part of MacGillâs life. Her influence extended from the factory floor to national discussions about equality. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Dr Reddyâs gets USFDA nod for first generic twice-yearly injectable HIV prevention drug Lenacapavir
text: A file shot of Dr Reddy's Labs headquarters in Hyderabad. Hyderabad: Dr Reddyâs Laboratories said Monday US Food and Drug Administration has granted tentative approval for its twice-yearly injectable lenacapavir for pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, to reduce the risk of sexually acquired HIV-1 in adults and adolescents weighing at least 35 kg. The approval, issued under USFDAâs Presidentâs Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) programme, moves the long-acting HIV prevention medicine closer to use in 120 countries outside the United States covered by Gilead Sciencesâ voluntary licence. Dr Reddyâs said the first supplies are expected to reach countries before the end of 2026, with broader availability in eligible markets in 2027. Lenacapavir is a first-in-class HIV-1 capsid inhibitor designed to act at multiple stages of the virus lifecycle. Gilead granted Dr Reddyâs a voluntary licence in October 2024. In September 2025, Unitaid, Wits Reproductive Health (Wits RHI) and HIV Institute and Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) agreed to support product development, speed regulatory work and enable access at $40 per person per year. Deepak Sapra, chief executive officer for API and Services at Dr Reddyâs, said the approval validates the companyâs work to develop and manufacture a complex long-acting injectable at an affordable price. Unitaid, CHAI and Wits RHI said accelerated generic approval could help expand prevention options, particularly for underserved populations. âUnitaidâs early risk-taking is helping shorten the time between a scientific breakthrough and real access in countries,â said Dr Philippe Duneton, executive director, Unitaid, saying lenacapavir could help young women in Africa avert infections. âFor someone at risk of HIV, taking a pill every day to prevent a disease they donât have is a hard thing to ask,â said Dr Neil Buddy Shah, CEO, CHAI, calling two injections yearly âalmost 100% effectiveâ and a ânew standard for global health.â âGeneric lenacapavir has the potential to transform HIV prevention,â said Prof Saiqa Mullick of Wits RHI, pointing out that countries need ready health systems, trained providers and engaged communities. World Health Organization recommends twice-yearly lenacapavir for HIV prevention. Dr Reddyâs said wider rollout still requires WHO prequalification and national regulatory approvals with HIV-negative status to be confirmed before initiation and before each subsequent injection. title: Avengers Assemble! US rolls out Stinger missiles to shield Trump's Florida estate from drone threats
text: Avenger air defense systems seen at Mar-A-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida (TWZ) The United States has deployed Avenger short-range air defence systems armed with Stinger missiles around President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, adding another layer of protection against potential aerial threats, including drones and low-flying aircraft. According to a report by The War Zone (TWZ), the systems were deployed around two weeks before October 30, following a request from the US Secret Service. The deployment was carried out by the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) and US Northern Command (USNORTHCOM). The missile systems have been positioned at multiple locations around the estate, including a floating platform in Lake Worth Lagoon, a nearby beach and Donald J Trump International Airport, approximately three miles west of Mar-a-Lago. Photographs published by TWZ show multiple Avenger systems deployed at these locations. Watch 94 Years Of The IAF: The Road Ahead For India's Air Arm NORAD and USNORTHCOM have also confirmed deploying counter-unmanned aircraft system (C-UAS) capabilities as part of the security arrangement. These systems are designed to detect, identify and track drones that could pose a threat to the president or restricted airspace. The deployment comes amid heightened security concerns over potential aerial threats and follows a series of airspace violations around Palm Beach. According to TWZ, more than 160 aircraft and drones have breached restricted airspace over the area since October 2025. What is the Avenger air defence system? The AN/TWQ-1 Avenger is a mobile, short-range air defence system developed by Boeing for the US Army to protect military forces and strategic locations against low-altitude aerial threats. Mounted on an M1097-series High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle (HMMWV), commonly known as a Humvee, the system combines surface-to-air missiles, a machine gun and advanced target-detection and tracking equipment on a single mobile platform. According to the US Army's Weapon Systems Handbook 2020-2021, the Avenger is designed to engage unmanned aerial systems (UAS), cruise missiles, helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft operating at low altitudes. It can operate during both day and night, in adverse weather conditions and while the vehicle is moving. The system is operated by a two-member crew and features a rotating turret equipped with two missile launcher pods, each carrying four FIM-92 Stinger surface-to-air missiles, giving it a total capacity of eight ready-to-fire missiles. Each Stinger missile uses infrared guidance to lock onto the heat signature of an aerial target and independently guide itself after launch. This fire-and-forget capability allows the operator to engage a target without having to continuously guide the missile. The Avenger also carries an M3P .50-calibre automatic machine gun, which provides an additional weapon for engaging close-range aerial threats and ground targets. The machine gun has a basic ammunition load of 250 rounds. The US Army handbook lists the system's target-tracking range at approximately 10 km, while its Stinger missiles have an engagement range of more than 6 km. The M3P machine gun has an engagement range of more than 1 km. Drones emerge as growing threat to Trump's security The growing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in modern warfare has emerged as an additional security concern for US President Donald Trump, prompting authorities to strengthen aerial protection around his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. The proliferation of relatively inexpensive drones, including first-person-view (FPV) and fibre-optic-controlled systems, has made it increasingly difficult to detect and counter potential aerial threats. According to The War Zone, Iran has both used and supplied such weapons, raising concerns about the possibility of their use against high-security locations. The threat is particularly significant because Mar-a-Lago is located close to the Atlantic coastline, potentially exposing the estate to aerial threats approaching from the sea. The War Zone noted that long-range kamikaze drones, which are designed to crash into targets carrying explosive payloads, could pose a particular challenge. Unlike conventional aircraft, small drones can fly at low altitudes and may be harder to detect using traditional air surveillance systems.

title: GPCB eases regulatory norms for eligible CBG, bio-CNG plants
text: Bio CNG plant Gandhinagar : In a move to accelerate clean energy projects, Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) has exempted eligible compressed biogas (CBG) and bio-CNG plants from obtaining individual exemption letters, simplifying regulatory procedures for the sector. The GPCB issued a notification on Oct 28, implementing the revised white category classification introduced by Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB). Eligible plants using specified feedstock and meeting prescribed conditions are exempt from obtaining Consent to Establish (CTE) and Consent to Operate (CTO). The notification means project developers will no longer need to approach the GPCB separately for exemption letters. An official statement said govt departments and registration authorities have also been advised not to insist on CTE, CTO or a separate no-objection certificate (NOC) for eligible units while processing registrations, permissions and applications for financial assistance. The move is expected to reduce paperwork, avoid procedural delays and expedite applications under govt schemes, including registration on the âGobardhanâ unified registration portal, the statement said. The exemption does not absolve units of their environmental responsibilities, the statement added. Under the union environment ministryâs Nov 12, 2024 notification, eligible white category units must notify the state pollution control board as prescribed and submit self-declarations confirming compliance with applicable environmental laws and regulations. (Facebook/Dave Billings) A British man has spent 11 years turning the garden of his Derbyshire home into an underground space inspired by World War II escape tunnels. Dave Billings, 43, has built two bunkers connected by a 35-foot passage, along with a lift disguised as a beer keg to carry drinks underground. By October 2024, he had spent around Â£30,000 on the project and expected the final construction cost to reach Â£35,000. According to The Sun's report, the underground rooms weren't yet connected to his bungalow, but Billings had plans to change that. He wants to create a concealed entrance inside his home, allowing him to reach the bunkers without stepping outside. The proposed route would eventually lead through the tunnel and back into the garden through an old well. For Billings, a fabricator, the project began with an interest in the history of his property. His home stands on land that was once part of a World War II army base. He had hoped to discover an existing bunker there, but when he found none, he decided to build one. âIâve always wanted to find a bunker on the property, but when I didnât I thought Iâll build one myself. Itâs a bit of a childhood dream, really,â he told DerbyWorld. Small underground room becomes larger project The first stage of construction began around 2013. At the time, the garden contained an old well, which Billings incorporated into his plans. He constructed stairs leading down to a bunker measuring approximately 13 square metres. For several years, this was the main underground space on the property. But Billings eventually decided that he wanted something bigger. In 2023, he began work on a second bunker, this time with approximately 25 square metres of space. He decided to connect it to the existing bunker. This meant digging a tunnel stretching 35 feet between the two structures. The idea came partly from The Great Escape, the 1963 film based on the escape of Allied prisoners of war from Stalag Luft III during World War II. The prisoners had dug underground passages in an attempt to escape captivity. Billings wanted to recreate the appearance of those tunnels, including wooden lining along the passage. A hidden entrance and an unusual way to deliver beer The tunnel is only one part of the underground arrangement Billings hoped to create. His longer-term plan involved extending his bungalow closer to the bunker and installing a secret door that would provide access from inside the house. This would make it possible to enter the underground rooms from the bungalow, move through the connecting passage and return to the surface through the well. Billings also wanted visitors to be able to use the underground route without disturbing other people in the house. There is already another feature designed to make life below ground more convenient. Carrying drinks down the stairs proved difficult, so Billings constructed a lift that resembles a beer barrel. The device allows him to lower drinks into the bunker without having to carry them down himself. It is among the more unusual additions to a project that began as a simple underground shelter. Construction costs and plans for finished bunker Despite carrying out the construction himself, Billings has spent a substantial amount on materials. According to The Sun, around Â£4,000 went towards bricks, while concrete, waterproofing and insulation added to the overall cost. His decision to do much of the work without hiring builders has helped reduce expenses. He also prepared the designs using Computer-aided design, with a structural engineer checking the specifications. By October 2024, the project had cost approximately Â£30,000. Billings estimated that completing the new bunker would bring the total to around Â£35,000. Billings also planned to install a projector and gaming simulator, along with other electronic devices. One of his ideas involved a remote-controlled fridge that could travel towards a person carrying a beer. At the time of the reports, he had not worked out how to make the device. Billings was aiming to finish the larger bunker by Christmas 2024, although he did not expect the project to end there. He was already considering further additions, including the possibility of another tunnel. âItâll never be fully finished. Iâll always be adding new inventions and maybe even another tunnel,â he said, as quoted by DerbyWorld, reflecting his determination to keep expanding the unusual underground retreat for years to come. title: Shakira's Barefoot Foundation has supported over 224,000 disadvantaged children, with 8 in 10 graduates pursuing higher education; its funding is building schools, training teachers and supporting Indigenous communities
text: Shakira's Barefoot Foundation has supported more than 224,000 children and young people in Colombia, helping expand access to education through school construction, teacher training and educational programmes. Founded by the Colombian singer in 1997, FundaciÃ³n Pies Descalzos works with communities facing economic and social barriers to quality education. The organisation reports that 8 in 10 students graduating from its supported schools continue to higher education, compared with approximately four in 10 young people nationally. Its work also includes improving educational facilities in underserved areas, providing school supplies and supporting Indigenous communities. Shakira's foundation focuses on education as a path out of inequality Shakira established FundaciÃ³n Pies Descalzos in 1997 to help children in Colombia access quality education. The organisation, also known as the Barefoot Foundation, focuses on children and young people in vulnerable communities, where financial difficulties and limited educational infrastructure can restrict opportunities. Rather than concentrating exclusively on school construction, the foundation combines infrastructure projects with teacher training, educational support and programmes intended to help students continue their studies. Its approach also involves working with public schools and local communities to improve learning environments. According to the foundation, its projects aim to ensure that children can develop the knowledge and skills needed to pursue further education and build better prospects for themselves and their families. Eight in 10 graduates continue to higher education One of the foundation's most notable reported outcomes is the proportion of students who continue their education after graduating from its supported schools. According to its official impact page, eight in 10 graduates from Pies Descalzos schools continue to higher education. The foundation contrasts this with the national picture, citing data from Colombia's National Administrative Department of Statistics (DANE) indicating that approximately four in 10 young people continue to this level of education. In a November 2025 publication, the foundation said between 70% and 80% of students graduating from schools it supports continue into tertiary education. This includes technical, technological and university-level programmes. Building schools in underserved communities Improving access to educational infrastructure is a central part of the foundation's work. Its projects include constructing new schools and upgrading existing facilities in areas where children face barriers to quality education. In 2024, the foundation reported supporting 28,157 students across 24 Colombian municipalities through educational and school-infrastructure projects. This was in addition to approximately 6,700 children and young people enrolled in schools supported by the organisation and bearing its name. One of its projects that year was a new school in the Villas de Aranjuez neighbourhood of Cartagena. The facility was designed to serve approximately 1,000 students annually, helping expand educational provision in the area. The foundation also worked with Colombia's Ministry of National Education to improve two schools in Riohacha and Uribia, in the department of La Guajira. These projects focused on strengthening educational access for communities that include Indigenous students and migrants. Supporting Indigenous WayÃºu students and migrant families In 2024, the organisation and Colombia's Ministry of National Education completed interventions at two schools in Riohacha and Uribia. The facilities served more than 1,500 students, most of whom belonged to the WayÃºu Indigenous community or were migrants from Venezuela. The projects used an ethno-educational approach, recognising the importance of cultural context in education. This is particularly relevant for Indigenous communities, where education programmes must account for local identities and circumstances. Training teachers and providing learning materials The foundation also invests in teachers, recognising that educational facilities alone cannot guarantee effective learning. Its official impact figures report that more than 12,824 teachers have received training, with women accounting for 85% of those trained. The organisation says these programmes are intended to strengthen teaching practices and help educators introduce new skills into their classrooms. In 2024, the foundation reported that 690 teachers participated in its training programmes. The organisation also distributed 10,965 kits, uniforms and reading materials to students, teachers, school leaders and coordinators that year. Such supplies can help schools and families meet some of the practical requirements of education. These initiatives complement the foundation's infrastructure projects by supporting the people and resources involved in students' day-to-day learning. Foundation reports more than 282,000 beneficiaries Although the foundation's impact page reports that it has supported more than 224,000 children and young people, its English-language homepage now lists a higher cumulative figure. The homepage reports more than 282,160 children and young people benefited, over 13,387 teachers trained and more than 300 public schools supported in Colombia. It also lists 22 schools built or improved in Colombia, two in Haiti and one in Soweto. The foundation also reports working with 1,131 families and caregivers, 80% of whom are women, according to its impact page. This highlights another dimension of its work: involving families in supporting children's development and education. Shakira's foundation expands support beyond the classroom The organisation's work has also extended into partnerships intended to help young people navigate education and prepare for their futures. In April 2026, Colombia's student-loan and educational-support agency ICETEX announced a three-year partnership with FundaciÃ³n Pies Descalzos under its Comunidad ICETEX project. The collaboration aims to support young people as they prepare for higher education, continue their studies and move towards employment. Its planned areas of work include financial education, emotional wellbeing, career guidance, gender equality, entrepreneurship, leadership and employability. You use AI every day. title: âFight with Indian solutionsâ: New IAF chief Ashutosh Dixit pushes self-reliance, combat readiness
text: From Tejas to AMCA: New IAF chief spells out priorities under âVAYUâ vision NEW DELHI: Newly appointed chief of the air staff air chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit on Sunday outlined his priorities for the Indian Air Force (IAF), placing emphasis on combat readiness, restoring sanctioned squadron strength, boosting indigenous defence capabilities, technological innovation and jointness among the armed forces. Addressing personnel at the Parade Ground of Air Force Station, Dixit said rebuilding the IAF's combat strength to its sanctioned level would be one of his foremost priorities. He stressed that every squadron, radar unit and air defence unit must remain prepared to respond at short notice. Watch From Test Pilot To IAF chief: Air Chief Marshal AP Singh's Long Association With The Tejas Unveiling his âVAYUâ vision, Dixit said the IAF's priorities would revolve around vigilance and readiness, self-reliance, innovation and unity of effort. Explaining the vision, he said, "Our priorities shall be summed up in one word: VAYU. V for Vigilance and Readiness. Every squadron, every radar, every air defene unit along with each and every Air Warrior, must be ready to respond at a moment's notice. Restoring our combat strength towards the sanctioned level will also be my foremost task. A for Aatmanirbharta. The Tejas MklA and lI, the AMCA, Indian sensors and Indian weapons are our highest priority. We will fight with Indian solutions, and we will hold them in numbers and that meet sustain operations demands. Our responsibility is to fight and win, but most importantly it is to deter conflict through credible Air Power." On technological advancement, Dixit highlighted the role of artificial intelligence-enabled command and control systems, layered counter-drone defence, responsive maintenance and the use of near-space as an operational domain. "Y is for Yukti, our ingenuity. Innovation in doctrine, procedures and in technology: networked, Al-enabled command and control; layered counter-drone defence; responsive maintenance, force protection, resilience a n d use of near-space as operational domains for the Air Force, are all areas which will b e constantly monitored a n d progressed. U is for Unity of effort. In step with the vision of JAl, Jointness, Aatmanirbharta and Innovation, we will plan and fight as one along with our Army, our Navy and our National Agencies. " Highlighting the changing nature of warfare, the new air chief said technologies such as drones, long-range precision weapons, space and cyber capabilities were reshaping the security environment. He stressed that the IAF must continue to transform while remaining prepared to fight and win. He also acknowledged the role of his predecessor, air chief Marshal AP Singh, in leading the force during Operation Sindoor. "I take over from air chief Marshal A P Singh, under whose leadership in Operations Sindoor, the Air Force displayed, what precise and decisive air power can achieve. I thank him for handing over a force in a high state of readiness. Our security environment remains demanding. In addition, the character of war is being reshaped by new technologies & systems like drones, long-range precision weapons, space, cyber, Al a n d the electromagnetic spectrum. The Air Force while transforming into the force that India will need in the next decade , must always be ready to fight and win," Dixit said. Dixit said the welfare, training, professional development and morale of Air Warriors, Agniveervayu personnel, civilian staff, veterans, Veer Naris and their families would also receive his personal attention. "Air power delivers most when it is integrated from the very first plan. Underpinning all of this are our people: our Air Warriors, Agniveervayu, Civilians, Veterans, Veer Naris and their families. Their training, professional excellence, morale, safety, welfare and dignity will have my personal attention. To the fellow citizens of my motherland, please trust that: your Air Force is vigilant, ready and resolute. Our commitment is clear ; to remain ready, to keep transtorming and to deliver whenever the nation calls," he added. Air chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit took charge as the 29th Chief of the Air Staff at the Parade Ground of Air Force Station on Sunday. He received a Guard of Honour after assuming office. Earlier in the day, he laid a wreath at the National War Memorial in New Delhi and paid tribute to personnel who laid down their lives in service of the country. Dixit succeeds air chief Marshal AP Singh, PSM, AVSM, who retired after 42 years of service. An alumnus of the National Defence Academy, Dixit was commissioned into the Fighter Stream of the Indian Air Force on December 6, 1986. During his four-decade career, he has served in several roles spanning operations, flight testing, capability development and joint staff assignments, according to the official release.

title: 3 Wall Street firms agree to pay up to $100,000 a month to get Trumpâs posts faster: How it works
text: 3 trading firms agree to pay Trumpâs Truth Social for faster access US President Donald Trumpâs paid social media service, Truth API, has found customers, with Bloomberg and two high-frequency trading firms paying for faster access to his posts. The service costs financial institutions up to $100,000 a month. Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter, cited by Reuters, said Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading, both of which specialise in algorithmic and automated trading strategies, have also signed up for the service. The deals give subscribers a timing advantage over people who monitor Trumpâs posts on the app themselves. The arrangement has raised concerns about the sale of faster access to statements by a sitting president, particularly because his posts can influence financial markets. It also comes as Trump Media and Technology Group, the company behind Truth Social, faces legal challenges over the paid service and questions about the potential use of presidential communications for commercial gain. How Truth API works Trump Media and Technology Group announced the faster-access product in July, pitching it to trading firms and other financial institutions. The service is designed to deliver Trumpâs posts more quickly than a person could obtain them by repeatedly checking Truth Social. Trump Media officials have put the timing advantage at 50 milliseconds. For financial firms using automated trading systems, that difference can matter when a presidential statement triggers a change in asset prices. High-frequency traders rely on software to scan news headlines, company announcements and government statements for information that could move markets. Their systems can read and analyse the information before executing trades in thousandths of a second. The potential consequences of Trumpâs social media posts were evident in April, when oil futures fell after he announced a ceasefire in the Iran war on Truth Social. An application programming interface, or API, acts as a digital bridge that allows one computer system to communicate with another. In this case, the product gives subscribers faster access to the presidentâs posts, which they can use in their trading or financial information systems. Who is paying for the service? According to a Reuters report, Bloomberg, Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading are among the organisations that have signed up for Truth API. In August, Trump Media told investors it had "signed more than 10 customer agreementsâ. Reuters was unable to independently confirm that figure. The company did not identify its customers but said they were primarily Wall Street trading firms paying between $60,000 and $100,000 a month. The latest deals indicate that the product has attracted both financial trading firms and a news and data provider. Reuters, which competes with Bloomberg in financial news, said in a statement: "We will assess the service, but have no current plans to subscribe." Trump Media defended the product in a statement, saying: âTruth Social offers an industry-standard API product for which there is significant demand across industries. We take customer confidentiality seriously. This reporting is based on misleading information being peddled by anonymous sources aimed at harming our company, customers and shareholders.â The company has not publicly named the subscribers in its August investor update, and the three firms named in the report declined to comment. Why the paid feed has drawn criticism The paid service has drawn criticism for giving subscribers faster access to a presidentâs statements, potentially offering financial firms an advantage when his posts move markets. The deals are likely the first time a business linked to a sitting president has sold access to his statements. In July, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Adam Schiff of California asked the US Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether the service violated securities laws. They called it a âshocking abuseâ of office by a president seeking personal gain. A Trump Media and Technology Group spokesperson said, âCongressional Democrats continue to mischaracterize Truth API either out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information.â In August, Intercept Media and the non-profit Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump, seeking to stop the White House from posting official government announcements exclusively on Truth Social. The ongoing lawsuit describes the service as "profoundly corrupt" and alleges violations of the First and Fifth Amendments. Trump Mediaâs financial portfolio The commercial arrangement has also drawn attention to the ownership of Trump Media. The presidentâs family trust owns 41% of the company, and Trump is the trustâs sole beneficiary. The Truth API deals come as Trump Media faces a steep decline in its stock market value. Shares of the company have fallen more than 50% so far this year. Its market value has also been volatile since it went public in March 2024. The company closed at a market value of about $8 billion on its debut in March 2024, but is now worth about $1.8 billion. title: In 2010, a Texas father opened an accessible theme park inspired by his daughter; Morganâs Wonderland has since welcomed more than 3.8 million guests from 50 states and 123 countries
text: Gordon Hartman, founder of Morganâs Wonderland, established the inclusive theme park in San Antonio, Texas, in 2010. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons Many mainstream theme parks emphasize thrill, capacity and spectacle, features that can create barriers for some disabled visitors. For families with a child who uses a wheelchair, is sensitive to sound, or cannot speak, a theme-park visit can become an organizational challenge. Although there are arrangements at the parks to accommodate such visitors, there is usually nothing that is pre-planned according to their requirements. In San Antonio, Texas, one individual decided to create something new by considering the opposite approach. As a homebuilder rather than an amusement-park operator, he drew inspiration from a deeply personal experience. Namely, he saw how his daughter was excluded from the playground. This experience led him to create a playground designed for everyone. From a foundation in 2005 to opening day on April 10, 2010 The Gordon Hartman Foundation was established in 2005 by Gordon Hartman, a former real estate developer, to assist people with disabilities, Gulf News reports. In 2007, after realizing that other children often avoided Morgan because she could not speak, Gordon decided to create an inclusive park. Morganâs biography of Hartman says that Morganâs Wonderland opened on April 10, 2010, as the worldâs first Ultra-Accessible theme park and the parkâs own account puts the journey from the 2007 decision to opening day at 39 months. Hartman thought that families like his required a space that was less bustling than the traditional parks but was not sure that people were going to show up. A 25-acre park with a core of 25 attractions and free entry for guests with a disability The park covers 25 acres and Morganâs 2024 press release describes a core of 25 attractions that existed before the expansion. In 2024, Morganâs Wonderland unveiled the largest expansion since its 2010 opening and Visit San Antonioâs release on the plan covers the four new attractions. A report carried by Intergame Online says the park caps daily attendance so it never gets too loud or the lines too long and admission is free for guests with special needs. Morganâs March 2024 press release put the expansion at $6.5 million, while the plan announced the previous October had estimated $6 million, a figure Blooloop repeated. Morganâs Wonderlandâs 2024 announcement lists the four new attractions as the 4D Magic Cinema, Pirateâs Island Cruises, Rocketâs Sky Flight Adventure, which is a four-seat zip line and Jetteâs Magic Bikes. According to Health Club Management, the Magic Cinema uses electric actuator-based motion effects, which can be disabled for guests who do not want motion effects. From 1.6 million guests in the first decade to more than 3.8 million today The family travel site Taking the Kids reported that more than 1.6 million guests from 50 states and 73 countries had visited the park during its first decade. During the 2024 expansion announcement, Hartman cited the figure as 2.7 million guests from 50 states and more than 120 countries. The parkâs website currently reports more than 3.8 million guests over 16 years of operation, from 50 states and 123 countries. The number of countries represented has risen from 73 to 123, while total attendance has more than doubled. What a 2023 review of 14 playground auditing tools found The wider research context helps explain why a park like this stands out. A 2023 paper in Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences , A Scoping Review of Tools to Evaluate Existing Playgrounds for Inclusivity of Children with Disabilities , was led by Leah G. Taylor. The authors also draw attention to the fact that there are almost 240 million children who suffer from disabilities throughout the world and have problems properly participating in society. In the 2023 scoping review, there were 14 resources from both academic and grey literature on playground auditing tools found. The team synthesized features of those tools into 13 recommendations for inclusive playground design. Just two tools covered 12 of those 13 recommendations and the tools applied the notion of inclusion differently, mostly in terms of physical inclusion. A display at Morganâs Wonderland introduces Morgan Hartman, the parkâs inspiration. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons The paper also notes that most of the tools were at an early stage of development and few had been formally tested for reliability and validity. Most of the tools also paid little attention to sensory, social and communication barriers. For its part, the parkâs biography says it was not meant to be a separate place for people with disabilities, but a place where disabled and non-disabled visitors could share the same rides. A 2022 observation study and the 71% active play figure A second paper , published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, looked at how children actually behave in an inclusive setting. The study, Childrenâs Usage of Inclusive Playgrounds: A Naturalistic Observation Study of Play , used two trained observers and a modified version of the System for Observing Play and Recreation in Children tool at a playground built for all ages and abilities. The study also found that 71% of the children observed were engaged in active play. Moreover, it should be noted that there were children without disabilities who seemed to be attracted to the playground. Both papers discuss further research into the interactions between the children with disabilities and playgrounds. The study observed not only the childrenâs activity but also their interactions and found that most were social or parallel rather than solitary. Nevertheless, neither of these two papers considered Morgan's Wonderland directly; instead, they create the background for the park. In the study of the auditing tool discussed above, it is stated that every space should be audited in regard to its current capabilities and shortcomings. It is true for every inclusive park. title: Opposition into politics of obstruction, must see anti-India pattern: PM Modi
text: PM said the next major priority is fully securing Indiaâs borders EKTA NAGAR, KEVADIA: PM Narendra Modi Saturday attacked opposition for abandoning its constitutional duty and instead resorting to politics of âobstructionâ, driven by âdespair and disappointmentâ. Addressing the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas parade â organised annually on the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel â Modi recalled how Sardar Patel and BR Ambedkar had, while framing the Constitution, clearly laid down duties and roles of govt and opposition. âOpposition is exercising politics of âobstructionâ, in complete disregard of constitutional boundaries and propriety,â he added. Warning against divisive forces that have come out in the open after more than a decade of political frustration to plot conspiracies, pit citizens against one another, and weaponise social media to spread rumours and tarnish Indiaâs image, the PM urged citizens to recognise the patterns of such forces conducting secret foreign meetings, their external backing by anti-India elements, and their rhetoric echoing the nationâs enemies. âWe have ended Naxalism in remote areas, but the threat from ideological extremists (dimagi Naxals) is not yet over, and the country has to remain ever vigilant against such entities,â he cautioned. Watch Rahul Gandhi Invites People For Ramlila Maidan March, Delhi Police Say No Permission Sought Stressing that the grand mission of national unity and the journey toward a strong and capable India must continue regardless of difficulties, the PM outlined the next major national priorities of fully securing Indiaâs borders, putting an end to infiltration and resulting demographic changes, and advancing toward a secular civil code. Acknowledging that major resolutions and bold decisions will inevitably face roadblocks and storms, he declared that the nation will not be deterred from the unwavering resolves of âEk Bharat, Shreshtha Bharatâ and a âViksit Bharatâ, working tirelessly with every breath and heartbeat toward the 2047 goal of a strong and capable India. Modi also referred to the instability and uncertainty facing the world in the current times, with some countries at war and major nations facing global supply chain disruptions and energy crises, while also recalling how India beat apprehensions that it would be among the worst affected by energy crisis. "Amid these apprehensions, some anti-india forces had also become active. But thanks to India's resilience, we did not let the people feel the hit of global energy crisis. This is a diplomatic and political victory of Indiaâ¦as well of the unity of its people," he stated. The prime minister, while attacking the earlier govt of electorally milking the promise of 'garibi hatao' without delivering on it, cited a recent World Bank report that stated that 50 crore Indians had beaten poverty over the past 10-12 year preceding 2024. Recalling that he had last year, while paying homage at the 'Statue of Unity', resolved not to rest until the country became Naxal-free, the prime minister said the goal has been achieved in the next one year. I"n 2015, 126 districts were Naxal-hit. By March 2026, not a single district was Naxal-hit. For decades, youths there who once faced an uncertain future, now have access to opportunities like education and employment," he said. title: Made in Karnataka, but no Kannada on product labels
text: A TOI report published on November 2, 2024, on the Karnataka Government's directive mandating Kannada labelling on products manufactured in the State. Bengaluru: Nearly two years after the state govt ordered mandatory Kannada labelling on products manufactured in Karnataka, the directive appears to have made little difference, as products continue to be sold with details printed in English and other languages, but not Kannada. The failure to implement the directive has once again come under scrutiny, with Kannada Development Authority (KDA) expressing concern over the lack of effective enforcement despite repeated efforts to ensure greater prominence for Kannada in everyday life. In Nov 2024, during the valedictory ceremony of the 69th Kannada Rajyotsava, the then chief minister Siddaramaiah had announced that all consumer, industrial and other products manufactured in Karnataka, whether by govt or private-sector entities, must carry their product names and labels in Kannada alongside other languages, if any. The directive was intended to ensure that Kannada received due recognition on products manufactured in the state and that consumers could identify and read product information in their mother tongue. However, the ground reality suggests that the initiative has remained largely ineffective, with little visible change in the labelling practices of manufacturers and companies. KDA chairperson Purushothama Bilimale said the authority had made efforts to follow up on the implementation of the govt order, including conducting field visits and coordinating with officials from other departments. âIâve personally toured 24 districts and followed up with food inspectors in those districts. But the problem is that most of these products are manufactured here, packaged elsewhere and marketed by companies from other states. Because of this, the govt order has failed to take proper shape in reality,â Bilimale said, pointing out that the absence of effective enforcement mechanisms and coordination among departments has undermined the initiative. The issue also highlights the challenges in ensuring the use of Kannada beyond govt offices, signboards and public institutions, particularly in the commercial space, where products manufactured in Karnataka often reach consumers without any identification in Kannada. title: How Cody Rhodes helped build All Elite Wrestling before returning to WWE: Inside the business decisions and career risks behind his defining wrestling comeback and championship pursuit
text: Cody Rhodes. Imagw via: WWE Cody Rhodes â wrestling career took a significant turn after he left WWE in 2016. Rather than immediately returning to the company, he rebuilt his reputation on the independent circuit, working with promotions around the world and helping demonstrate the commercial potential of wrestling outside WWEâs established system. That momentum contributed to All In in 2018, an independent event organised by Rhodes and The Young Bucks. Its success helped lay the groundwork for All Elite Wrestling (AEW), which launched in 2019 with Rhodes among its founding executive vice presidents; and his subsequent departure in 2022 and return to WWE marked another major turning point in his career. How Cody Rhodes helped build All Elite Wrestling Cody Rhodes played a major role in establishing All Elite Wrestling (AEW) as an alternative to WWE after helping demonstrate the drawing power of independent wrestling, and following his WWE departure in 2016, Rhodes competed across multiple promotions and developed a stronger identity beyond the character he had portrayed in WWE. His success helped build momentum for All In, the 2018 independent wrestling event he organised alongside The Young Bucks. The event attracted significant attention and helped establish the commercial potential for a new wrestling promotion. In 2019, Rhodes became one of AEWâs founding executive vice presidents alongside The Young Bucks and Kenny Omega, with Tony Khan providing the financial backing and leading the company. Rhodes took on responsibilities beyond performing in the ring. As an executive vice president, he helped shape AEWâs early identity while continuing to compete on its programmes. However, his dual role also placed him under scrutiny from fans who questioned the influence of the promotionâs executives over its creative direction. Why Cody Rhodes left All Elite Wrestling for WWE Rhodes departed AEW in February 2022 after contract negotiations failed to produce a new agreement. Although reports and subsequent comments have pointed to tensions surrounding his final months with the promotion, the departure should not be reduced to one confirmed disagreement over money or creative control. In later comments, Rhodes described feeling disrespected at a company he had helped build. He also indicated that his experience at AEW differed from his earlier frustrations in WWE because of his personal investment in the new promotion. His wife, Brandi Rhodes, was among those who encouraged him to consider moving on, according to his account. Leaving AEW represented a significant professional gamble. Rhodes was walking away from an executive position and the companyâs early growth to pursue a fresh chapter elsewhere. His decision also came without a guarantee that WWE would restore him to a prominent role.
